Part 3 — Organizations, locations, roles and permissions

Chapter 8 — The multi-tenant model

The Platform serves many clinic businesses from one installation and one database, and each business can have several branches. This chapter explains how the data of one clinic is kept apart from another, how a person can work for clinics, how a signed-in user ends up "inside" one clinic and one branch, and how the Platform decides what "today" means for a clinic. It is written for the product owner, who needs this model to reason about every other chapter.

8.1 Organizations, locations and the tenant boundary

Status: [Implemented]

In simple terms. An organization is one clinic business; it is the tenant. A location is one branch of that business. A dental group with three branches is one organization with three locations. Almost every record in the Platform (patients, appointments, invoices, staff assignments, queue sessions) carries the organization it belongs to, and most also carry a location.

Technically.

  • organizations is the tenant table. locations belongs to exactly one organization (organization_id, deleted with it by ON DELETE CASCADE). Each location has one location_settings row.
  • Tenant tables carry an organization_id column, and services always filter by the active organization. Data that differs per branch also carries location_id.
  • All tenants share one database and one schema. Isolation is done in application code (guards plus organization_id filters in every query), not by separate databases or database row-level security.
  • The super admin stands outside all tenants (users.global_role = 'super_admin') and can enter any active organization.

Figure 8.1 — The tables that define who belongs to which organization and location.

The diagram shows eight tables and their relationships. organizations (with id, slug, access_version, is_active) "has" zero or more locations (with organization_id, code, timezone, is_active). Each location is "configured by" at most one location_settings row (with location_id and tax_rate). users (with uuid, email, global_role) "owns" organizations through organization_ownership rows (with user_id, organization_id, is_primary_owner); an organization can have several owners and a user can own several organizations. An organization "defines" zero or more employment_roles (with organization_id, the permissions map and template_key). The employees table (with id, full_name, phone) has no organization column; a person "works through" zero or more employee_org_location_assignments. Each assignment links one employee to one organization ("employs") and one location ("staffs"), optionally to one employment role ("grants"), and optionally to one user account ("logs in as"); it also holds has_portal_access and is_active.

Technical references: backend/src/organizations/entities/organization.entity.ts · backend/src/locations/entities/location.entity.ts · backend/src/auth/services/authorization.service.ts

8.2 Ownership

Status: [Implemented]

An owner is a user linked to an organization through an organization_ownership row. Owners are not employees and have no role: the access resolver gives an owner every permission at its widest scope at every location of the organization (Chapter 11).

  • How owners are created. Self-signup creates the clinic and makes the new user its primary owner (is_primary_owner = true). Further owners are created from user administration with the "owner" account type and are stored with is_primary_owner = false.
  • Several owners, several clinics. A clinic can have several owners and one user can own several clinics; the pair (user_id, organization_id) is unique.
  • What an owner can enter. Every active location of every active organization the owner owns.

Technical references: backend/src/organizations/entities/organization-ownership.entity.ts · backend/src/user/user.service.ts · AuthorizationService.isOwner

8.3 The employee person record and assignments

Status: [Partial] — the data model supports one person at several locations and clinics, but the API only ever creates one assignment per employee.

In simple terms. The Platform separates the person from the job. The employee record holds who the person is (name, phone, national ID number, gender, date of birth, photo). Each assignment says where and how that person works: in which organization, at which location, in which role, with which salary, and whether the person may sign in there.

Technically.

  • employees has no organization_id. Phone is unique across the whole Platform, and so is the national ID number when given.
  • employee_org_location_assignments holds, per job: organization_id, location_id, employment_role_id (the role, may be empty), designation, employee_code (unique per organization), an optional queue token_prefix, salary fields, has_portal_access, user_id (the staff login, may be empty), is_primary and is_active. One person can have at most one assignment per location (unique on employee_id, location_id).
  • Permissions are tied to the assignment, not to the person: the same person can be a Doctor at one location and have no role at another.
  • What the API does today. POST /employees creates the person and exactly one assignment, at the location the creator is working in. It refuses a phone number that already exists anywhere on the Platform ("An employee with this phone number already exists"). No endpoint adds a second location or a second clinic to an existing employee; the multi-location model can only be filled outside the API [Partial].
  • Staff logins. User administration can create a login for an existing employee; that login is linked to all of the person's active assignments in the organization. A login only grants entry where the assignment is active and has_portal_access is on.

Technical references: backend/src/employees/entities/employee.entity.ts · backend/src/employees/entities/employee-org-location-assignment.entity.ts · EmployeesService.create · backend/src/user/user.service.ts

8.4 Who can enter which clinic and branch

Status: [Implemented]

At sign-in, and whenever a location is selected, the Platform works out the list of places a user may enter (AuthorizationService.resolveUserAccess):

Kind of user Organizations offered Locations offered
Super admin Every active organization Every active location of each
Owner Every active organization the user owns Every active location of each
Employee with a staff login Organizations where the user has an active assignment with portal access, if the organization is active Exactly those assigned locations that are active

The table shows the three ways to gain entry. When one user is both owner and employee in the same organization, the owner entry wins. Deactivated organizations and locations disappear from the list. The same rules are checked again on every request by validateAccess (section 8.5): an owner passes for any active location of the organization, an employee needs an active, portal-enabled assignment at exactly that location.

Technical references: AuthorizationService.resolveUserAccess · AuthorizationService.validateAccess

8.5 The tenant context on every request

Status: [Implemented]

In simple terms. The web app always tells the API which clinic and which branch the user is working in. The API checks that the user is allowed there before doing anything else.

Technically.

  • The access token (a JWT, valid 15 minutes) carries only the user id, email, global role and session id. It does not carry the organization or location.
  • The web app's axios instance adds two headers to every request from the in-memory auth store: x-organization-id and x-location-id (lab portal requests carry x-lab-id instead).
  • TenantContextGuard, the second of the five global guards, reads the headers and calls validateAccess. Missing headers give 400 "Missing tenant context. Please select an organization and location."; no access gives 403. On success it stores request.tenantContext.
  • Controllers read the context with @ActiveTenant() and pass the organization id (and, where relevant, the location id) to the service, which filters every query by it.
  • The guard steps aside for @Public() and @ContextFree() routes and for super admins, and checks the super-admin role for @RequireSuperAdmin() routes. It has no path-prefix exceptions.
  • The organization and location in the headers also select the access context (Chapter 11) and the active features (Chapter 10).

Technical references: backend/src/auth/guards/tenant-context.guard.ts · TenantContextGuard · backend/src/common/decorators/active-tenant.decorator.ts · web-app/src/lib/api.ts

8.6 Sign-in, choosing a location and switching

Status: [Implemented]

Figure 8.2 — Sequence from sign-in to the first page, and a later location switch.

The diagram has four participants: the Staff user, the Web app, the API and PostgreSQL. (1) The user enters email and password and signs in. (2) The web app calls POST /auth/login. (3) The API checks the password and account status and creates a session. (4) It resolves the user's access: ownerships, active portal assignments, active organizations and locations. (5) It returns an access token valid for 15 minutes, sets a refresh cookie valid for 1 day (30 days when the user ticks "keep me signed in"), and returns the list of organizations with two flags saying whether an organization or a location must still be chosen. An "alt" box shows two paths. If the user has exactly one organization with one location, the web app stores them as active. Otherwise, or for any super admin, the web app shows /select-location with "Select Organization" and then "Select Location"; the user picks a location and clicks Continue; the web app calls POST /auth/select-location; the API runs validateAccess and saves the last accessed organization and location; it returns the active ids. After the box, the web app calls GET /me/access with the two tenant headers and receives the permissions, features, roles and home page, then opens the role's home page. The last part shows a later switch: the user picks another location in the location switcher, the web app calls POST /auth/switch-location, the API checks access and saves the choice, returns the new ids, and the web app invalidates every cached query so all data and the access context are fetched again.

Rules behind the figure:

  • Automatic choice. One organization with one location is selected automatically. A super admin always chooses an organization first. When a choice is needed, the API pre-fills the last organization and location the user worked in (users.last_accessed_organization_id / last_accessed_location_id), if they are still allowed.
  • Where the browser goes. The root route (__root.tsx) redirects: not signed in → /login; signed in but no location chosen → /select-location. Super admins may open the setup pages (Organizations, Locations, Lab Directory, Config Studio, Subscriptions) without a location. Users who only belong to a lab go to the lab portal.
  • Session restore. The auth store is in memory only. On page load the web app calls POST /auth/refresh; the refresh cookie returns a new token and the same selection data.
  • Switching. The location switcher in the top bar lists every organization and location the user may enter, grouped by organization. With only one location it shows the name without a menu.

Figure 8.3 — Select organization and location (screenshot pending).

The page appears after sign-in when a choice is needed. Its header reads "Select Organization" or "Select Location", with a welcome line using the user's name ("Choose an organization to continue" or "Choose where you'd like to work today"). The organization step shows one card per organization; picking an organization with a single location selects it at once. The location step shows one card per location of the chosen organization and a Continue button. If the organization has no locations yet, the page says "No locations yet" and offers Create First Location, which opens the Locations page. On success a toast says "Location selected" and the user lands on the home page. (The only existing screenshot of this page is excluded from the handbook because it shows compliance badges that the current code no longer displays.)

Technical references: backend/src/auth/auth.service.ts (login, selectLocation, switchLocation) · web-app/src/routes/__root.tsx · web-app/src/features/auth/components/LocationSelector.tsx · web-app/src/components/layout/LocationSwitcher.tsx

8.7 Clinic time: the location's timezone

Status: [Implemented]

In simple terms. A clinic's day starts at midnight where the branch is, not where the server is. Each location stores its own timezone, and every "today", "now" and opening-hours check uses it.

Technically.

  • locations.timezone holds an IANA timezone name. New locations created through POST /locations default to UTC; the setup wizard copies the organization's timezone (default Asia/Karachi) to every location. The value is not validated; an unknown name falls back to UTC.
  • ClockService (common/clock/) is the single source of clinic time. timezoneFor(locationId) reads the timezone (cached for 60 seconds); today(tz) gives the local date; dayRange(tz, date) gives the UTC start and end of a local day; at(tz, date, time) converts a local wall-clock time; wallClock(tz, instant) gives the local weekday and time.
  • It is used by appointments (working hours, availability, same-day checks), the queue (the queue day and token day), billing, payroll, reports, notifications, employees and the lab modules.
  • Scheduled jobs are triggered by the server clock (Chapter 6); jobs that need a clinic day compute it through ClockService.

Technical references: backend/src/common/clock/clock.service.ts · ClockService · backend/src/common/clock/tz.util.ts

8.8 Limitations and known gaps

  • One person cannot be given a second location or clinic through the API (section 8.3) [Partial].
  • Deactivating an organization or a location hides it at the next sign-in or selection, but does not end sessions that are already working there; requests keep passing the tenant guard for an owner of a deactivated organization, because validateAccess checks the location but not the organization's status for owners [Partial].
  • Locations created from the Locations screen get timezone UTC and currency USD unless changed, because that form has no timezone or currency field (Chapter 9).
  • Isolation relies on every service filtering by organization; there is no database-level row security.

Chapter 9 — Organizations and locations

This chapter describes the two records that frame every clinic on the Platform: the organization (the clinic business, the tenant) and its locations (the branches). It covers their fields, who can create and change them, their settings, and how they are switched off. It is written for the product owner; subscriptions, trials and plan limits get their own chapter (Chapter 45), and only read-only mode is summarised here.

9.1 What these records are for

Status: [Implemented]

  • An organization answers "who is the clinic?": name, contact details, default timezone and currency, specialties, plan and subscription dates.
  • A location answers "where does it operate?": address, a short branch code, its own timezone (which defines "today" for queues and reports), its own currency, and per-branch settings such as the tax rate.

The super admin manages organizations. Locations are managed by anyone holding the permission admin.locations.manage in that organization: owners and super admins always hold it, the system Admin role holds it, and a custom role can be given it. The owner's one-time setup wizard (/setup, Chapter 45) also edits the organization and its main location.

Sidebar: "Organizations" (super admin only, /organizations) and "Locations" (/locations, needs admin.locations.manage).

Technical references: backend/src/organizations/ · backend/src/locations/ · web-app/src/features/organizations/ · web-app/src/features/locations/ · backend/docs/modules/01-organizations-locations.md

9.2 Organization fields

Status: [Implemented]

Field Meaning
name, slug Display name; slug is unique, generated from the name on creation and never regenerated.
email, phone, website Contact details.
subscription_plan free, starter, professional or enterprise. Default free. The plan limits are defined in code (subscriptions/plans.ts).
clinic_type Free text. No API writes it.
specialty_tags List of general, dental, skin, ortho, physio, eye. Default general. Written by the setup wizard; the web app uses it to show specialty-specific screens.
timezone, currency Organization defaults: Asia/Karachi and PKR. The setup wizard copies them to every location.
max_locations, max_users Per-organization overrides of the plan limits; empty means "use the plan's limit".
trial_ends_at, paid_until Subscription period. Both empty means an unmanaged clinic: no expiry and no limits.
onboarding_pending True for self-signup clinics until the owner finishes /setup.
access_version Counter raised on every access change (roles, assignments, features, ownership); used to invalidate access caches (Chapter 11). Never written by normal saves.
is_active Soft switch-off.

The table explains each column of organizations in business terms. Three related tables hang off an organization: organization_ownership (its owners), organization_settings (legacy settings, section 9.4) and subscription_payments (Chapter 45).

Technical references: backend/src/organizations/entities/organization.entity.ts · Organization

9.3 Managing organizations (super admin)

All endpoints are in OrganizationsController and carry @RequireSuperAdmin(), so only the super admin can call them, for any organization.

9.3.1 Create an organization

Status: [Partial] — the endpoint works; the screen's form has fields the API refuses.

What it does. Creates a clinic with a name and optional contact details and plan.

How the user does it. On the Organizations page, click Create, fill the form and save.

Behind the scenes. POST /organizations saves the row, then seeds the organization's feature flags from the catalog defaults (Chapter 10) and the 5 system roles (Chapter 11). The two steps are not one transaction. No owner, no location and no subscription dates are created: the clinic is "unmanaged" until the super admin sets dates or records a payment.

Rules. Name is required (at most 255 characters); email must be valid; phone at most 20, website at most 500 characters; plan must be one of the four enum values. Duplicate slug gives 409.

Known problems (by reading the code, not executed). The form also offers Clinic Type, Timezone and Currency, which the create DTO does not accept, so filling them makes the request fail with 400. The plan selector offers "FREE", "BASIC", "PREMIUM" and "ENTERPRISE", which do not match the API's lower-case values, so choosing a plan also fails with 400. No audit row is written.

Technical references: OrganizationsController.create · OrganizationsService.create · CreateOrganizationDto · web-app/src/features/organizations/OrganizationManagementView.tsx

9.3.2 List and view organizations

Status: [Implemented]

GET /organizations lists active organizations by name; GET /organizations/:id returns one. Deactivated organizations do not appear in the list.

Technical references: OrganizationsController.findAll · OrganizationsController.findOne

9.3.3 Edit an organization

Status: [Partial] — the endpoint works; the screen sends fields the API refuses.

PATCH /organizations/:id accepts name, email, phone, website, plan and isActive. The edit dialog sends the whole organization row (including id, slug and timestamps), which the strict validation pipe refuses with 400 (by reading the code, not executed). A plan change made here is not audited and does not touch the subscription dates.

Technical references: OrganizationsController.update · UpdateOrganizationDto

9.3.4 Deactivate an organization

Status: [Implemented]

The trash action asks "Deactivate organization?" and calls DELETE /organizations/:id, which sets is_active = false. Data is kept. The organization disappears from sign-in and selection lists. Sessions that are already working in it are not ended. There is no screen to reactivate it; only PATCH /organizations/:id with isActive: true does that.

Technical references: OrganizationsController.deactivate · OrganizationsService.deactivate

Figure 9.1 — Organizations (screenshot pending).

The page is titled "Organizations" with the subtitle "Manage clinic organizations and their settings" and a Create button at the top right. The create and edit dialog contains Name, a read-only Slug, Clinic Type, Timezone, Currency and Subscription Plan. Non-super-admins who open the URL are sent to the dashboard.

9.4 Organization settings (legacy)

Status: [Not implemented] — the settings are stored and editable, but no backend code reads them.

organization_settings has one row per organization, created on first read. It holds old feature switches (feature_appointments, feature_inventory, feature_finance, feature_reminders, feature_whatsapp, feature_patient_portal), allow_location_override, and booking defaults (default_slot_duration, advance_booking_days, cancellation_notice_hours).

  • GET /organizations/:id/settings is allowed to the super admin and to owners of that organization.
  • PATCH /organizations/:id/settings is super-admin only. Limits: slot duration 5–480 minutes, advance booking 1–365 days, notice 0–168 hours.
  • No backend code reads any of these values. Real feature gating is the feature system (Chapter 10). The web app uses allow_location_override only to grey out three inputs on the location settings page.
  • The settings screen sends the whole row, which the API should refuse with 400 (by reading the code).

Figure 9.3 — Organization settings (screenshot pending).

The page has a back button to Organizations and two cards. "Global Overrides" holds one switch, Allow Location Override. "Booking Defaults" holds three number inputs: Default Slot Duration (mins), Advance Booking Days and Cancellation Notice (hours). A Save button stores the card values. None of these values changes how bookings behave.

Field Meaning

9.6 Managing locations

All location endpoints are in LocationsController. The controller is @ContextFree(), because an owner manages locations before choosing one; each handler therefore checks admin.locations.manage itself, in the organization of the location being acted on (or, for create and list, the organization in the body or the x-organization-id header). An invalid organization gives 400 "Select an organization first"; a missing permission gives 403 NO_PERMISSION.

9.6.1 Add a location

Status: [Implemented]

How the user does it. On the Locations page, click Create Location and fill Name, Code, Address, City, Country, Phone and Email. A super admin also picks the organization ("Organization (Required)").

Behind the scenes. POST /locations first checks the plan's location limit (SubscriptionsService.assertCanAddLocation, skipped for super admins), then saves the location and a default settings row as two separate saves (not one transaction). No audit row is written.

Rules and errors. Name and code are required; code at most 50 characters and unique in the organization (409 on duplicates). Plan limit reached gives 403 PLAN_LIMIT; an expired subscription gives 402 SUBSCRIPTION_EXPIRED.

Technical references: LocationsController.create · LocationsService.create · CreateLocationDto

9.6.2 List, view and edit locations

Status: [Partial] — list and view work; the edit screen sends fields the API refuses.

GET /locations returns, for a super admin, every active location of every organization; otherwise the active locations of the active organization (or of every organization where the user holds the permission organization-wide). GET /locations/:id returns one. PATCH /locations/:id accepts the create fields except code and the organization, plus isActive. The edit dialog sends the whole row, which the API should refuse with 400 (by reading the code). Setting isActive: true reactivates a location without the plan-limit check.

Technical references: LocationsController.findAll · LocationsController.findOne · LocationsController.update · UpdateLocationDto

9.6.3 Deactivate a location

Status: [Implemented]

The trash action asks "Deactivate location?" and calls DELETE /locations/:id (is_active = false). Nothing stops deactivating the last location or the main one. Staff assignments, appointments and queue sessions at that location are left as they are; the location stops being offered at sign-in and in the switcher. The list hides inactive locations, so the screen cannot reactivate one.

Technical references: LocationsController.deactivate · LocationsService.deactivate

Status: [Partial] — the tax rate and a few other values are used; the edit screen's save is expected to fail, and several stored values do nothing.

Setting Used by

9.8 Subscriptions and read-only mode (summary)

Status: [Implemented]

An organization with subscription dates is "managed": it is on a trial (self-signup gives 14 days with Professional limits) or paid until a date, and after that date it gets 3 grace days. When the grace days have passed, the clinic is in read-only mode: the fifth global guard, SubscriptionGuard, refuses every write with 402 SUBSCRIPTION_EXPIRED, while reads, sign-in, the account and setup pages and the super admin keep working. Recording a subscription payment (a manual super-admin action) lifts read-only mode at once; the status is computed on each request and cached for 30 seconds per process. Chapter 45 covers plans, limits, payments and the setup wizard in full.

Technical references: backend/src/subscriptions/subscription.guard.ts · backend/src/subscriptions/plans.ts · SubscriptionsService.isReadOnly

9.9 Limitations and known gaps

  • Several edit screens (organization edit, organization settings, location edit, location settings) send whole rows and are expected to fail with 400 under the strict validation pipe; this was found by reading the code and not executed.
  • Organizations and locations cannot be reactivated from any screen.
  • New locations default to UTC and USD; timezone and currency are not validated.
  • is_main_branch is not exclusive, and the last or main location can be deactivated.
  • Organization and location create, edit and deactivate write no audit rows; only subscription changes are audited.
  • organization_settings and most location settings are stored but unused.

9.10 Owner's FAQ

Can an owner create a new organization? No. Only the super admin can, or a new owner through self-signup, which creates a separate clinic.

Can an owner add a branch? Yes, from Locations, as long as the plan's location limit allows it and the subscription has not expired.

Can a branch code be changed? No. The code is fixed at creation; the token prefix falls back to it.

Where is the sales tax rate set? In the location's settings (Tax Rate %) or in the setup wizard's location step. Each branch has its own rate.

What happens to patients and staff when a branch is deactivated? Nothing is deleted or moved. The branch is no longer offered at sign-in and in the location switcher.

What does "unmanaged" mean? An organization with neither trial end nor paid-until date. It never expires and has no plan limits. Organizations created by the super admin start this way.

Chapter 10 — Features: entitlement, enablement and location overrides

A feature is a named part of the Platform, such as "Invoices" or "Lab Management", that can be on for one clinic and off for another. This chapter explains the three switches that decide whether a feature is active (the super admin's entitlement, the owner's switch and a per-location override), the 24 features that exist, how the backend enforces them and which screens control them. It is written for the product owner, who sells and configures features per clinic.

10.1 The three switches

Status: [Implemented]

In simple terms. The platform operator decides what a clinic is allowed to have; the clinic owner decides what the clinic actually uses; and the owner can switch a feature off at one branch. A feature works at a branch only when all three agree.

Switch Who sets it Stored in Meaning
Entitled Super admin org_feature_flags.is_entitled, optional entitled_until The feature is part of this clinic's plan. With entitled_until, it is a trial that ends at that moment.
Enabled Owner (or anyone with admin.features.manage); the super admin can also set it org_feature_flags.is_enabled The clinic has switched the feature on. Only possible while entitled.
Location override Owner (same permission) location_feature_overrides.is_disabled Switches the feature off at one location. It can never switch on something the organization has off.

The table lists the three switches, who controls each, where it is stored and what it means. A feature is active for an organization when its catalog entry is active, it is entitled (and the trial has not ended), and it is enabled. It is active at a location when, in addition, that location has not switched it off.

Defaults and missing rows.

  • When an organization is created (by the super admin or by self-signup), the Platform writes one org_feature_flags row per active catalog feature: features that are "on by default" in the catalog are both entitled and enabled; all others are neither.
  • If an organization has no row for a feature, it counts as entitled, and enabled according to the catalog default. This keeps organizations that predate entitlement working.
  • A trial end date must be in the future when set. When it passes, the feature becomes "not entitled" with the reason trial_expired; the owner sees it locked.

Figure 10.1 — The decision path from a catalog feature to "active at this location".

The flowchart reads left to right. It starts from "Feature in the active catalog" and reaches the first decision, "Entitled? is_entitled and trial not ended", which the super admin controls by entitling with an optional trial end. If the answer is no, the feature is "Not active" with the reason not_entitled or trial_expired. If yes, the second decision asks "Enabled? owner switch, else catalog default"; the owner (or the super admin) controls this switch. If no, the feature is "Off for the whole clinic". If yes, the third decision asks "Switched off at this location?", controlled by the owner's location override. If yes, the feature is "Off at this location only". If no, the feature is "Active here", and the final box says what that means: routes marked @RequireFeature open, and the permissions that belong to the feature are kept.

Technical references: backend/src/feature-flags/feature-state.ts · featureState · resolveEnabledFeatures · narrowByLocation · FeatureFlagsService.seedFlagsForOrg

10.3 How the backend enforces features

Status: [Implemented]

There are two mechanisms.

  1. Through permissions (the common case). Every permission names one feature. AccessResolver keeps a permission only if its feature is active at the request's organization and location (filterByFeatures). Turning a feature off therefore takes the permission away from every role without changing the roles; turning it back on restores access exactly as it was.
  2. Through @RequireFeature(key). Used where no permission expresses the feature, mainly on @AnyMember() routes. FeatureFlagGuard, the third global guard, collects every @RequireFeature key on the handler and its controller (both apply) and refuses with 403 'The "" feature is not enabled for this location' if any is not active. Super admins and @Public() routes skip the check. The location header narrows the set; the guard trusts it without a membership check, which is safe because a location can only remove features.

Caching. FeatureFlagsService keeps the active set per organization, and per organization and location, in process memory for 30 seconds. Every change clears the cache in the process that made it. The change also raises the organization's access version (automatically for org_feature_flags writes, explicitly for location overrides), which is broadcast over Redis so every other process drops its cache at once, and the web app gets access.changed and refetches. If Redis is down, other processes catch up within the 30-second lifetime.

Every change is audited in audit_logs (entity types org_feature_flag and location_feature_override), in the same transaction as the change, with the before and after values.

Technical references: backend/src/feature-flags/guards/feature-flag.guard.ts · FeatureFlagGuard · requiredFeaturesOf · FeatureFlagsService.getEnabledFeatures · FEATURE_CACHE_TTL_MS · AccessVersionSubscriber · FeatureAdminService

Per feature, the Entitled switch grants or withdraws it, a date picker ("No trial end") sets a trial end, and the Enabled switch flips the owner's switch. 10.7 Limitations and known gaps

  • Three active keys (comms.whatsapp, comms.in_app, hr.commissions) have no effect; an owner can switch them without any change in behaviour.
  • inventory.alerts only produces a server log line, no notification.
  • Catalog editing has no screen.
  • The legacy organization_settings.feature_* switches (Chapter 9) are unrelated to this system and do nothing.

10.8 Owner's FAQ

What happens to roles when I turn a feature off? Nothing is deleted. The feature's permissions stop working for everyone; turning the feature back on restores them exactly.

Can I turn a feature on at one branch only? Not directly. Turn it on for the clinic and switch it off at the other branches.

Why can't I switch a feature on? It is not in your plan, or its trial has ended. Only the super admin can entitle it.

What happens when a trial ends? The feature becomes inactive at once (within the 30-second cache), and the owner's switch shows it locked with "trial ended".

Does turning a feature off log people out? No. Open screens receive an access update and lose the related menu items and buttons.

Chapter 11 — Roles and permissions

This chapter explains who may do what inside a clinic on the Platform. It covers the fixed list of 70 permissions, how they are grouped into roles, the five system roles every clinic starts with, how a clinic builds its own roles safely, and how the backend and the web app check permissions on every request and every screen. It is written for the product owner; the deeper customization screens (sidebar builder, theme, the owner's Features page) are covered in the Customization chapter, Chapter 58.

11.1 The model in one paragraph

Status: [Implemented]

The Platform never checks role names. It checks permissions, such as billing.invoice.void. A role is a clinic-owned bundle of permissions, stored as a map { permission: scope or true } in employment_roles.permissions. An employee gets a role through an assignment at one location (Chapter 8), so the same person can have different roles at different branches. Owners and super admins have no role: they always get every permission at its widest scope. A permission whose feature is not active (Chapter 10) is dropped at resolution time. Anything not granted is denied (fail-closed).

Technical references: backend/src/access/ · backend/src/access/catalog/permissions.ts · docs/access-control/README.md

Status: [Implemented]

The catalog is fixed in code; clinics combine its keys into roles but can never invent new ones. Each permission has a label, a module group, a feature, optionally a list of permissions it implies, optionally a set of scopes, and optionally a high-risk mark.

Module (group) Permissions Feature
Patients (12) patients.view*, patients.create, patients.edit, patients.delete!, patients.export!, patients.price.view, patients.clinical.view, patients.clinical.edit, patients.documents.manage, patients.chart.edit, plans.manage, plans.templates.manage patients.core; documents → patients.documents; chart → patients.teeth_chart; plans → patients.treatment_plans

Discounts (2) billing.discount.apply, billing.discount.custom! billing.discounts
Expenses (2) expenses.view, expenses.manage billing.expenses
Commissions (3) earnings.own.view, earnings.all.view, compensation.manage! billing.commissions

Reports (4) reports.clinical.view, reports.financial.view, reports.export!, finance.overview.view reports.clinical, reports.financial, reports.exports
Admin (9) admin.features.manage!, admin.roles.manage!, admin.users.manage!, admin.nav.manage, admin.settings.manage, admin.locations.manage, admin.audit.view, admin.theme.manage, notifications.settings.manage core (always on)

The table lists every permission by module, with its feature. An asterisk (*) marks the 7 scoped permissions; an exclamation mark (!) marks the 13 high-risk permissions. "Core" permissions belong to no feature and can never be switched off.

Scopes. A scoped permission is granted with how far it reaches:

  • own — only records tied to the user as an employee (for example patients the doctor has seen through an appointment or the queue);
  • location — records of the active location;
  • org — every record of the organization.

A wider scope includes the narrower ones. Unscoped permissions are stored as true and reach the whole organization.

Implies. Granting a permission also grants what it implies, transitively. Examples: patients.create implies patients.view; consultation.conduct implies patients.clinical.edit, which implies patients.clinical.view; queue.doctor.any implies queue.doctor.own; compensation.manage implies earnings.all.view, which implies earnings.own.view; appointments.override_rules implies appointments.book. An implied scoped permission takes the granting permission's scope when it supports it, otherwise its narrowest scope.

11.3 Bundles: None, Basic and Full, and Advanced mode

Status: [Implemented]

So that owners do not tick 70 boxes, the roles screen offers three ready levels per module:

  • None — nothing from the module.
  • Basic — a sensible everyday set. For example: Patients Basic = view at location, register, edit, manage documents; Appointments Basic = view at location, book, reschedule, cancel; Queue Basic = board, check-in, manage entries; Consultation Basic = conduct at own, write prescriptions; Billing Basic = desk, view invoices at location, collect payments; Reports Basic = clinical reports at location; Admin Basic = clinic settings and audit log.
  • Full — every permission of the module at its widest scope.

Advanced opens the module's full list of permissions, each with a checkbox and, for scoped ones, a scope selector. When a role's grants in a module match no level exactly, the module shows Custom.

Action Endpoint

A legacy /employment-roles controller serves the employee form's role picker (employees.view) and applies the same rules to writes.

Rules and validations.

  • Escalation protection. A user who is not an owner or super admin cannot grant a permission they do not hold, or a wider scope than they hold. Only newly added or widened grants are checked, implies included. Refusal: 403 ESCALATION listing the permissions.
  • Reason for high-risk grants. Newly granted high-risk permissions need a reason, or 400 REASON_REQUIRED.
  • Valid maps only. Unknown keys, a missing scope on a scoped permission, or a scope on an unscoped one give 400 INVALID_PERMISSIONS.
  • System roles are read-only (403 SYSTEM_ROLE_READ_ONLY) and cannot be deleted.
  • Unique names per organization (409 ROLE_NAME_TAKEN). A clone without a name becomes " (copy)", "(copy 2)" and so on.
  • No delete while in use. A role with active members cannot be deleted (409 ROLE_HAS_MEMBERS). Deletion is permanent.
  • Home page must be an in-app path starting with a single /.

11.6 Resolving access: AccessResolver, cache and access version

Status: [Implemented]

In simple terms. For each user, clinic and branch, the Platform works out once what the user may do, remembers the answer, and throws the answer away as soon as anything relevant changes.

Figure 11.3 — The access resolution path from a request to the permission checks in the backend and the web app.

The flowchart reads top to bottom. A request brings a user, an organization and a location. The resolver first reads the organization's access_version (cached for 15 seconds). It then asks whether a cached context exists for this user, organization, location and version that is less than 5 minutes old; if yes, it goes straight to the AccessContext. If not, it asks "Super admin or owner?". If yes, the user gets every permission at its widest scope. If no, it asks whether the user has an active assignment at this location with portal access and an active role. If no, the user gets no permissions; if yes, the role's grants are normalized and expanded with everything they imply. All three branches meet at "Drop permissions whose feature is not active here", which produces the AccessContext, offering can, scope, applyScope and decide. The context feeds two final boxes: the backend (@Can on handlers, applyScope on queries, @VisibleIf on fields) and the web app (GET /me/access, useAccess().can, the route gate, the sidebar and the buttons).

Technically.

  • AccessResolver.resolve(user, organization, location) builds an AccessContext holding: the user, organization, location, version, isSuperAdmin, isOwner, isMember (super admin, owner or portal-enabled assignment), the employee id, active features, granted permissions, the role and its home page.
  • The cache lives in process memory: at most 10,000 entries, 5 minutes each, keyed on user, organization, location and access version.
  • organizations.access_version is raised by one after any committed change to employment roles, assignments (role, location, organization, active flag, portal access, login), organization feature flags or ownership. An entity subscriber does this automatically for TypeORM writes, once per transaction after commit; location overrides and raw SQL bump it explicitly.
  • A bump is broadcast over Redis to every process, which drop their cached contexts and feature sets, and the Socket.IO gateway emits access.changed to the room org:<id>; open browser tabs refetch their access. If Redis is down, other processes catch up within 15 seconds (the version cache).
  • Fail-closed. A missing key is no access. Roles with only old-style boolean flags give nothing. A role that is inactive, or belongs to another organization, gives nothing. A location header that is not a valid id means no location, so staff get no role permissions.

Technical references: backend/src/access/access.resolver.ts · AccessResolver · backend/src/access/access-context.ts · AccessContext · backend/src/access/version/ · AccessVersionService · AccessVersionSubscriber · AccessChangeBus

11.7 Checking access in the backend

Status: [Implemented]

Every HTTP handler must say who may call it, with exactly one of these markers (on the method or its controller):

Marker Meaning Checked by
@Can('perm', ...) All listed permissions are required; class and method lists merge. AccessGuard (403 NO_PERMISSION with the missing keys)
@AnyMember() Any active member of the location (owners and super admins too). AccessGuard
@Public() No sign-in (the route must also be in PUBLIC_ROUTES). JwtAuthGuard list, all guards skip
@RequireSuperAdmin() Super admin only. TenantContextGuard
@ContextFree() The handler checks access itself (for example /locations, GET /me/access). the handler

The table lists the five markers, what they mean and which component enforces them. A controller protected by its own @UseGuards(...) (lab portal, magic links) also counts.

  • The coverage test. access-coverage.spec.ts loads every controller and fails if any handler outside the auth and session controllers has none of the markers, or still uses the removed @Roles(). At runtime, a handler without a marker would pass the access guard, so this test is the safety net.
  • Row scope. Handlers that list data take @Access() access and call access.applyScope(queryBuilder, 'patients.view', columns). For own it adds the caller's employee condition, for location the active location condition, for org nothing extra; with no grant it adds a condition that matches no rows. Patients, for example, are "own" when the doctor has an appointment or queue entry with them, and "location" when their primary location or an appointment or queue entry is at the active location.
  • Field hiding. A response property marked @VisibleIf('perm') is removed by a global interceptor when the caller lacks the permission; with no access context every guarded field is removed. It is used today for treatment and treatment-plan prices (patients.price.view).
  • Range decisions. access.decide(perm, { value, min, max }) returns allow, deny or "needs approval". It is used for discounts: changing a preset discount outside its range needs billing.discount.custom.
  • Rule for developers. Code never checks role names; it asks can(...).

Technical references: backend/src/access/access.guard.ts · AccessGuard · backend/src/access/decorators/access.decorators.ts · backend/src/access/access-coverage.spec.ts · backend/src/access/visible-if/visible-if.ts · backend/src/patients/access/patient-scope.ts

11.8 Checking access in the web app

Status: [Implemented]

  • GET /me/access returns, for the active organization and location: the version, owner and super-admin flags, active features, granted permissions with scopes, the role, the employee id, the home page and the clinic's sidebar layout. AccessProvider loads it (fresh for 30 seconds, refetched on window focus and on every access.changed event) and serves it through useAccess().
  • Buttons and widgets ask useAccess().can('perm') or wrap content in <Can perm="...">.
  • Routes declare staticData: { can: ... } (one permission, or an array meaning any of them). One gate in the root route, RouteAccessGate, checks every matched route and shows the No access page instead of the screen when the check fails.
  • The sidebar is built from a developer-owned registry of 39 items, each with its own requirement (a permission, super admin only, owner or super admin, or lab member). Items the user may not open are hidden. The clinic's saved sidebar layout only arranges items; it never grants access.
  • The permission list in the web app is a generated copy of the backend catalog (features/access/generated/catalog.ts), refreshed with npm run access:export.

The main area is titled "No access" and shows a shield icon, the Roman-Urdu headline "Aapke paas is page ki permission nahi" ("You do not have permission for this page"), the English text "You don't have permission to open this page. Ask your clinic owner to add it to your role." and a button "Go to my home page", which opens the role's home page, or the dashboard when none is set.

11.9 Limitations and known gaps

  • A system role deleted directly in the database is recreated on the next start; a clinic cannot permanently remove a system role (the API refuses to delete one anyway).
  • Missing markers are caught by a unit test, not at runtime.
  • POST /auth/switch-location still returns eight old permission flags derived from the new permissions; the web app ignores them.
  • Permissions follow the assignment's location: a staff member with no assignment at the active location gets no role permissions there.

11.10 Owner's FAQ

Can a receptionist see treatment prices? Yes with the default Receptionist role, which holds patients.price.view. Without it, prices are removed from the API responses, not only hidden on screen.

Can I give my manager the right to edit roles without making them all-powerful? Yes: grant admin.roles.manage. They still cannot grant anything they do not hold themselves.

Why can't I edit the Doctor role? System roles are read-only templates. Clone it and edit the copy, then assign the copy.

How quickly does a role change take effect? On the next request: the change raises the access version, every server drops its cached answer, and open screens refetch their access.

What does a doctor see with patients.view at scope own? Only patients they have an appointment or queue entry with.

Where is the history of role changes? In the audit log, as employment_role entries with before and after values and the reason given for high-risk grants.

Part 4 — Data model

Chapter 12 — Data model overview

This chapter explains how the Platform's database is organised as a whole: who owns the schema, which naming and money conventions the tables follow, and how tenant data is kept apart. It is written for the product owner who needs to reason about the data before changing a feature or answering a support question. Chapters 13 to 27 then walk through each business domain table by table; this chapter is the map they share.

12.1 The database in numbers

The Platform stores all of its data in one PostgreSQL database. The backend defines 153 entity classes, one per table, spread across 31 owning modules (a module "owns" a table when the table's entity class lives in that module's folder). The schema has 278 enforced foreign keys. It has no views, no table inheritance and no many-to-many junction tables generated by the ORM; every link between two tables is an ordinary column.

The field-level reference for every table is the generated entity catalog, backend/docs/data-model/ENTITY_CATALOG.md. It lists every column, type, default, index, constraint and foreign key, and it was produced from the same metadata the ORM uses to build the schema. This handbook names only the key columns of each table; when you need the full column list, open the catalog. The catalog has two known defects: the "Notes" column of the ten inventory tables is shifted one row down, and one note claims a trigger on form_schema_versions that does not exist.

12.2 Who owns the schema

12.2.1 Entities are the source of truth

Status: [Implemented]

The shape of every table — its columns, primary key, foreign keys, unique keys, indexes, CHECK constraints and EXCLUDE constraints — is declared in TypeORM entity classes in the backend code. Nobody writes CREATE TABLE statements by hand for normal tables.

  • In development, the API process builds and updates the schema itself on start-up. The setting in app.module.ts is synchronize: true whenever the process owns the schema and NODE_ENV is not production. The ORM compares the entities with the database and applies the difference.
  • In production, synchronize is off. An engineer runs npm run schema:log:prod to print the SQL the entity changes would need, reviews every statement (watching especially for DROP COLUMN, DROP TABLE and type changes), takes a backup, and then applies it with npm run schema:sync:prod.

Only the API process owns the schema. The background worker process never synchronizes and never runs migrations.

Two entity classes are not registered by any running module: chairs and inventory. The running app only knows tables that some module registers, so in development these two tables are not created. The command-line data source used by schema:sync:prod loads entity files by file pattern, so it does include them. A development database and a production database can therefore differ by exactly these two tables.

12.2.2 Migrations: three files, two that run

Status: [Implemented]

The folder backend/src/migrations/ holds three files. Migrations do the work that synchronize cannot do: triggers, SQL functions and data backfills.

File What it does Runs?
1776356529788-create-table A partial schema diff taken from an early development database. Describes 17 tables in a shape that no longer exists. Never. Start-up records it as already applied without executing it.
1792403456699-doctor-compensation Creates the commission tables if they are missing, installs the append-only trigger on commission_entries, and backfills data. Yes, once. Hand-written and idempotent.
1792490000000-lab-management-foundation Creates audit_logs, status_history, number_sequences, labs, lab_members and lab_clinic_links if missing, installs uuid_generate_v7() and the append-only triggers on audit_logs and status_history. Yes, once. Hand-written and idempotent.

The table lists the three migration files, what each contains and whether it executes. The first file is the "legacy baseline": it is kept in the folder, recorded as applied by a helper called recordLegacyBaseline, and must never be edited or deleted. The other two are written so that they give the same result whether or not synchronize already created the tables; they skip table creation when the table exists and always (re)install their triggers.

On API start-up the order is fixed: first the required database extensions and functions are created, then synchronize runs (development only), then pending migrations run, each in its own transaction. Because 136 of the 153 tables appear in no migration at all, the migration folder cannot be used to rebuild the schema; the entities are the only complete description.

12.2.3 Database objects that live outside the entities

A few database objects cannot be expressed in an entity class. They are created by start-up code or by the two running migrations:

  • btree_gist extension. Needed by the GiST EXCLUDE constraints that compare uuids, such as the rule that stops one doctor from having two overlapping appointments (appointments.no_doctor_overlap). Created at start-up before synchronize.
  • uuid_generate_v7() SQL function. Produces time-ordered uuids; it is the primary-key default of the newer tables. Created at start-up and also by the lab-management migration.
  • commission_entries append-only trigger. Blocks every DELETE and blocks UPDATE except setting or releasing the settlement link while the settlement is still pending.
  • audit_logs and status_history append-only triggers. Block every UPDATE and DELETE.
  • migrations table. TypeORM's bookkeeping of which migrations ran.

There are no views, no row-level security policies and no other triggers anywhere in the backend. Several other tables are described as "append-only" or "immutable" in code comments (for example queue_events, patient_consents, prescription_history, ledger_entries), but for those the rule is kept by the application only; the database would accept an update.

12.3 Conventions

12.3.1 Primary keys

Kind of primary key Tables Where it is used
uuid v4, generated by TypeORM (uuid_generate_v4()) 84 The older modules: identity, organizations, locations, staff, patients, appointments, queue, prescriptions, billing, inventory and others.
uuid v7, default uuid_generate_v7() 55 The newer modules: every lab table, the workflow engine, notifications, the general-ledger journals, audit_logs, status_history and config_values.
bigint identity 2 outbox and queue_events, where strict insertion order matters.
Supplied by the application (natural or composite key) 12 For example idempotency_keys (organization + key), location_billing_settings (the location id), notification_events (an event code), patient_comm_prefs (the patient id).

The table counts the four kinds of primary key across all 153 tables and names where each appears. A uuid v7 starts with a timestamp, so new rows sort by creation time and indexes stay compact; a uuid v4 is fully random. Both look the same to the application. One naming quirk: the four identity tables (users, oauth_providers, security_logs, user_sessions) call their primary-key column uuid; every other table calls it id.

12.3.2 Column naming

Columns use snake_case (organization_id, created_at) in every module except one. Ten of the eleven tables of the inventory module use camelCase column names such as organizationId, locationId and inventoryItemId. Queries written by hand against these tables must quote the names. The eleventh table, the unregistered inventory table, uses snake_case. The Inventory chapter (Chapter 23) covers those tables.

12.3.3 Money

The Platform stores money in two ways, and a reader must check which one a column uses:

  • Integer paisa (bigint or integer columns whose names end in _paisa). One rupee is 100 paisa, so 1,250.50 PKR is stored as 125050. The newer money-handling code uses this form: payroll breakdowns, commissions and compensation plans, the general-ledger journals, and every lab billing and payables table.
  • Numeric with two decimals (numeric(12,2) or numeric(10,2)). The amount is stored in rupees with two decimal places. Billing v2 (charges, invoices, payments, refunds), subscriptions, inventory, insurance, treatment plans and the legacy treatments.cost use this form.

Some tables carry both. payroll_records keeps base_salary_paisa, commission_paisa and total_paisa in paisa and also salary_amount in rupees, which mirrors the total for older screens. "PKR" is the default currency of a new organization, not a limit: organizations.currency and locations.currency hold the currency code.

12.3.4 Timestamps and dates

Most tables have created_at and many have updated_at, filled automatically by the ORM. Older tables store these as timestamp without time zone (about 50 tables); newer tables use timestamp with time zone (about 70 tables). Business moments that matter to the clinic — appointment start and end, check-in, payment time — are timestamp with time zone throughout. Calendar days that belong to a clinic day, such as queue_sessions.service_date, are stored as date and are computed in the location's timezone (locations.timezone), not the server's.

12.3.5 Soft delete

The Platform hides records in three ways:

  • is_active flag. Organizations, locations, employees, assignments, roles, catalogs and templates are switched off with is_active = false; the row stays. Deactivating an organization or a location is always a soft delete.
  • deleted_at column. Three tables use TypeORM's soft-delete column: patients, patient_documents and patient_treatment_plans. A row with deleted_at set is excluded from normal ORM reads.
  • Hard delete. Some actions really delete rows and rely on ON DELETE CASCADE to remove children. For example, permanently deleting a patient deletes the patient row and every child row whose foreign key cascades. Child rows whose foreign key is RESTRICT block the delete instead.

patients has both a deleted_at column and an is_active flag. The user-facing activate/deactivate switch uses is_active.

12.3.6 Tenant columns

Every row that belongs to one clinic carries organization_id, and every row that belongs to one branch also carries location_id. The column names are the same in every snake_case module. Whether the column has a foreign key varies by module:

  • The older modules (organizations, staff, patients, appointments, encounters, treatments, prescriptions) declare real foreign keys to organizations and locations, almost always with ON DELETE CASCADE.
  • The queue tables, nearly all billing v2 tables, the lab tables, plan_templates, audit_logs and status_history keep organization_id (and often location_id) without a foreign key. The database accepts any uuid there; the application is responsible for writing the right one.

12.4 Tenant scope rules

The catalog classifies every table by which tenant columns it carries. The classes are:

Scope class Meaning Examples
Global — platform Shared by all tenants; no tenant column. users, user_sessions, feature_catalog, specialties, notification_events, workflow_effects
Global — person or lab Shared across organizations by design. employees (one person can work for several clinics), labs, lab_members, lab_services
Organization organization_id only. patients, employment_roles, org_feature_flags, medicine_directory, services
Organization + location Both columns. appointments, queue_sessions, charges, invoices, payroll_records, prescriptions
Location only location_id only; the organization is reached through locations. chairs (unregistered)
Cascading scope A scope_type + scope_id pair that points to the platform, an organization or a location. config_values
Platform or organization Nullable organization_id: null means a platform default shared by all, a value means a clinic's own copy. form_schemas, workflow_templates, stage_templates, notification_templates
No tenant column A child table scoped only through its parent. the ten tables listed after this table

The table shows each scope class, what it means and typical tables. Ten tenant-data tables have no organization column and are isolated only through their parent: treatment_plan_items (through patient_treatment_plans), prescription_history and prescription_medicines (through prescriptions), treatment_plan_template_medicines (through treatment_plan_templates), cash_close_lines (through cash_closes), commission_rules (through compensation_plans), and the inventory children consumption_template_items, patient_consumption_items and purchase_order_items. Any query on these tables must join the parent to stay inside one tenant.

The rule that keeps tenants apart at runtime is not in the database. The guard chain resolves the active organization and location from the request headers, and every service filters by organization_id (and location_id where relevant). The multi-tenant model is described in Chapter 8; this chapter only describes the columns that make it possible.

12.5 The domains and how they connect

Figure 12.1 — Domains of the data model and the key links between them.

The figure draws the 153 tables as fourteen domain boxes, each labelled with the domain name and two to four of its most important tables. Arrows point from the side that is referenced (the parent) to the side that holds the reference (the child). Solid arrows are links backed by a foreign key; the two dotted arrows are logical links that have no foreign key. The left side holds the foundation: Identity, Organizations and locations, and Access and features. The middle holds the clinic's daily work: Staff and payroll, Patients, Appointments-queue-encounters, Prescriptions and plans, Billing, Inventory, Common and the Workflow engine. The right side holds Compensation and Labs, which consume data from several middle domains. Notifications sits near Identity because its main link is the user's in-app inbox. Every link drawn is explained in the next section.

12.5.1 Every link in the figure

  • Identity → Organizations and locations ("ownership"). organization_ownership.user_id links a user account to the organization it owns. Deleting the user or the organization deletes the ownership row (CASCADE).
  • Identity → Staff and payroll ("staff login"). employee_org_location_assignments.user_id links an employee's assignment to the user account they log in with. The link is optional; deleting the user sets it to null.
  • Organizations and locations → Patients ("tenant root"). patients.organization_id is a foreign key with CASCADE. The same kind of link, organization_id and often location_id, exists on almost every tenant table in every domain; the figure draws it once to keep the picture readable.
  • Organizations and locations → Access and features ("roles, flags, layouts"). employment_roles, org_feature_flags and nav_layouts each belong to one organization (CASCADE); location_feature_overrides belongs to one location (CASCADE).
  • Access and features → Staff and payroll ("role of an assignment"). employee_org_location_assignments.employment_role_id names the role a person has at a location. Deleting the role sets it to null.
  • Staff and payroll → Appointments, queue, encounters ("doctor"). appointments.doctor_id and queue_sessions.doctor_id point to employees, both with RESTRICT, so a doctor who has appointments or queue sessions cannot be hard-deleted.
  • Patients → Appointments, queue, encounters ("patient"). appointments, queue_entries, patient_encounters and treatments all carry patient_id with CASCADE.
  • Appointments, queue, encounters → Prescriptions and plans ("encounter and appointment"). prescriptions.encounter_id and prescriptions.appointment_id are optional links; deleting the encounter or appointment sets them to null.
  • Prescriptions and plans → Appointments, queue, encounters ("plan template used"). treatments.plan_template_id points to plan_templates; deleting the template sets it to null.
  • Patients → Billing ("patient, RESTRICT"). charges, invoices, payments and refunds carry patient_id with RESTRICT. A patient who has any billing row cannot be hard-deleted.
  • Staff and payroll → Compensation ("plan per assignment"). compensation_plans.assignment_id ties a salary-and-commission plan to one assignment (CASCADE). In the other direction, commission_settlements.payroll_record_id links a settlement to the payroll record that paid it (RESTRICT).
  • Billing → Compensation ("charge earns commission"). commission_entries.charge_id points to the charge that earned a commission (RESTRICT), and charges.commission_plan_id records which plan applied.
  • Labs → Compensation ("lab line earns commission"). commission_entries.lab_invoice_line_id points to a lab invoice line (RESTRICT).
  • Patients → Labs ("patient"). lab_orders, lab_invoices, lab_payments and lab_refunds carry patient_id with RESTRICT.
  • Workflow engine → Labs ("workflow and forms"). lab_services and lab_orders point to workflow templates, workflow template versions, stage templates and form schemas (all RESTRICT).
  • Billing → Labs ("clinic service mapping"). service_mappings.clinic_treatment_id maps a clinic billing service in services to a lab service (RESTRICT).
  • Patients → Inventory ("consumption"). patient_consumptions.patientId records materials used for a patient (CASCADE).
  • Identity → Notifications ("in-app inbox"). user_notifications.user_id delivers an in-app notification to a user (CASCADE).
  • Identity → Labs ("lab member"). lab_members.user_id makes a user a member of a lab (RESTRICT).
  • Patients ⇢ Common ("entity_id, no FK", dotted). audit_logs and status_history record history for many kinds of rows through an entity_type + entity_id pair (and a subject_id that groups a patient's sub-records under the patient). The pair is polymorphic, so no foreign key is possible.
  • Billing ⇢ Appointments, queue, encounters ("service_id, no FK", dotted). treatments.service_id names the catalog service billing uses to price the treatment, without a foreign key. charges.encounter_id and charges.appointment_id are also logical links without foreign keys.

12.6 Where to read next

Each domain has its own chapter with an entity-relationship diagram and every relationship explained: identity (Chapter 13), organizations, locations and subscriptions (Chapter 14), access and features (Chapter 15), staff and payroll (Chapter 16), patients (Chapter 17), appointments, queue and encounters (Chapter 18), prescriptions and plans (Chapter 19), billing (Chapters 20 and 21), compensation (Chapter 22), inventory (Chapter 23), notifications (Chapter 24), labs (Chapter 25), and the workflow engine and common tables (Chapter 26). Overlapping concepts — two prescription tables, four "visit" tables, two outboxes, two sequence mechanisms — are compared in Chapter 27.

Chapter 13 — Identity and sessions

This chapter describes the four tables that hold the people who can sign in to the Platform and the record of what happened when they did. It is for the product owner who needs to know where a login account lives, how a session is kept, and how sign-in events are logged. These tables sit underneath every other domain: a staff login, an owner, a super admin and a lab member are all rows in users.

13.1 Context

The identity domain is global. Its tables carry no organization_id or location_id, because one person has one account and may work for several organizations. What a user may do inside a clinic is not stored here; it comes from ownership (Chapter 14) and from the user's assignments and roles (Chapters 15 and 16). The tables are owned by three small modules: user owns users, auth owns oauth_providers and security_logs, and session owns user_sessions. Every column of every table is listed in the entity catalog, backend/docs/data-model/ENTITY_CATALOG.md.

13.2 The tables

13.2.1 users — user account

Status: [Implemented]

One row per login account on the whole Platform. The key columns are:

  • uuid — the primary key. This table, and the other three in this chapter, name the key column uuid instead of id.
  • email — unique across the whole Platform. Two accounts can never share an email address.
  • password — the stored password hash; the column is nullable.
  • global_role — null for normal users; the value super_admin marks a super admin. No other value exists.
  • status — active, suspended or deleted, with suspended_at, suspension_reason and deleted_at recording when and why. The account is never removed by this flag; it is a status.
  • email_verification_token, email_verification_expires, email_verified_at — used only for self-signup accounts, so accounts created by an administrator are never asked to verify.
  • last_accessed_organization_id, last_accessed_location_id — the organization and location the user last worked in, so the next login can return there.
  • provider — local, google or github; defaults to local.
  • refresh_token — a deprecated single refresh token kept for backward compatibility. Sessions now keep their own refresh tokens in user_sessions.

There is an index on status for listing accounts by state.

13.2.2 oauth_providers — linked external sign-in

Status: [Not implemented] (table exists, nothing reads or writes it)

Designed to record external sign-in identities (Google, GitHub) linked to an account: user_id, provider, provider_id (the provider's own id for the person), and the email, display name, avatar and raw profile the provider returned. A user can have at most one row per provider (unique user_id + provider), and lookups by provider + provider_id are indexed.

The auth module registers the table, so it is created in the database, but no service injects or queries it. External sign-in itself is disabled: the Google and GitHub strategies exist as files but are not registered, and the module comment says Google/GitHub sign-in is disabled. Expect this table to be empty.

13.2.3 security_logs — security event log

Status: [Implemented]

One row per security-relevant event: a successful or failed login, logout, logout of all devices, password change or reset, email verification, session created, revoked or expired, token refreshed, account suspended, deleted or restored, a login from a new device, and suspicious activity. Key columns:

  • user_id — the account concerned; nullable, because a failed login for an unknown email has no account.
  • event_type — one of twenty event codes such as LOGIN_SUCCESS, LOGIN_FAILED, SESSION_REVOKED.
  • success and error_message — whether the event succeeded and why not.
  • session_id — the session involved, when the event concerns a session.
  • metadata — free-form JSON with event-specific detail.
  • The table also records the network address and browser string of the request. Those values are personal data and are not reproduced in this handbook.

Indexes on created_at and on user_id + event_type support "recent events" and "events of this kind for this user" queries. The table has only created_at; rows are never updated by design, but the database does not enforce that.

13.2.4 user_sessions — login session

Status: [Implemented]

One row per signed-in device or browser. Each session has its own refresh token, so a user can be signed in on several devices and sign one out without affecting the others. Key columns:

  • user_id — the account.
  • refresh_token_hash — a hash of this session's refresh token; the token itself is never stored.
  • expires_at — after this moment the session is expired.
  • is_revoked — a soft revocation flag: when true the session is no longer valid, and the row stays as history.
  • device, browser, os and a free-text location describe the device; an is_current flag is also stored.
  • last_active_at — updated on every save of the row.

An index on user_id + is_revoked makes "this user's live sessions" fast.

13.3 Entity-relationship diagram

Figure 13.1 — Identity and session tables.

The diagram has users in the centre, with the key columns uuid (primary key), email (unique), global_role, status, last_accessed_organization_id and last_accessed_location_id. Under it are three child tables. On the left, oauth_providers (uuid, user_id, provider, provider_id) hangs from users with a solid line labelled "links": one user, zero or more provider rows, and every provider row must have a user. In the middle, security_logs (uuid, user_id, session_id, event_type, success) hangs from users with a solid line labelled "logs" whose user end is optional. On the right, user_sessions (uuid, user_id, refresh_token_hash, expires_at, is_revoked) hangs from users with a solid line labelled "opens". A dashed line labelled "session_id, no FK" runs from user_sessions to security_logs. At the top, organizations and locations are drawn as context boxes with only their id; each has a dashed line to users labelled "last accessed, no FK". Solid lines are foreign keys; dashed lines are logical references the database does not enforce.

13.4 Relationships explained

Foreign-key relationships:

  • oauth_providers.user_id → users. Each provider row belongs to exactly one user; a user has zero or more (at most one per provider). Deleting the user deletes their provider rows (ON DELETE CASCADE).
  • security_logs.user_id → users. Each log row belongs to zero or one user; a user has zero or more log rows. Deleting the user keeps the log rows and sets user_id to null (ON DELETE SET NULL), so the security history survives the account.
  • user_sessions.user_id → users. Each session belongs to exactly one user; a user has zero or more sessions. Deleting the user deletes their sessions (ON DELETE CASCADE).

Logical relationships (no foreign key; the database accepts any value):

  • security_logs.session_id → user_sessions. The session an event concerns. Zero or one session per log row. If the session row disappears, the log keeps a dangling id.
  • users.last_accessed_organization_id → organizations and users.last_accessed_location_id → locations. A convenience pointer for the next login. If the organization or location is removed, the pointer is not cleared by the database.

Links into users from other domains (described in their own chapters):

  • organization_ownership.user_id (CASCADE) makes a user an owner of an organization (Chapter 14).
  • employee_org_location_assignments.user_id (SET NULL) gives an employee's assignment a staff login (Chapter 16).
  • lab_members.user_id (RESTRICT) makes a user a member of a lab (Chapter 25). Because of RESTRICT, a user who is a lab member cannot be hard-deleted.
  • user_notifications.user_id (CASCADE) is the user's in-app inbox (Chapter 24).
  • Many tables keep "actor" columns such as created_by, updated_by, approved_by or recorded_by. They hold a users.uuid but have no foreign key (see Chapter 12).

13.5 Tenant scope

All four tables are global: no organization_id, no location_id. A user's link to clinics is indirect, through organization_ownership and through assignments. This is why users.email is unique across the whole Platform rather than per organization. Only the super admin has a platform-wide role, stored in users.global_role.

13.6 Ownership and ambiguities

  • oauth_providers is registered but unused. The table is created, but no code path reads or writes it, and external sign-in is disabled. It is a leftover of a planned feature.
  • Two places for a refresh token. users.refresh_token is marked deprecated; the live mechanism is one hashed token per row in user_sessions.
  • security_logs.session_id has no foreign key, so a log row can point to a session that no longer exists. This is acceptable for a log but means joins must be outer joins.
  • Append-only by convention. Nothing in the database prevents an update or delete of security_logs rows.

Chapter 14 — Organizations, locations, subscriptions and settings

This chapter describes the tables that define a tenant: the organization (one clinic business), its locations (branches), who owns it, how it pays for the Platform, and where its settings are stored. It is for the product owner who needs to know what a "clinic" is in the database and which table to look at for a given setting. Almost every other table in the Platform points back to organizations, and most point to locations as well.

14.1 Context

Seven tables belong to this domain. organizations, organization_ownership and organization_settings are owned by the organizations module; locations and location_settings by the locations module; subscription_payments by the subscriptions module; and config_values by the settings-registry module. The business behaviour of organizations and locations is covered in Chapter 9 and subscriptions in Chapter 45; this chapter covers only the data. Every column is listed in the entity catalog, backend/docs/data-model/ENTITY_CATALOG.md.

14.2 The tables

14.2.1 organizations — organization (the tenant)

Status: [Implemented]

One row per clinic business. This is the root of tenancy: no other table sits over it. Key columns:

  • name and slug — the display name and a short machine name. slug is unique across the Platform.
  • clinic_type and specialty_tags — what kind of clinic this is. specialty_tags is a JSON list such as ["general"] or ["dental"] and is used to decide which features are relevant.
  • timezone (default Asia/Karachi) and currency (default PKR) — the organization-wide defaults.
  • subscription_plan — free, starter, professional or enterprise.
  • trial_ends_at and paid_until — the subscription window. When both are null the clinic is "unmanaged" (created by a super admin before subscriptions existed) and has no expiry.
  • max_locations and max_users — optional limits.
  • onboarding_pending — true for a self-signup clinic that has not yet finished the setup wizard.
  • access_version — a counter increased by one on every access change in the organization (roles, assignments, feature flags, ownership). Access caches use it as their key; it is written only by the access-version service.
  • is_active — the soft-delete flag. Deactivating an organization sets it to false; the application does not hard-delete organizations.

Indexes: unique slug, and an index on is_active.

14.2.2 organization_ownership — owner link

Status: [Implemented]

Links a user account to an organization it owns: user_id, organization_id and is_primary_owner. The pair (user_id, organization_id) is unique, so a user is listed at most once per organization. An owner holds every permission in the organization (Chapter 11). An organization can have more than one owner row; is_primary_owner marks the main one.

14.2.3 organization_settings — organization-wide settings

Status: [Partial] — stored and editable; the feature switches only hide sections on the location settings screen

One row per organization at most (organization_id is unique). It holds:

  • Booking defaults: default_slot_duration (30 minutes), advance_booking_days (30), cancellation_notice_hours (24).
  • allow_location_override — whether locations may set their own booking values. The location settings screen shows the organization's values instead when this is false.
