Every foreign key in the lab tables uses ON DELETE RESTRICT: no lab record can be deleted while anything refers to it. Records are voided, reversed, archived or switched off instead.

Directory, links and magic links:

  • An internal lab belongs to zero or one owner organization; an organization can own many labs.
  • Each lab link belongs to exactly one lab and one organization; one link per pair.
  • Each lab member belongs to exactly one lab and one user; one membership per pair.
  • Each magic link belongs to exactly one organization, one lab and one lab order; an order can have many links.

Catalog:

  • Each lab service belongs to exactly one lab, one specialty and one service category, and optionally to one form schema, one workflow template and one stage template.
  • Each service category belongs to exactly one specialty.
  • Each option and each price row belongs to exactly one lab service. A price row belongs to zero or one organization (empty = list price).
  • Each service mapping belongs to exactly one organization, one clinic service (services) and one lab service.
  • Each order template belongs to exactly one organization and one specialty, and optionally to one lab.

Orders:

  • Each lab order belongs to exactly one organization, location, specialty, patient, lab, lab link and pinned workflow version, and optionally to one doctor (employee).
  • Each order item belongs to exactly one order, one lab service and one pinned workflow version, and optionally to one form version and to one earlier item it remakes.
  • Each tooth row belongs to exactly one item; each item has at most one details row and at most one form-response row (both keyed by the item id). A form response may point at one form version.
  • Each message, revision and charge request belongs to exactly one order; messages and charge requests may also point at one item.

Production:

  • Each stage row belongs to exactly one order, one item and one pinned workflow version, and optionally to one stage-template step.
  • Each assignment belongs to exactly one item and one lab member.
  • Each shipment item belongs to exactly one shipment, one order and one item, and optionally one stage.
  • Each remake request belongs to exactly one order and one original item, and to zero or one new item (one-to-one).
  • Each warranty belongs to exactly one item (one-to-one through the unique item id).

Finance:

  • Each patient lab invoice belongs to exactly one patient and optionally one order; each line belongs to exactly one invoice and optionally one item or one charge request.
  • Each lab payment belongs to exactly one patient and may reverse exactly one earlier payment (one-to-one).
  • Each allocation belongs to exactly one payment and one invoice. Each credit note belongs to exactly one invoice.
  • Each lab refund belongs to exactly one patient and optionally one credit note; each refund source belongs to exactly one refund and one payment.
  • Each vendor bill and vendor payment belongs to exactly one lab; each bill line belongs to exactly one bill; each vendor allocation belongs to exactly one vendor payment and one bill.
  • Each lab statement belongs to exactly one lab; each statement line belongs to exactly one statement.

Logical relationships (no foreign key):

  • magic_links.shipment_id → shipments (unused, see 25.2).
  • order_templates.owner_user_id → users.
  • attachments.entity_id is polymorphic (order or item); attachments.order_id → lab_orders.
  • lab_order_items.clinic_treatment_id → services, option_ids → lab_service_options (array), lab_price_id → lab_service_prices, stage_template_id → stage_templates. Note that service_mappings.clinic_treatment_id has a foreign key to the same services table, but the item's copy does not.
  • lab_orders.appointment_id → appointments, treatment_id → treatments, order_template_id → order_templates.
  • order_messages.author_user_id → users.
  • item_assignments.lab_id, order_item_stages.lab_id, remake_requests.lab_id, shipments.lab_id → labs. These copies let the lab portal filter by lab quickly.
  • order_item_stages.appointment_id → appointments; remake_requests.warranty_id → item_warranties.
  • lab_credit_notes.patient_id → patients.
  • lab_invoice_lines.clinic_treatment_id → services, doctor_id → employees, performing_assignment_id → employee_org_location_assignments, commission_plan_id → compensation_plans.
  • vendor_bills.lab_order_id → lab_orders, statement_id → lab_statements, journal_id → ledger_journals.
  • vendor_bill_lines.lab_order_id, order_item_id, charge_request_id, remake_request_id → the matching lab tables.
  • lab_statement_lines.matched_bill_id → vendor_bills and matched_bill_line_id → vendor_bill_lines.
  • lab_statements.attachment_id → attachments (unused).
  • Actor columns (created_by, updated_by, decided_by, received_by and others) hold a user id.

25.9 Tenant scope

  • Global, lab-side: labs (internal labs carry an owner organization), lab_members, lab_services, lab_service_options. These are scoped by lab_id, not by organization.
  • Global, platform catalog: service_categories.
  • Organization and location: lab_orders, lab_invoices, lab_payments, lab_credit_notes, lab_refunds, vendor_bills, vendor_payments.
  • Organization only: every other lab table, including items, item parts, messages, revisions, charge requests, attachments, all production tables, invoice lines, allocations, refund sources, settings, bill lines, vendor allocations, statements and statement lines. lab_service_prices is organization-scoped when a negotiated price, global when a list price.
  • Only lab_clinic_links, magic_links, lab_service_prices, service_mappings, order_templates and lab_orders have foreign keys on their tenant columns. Everywhere else the organization id is stored without a constraint and the application enforces isolation.

Chapter 26 — Workflow engine and common tables

This chapter describes two groups of tables. The first is the workflow engine: twelve tables that store specialties, versioned forms, try-in stage templates and versioned state machines, which the lab module runs on. The second is the shared infrastructure in backend/src/common/: the generic audit log, the status history and the per-organization number counters, plus the unused chairs table. It is written for the product owner who needs to know which behaviour is configured as data rather than code, and which history can never be changed. The entity catalog (backend/docs/data-model/ENTITY_CATALOG.md) remains the field-level reference.

26.1 The workflow engine in one paragraph

A specialty (for example DENTAL) is the root. Under it, the Platform keeps form schemas (what the doctor fills in when ordering a lab item), stage templates (the try-in rounds a piece of work goes through) and workflow templates (state machines for lab orders, lab order items and stages). Forms and workflows are versioned: a version is a draft while it is edited, becomes published and then frozen, and is finally retired. Every lab order and item pins the exact version it started on, so editing a form or workflow never breaks work in progress. When a workflow version is published, its JSON definition is turned into rows of states, transitions and transition effects, which the runtime reads. Effects are code handlers listed in a registry; configuration can only choose among them, never add new code.

Status: [Implemented]. The super admin edits forms, workflows and stage templates in Config Studio (sidebar entries "Form schemas", "Workflows" and "Stage templates", super admin only). The lab order and production services run on the published versions.

Keys. All engine tables with an id use UUID version 7 keys (uuid_generate_v7()); the Labs chapter (Chapter 25) explains them. organization_specialties, transition_effects and workflow_effects have natural keys supplied by the application.

Figure 26.1 — Specialties, form schemas and versions, stage templates and steps, workflow templates, versions, states, transitions and effects.

The figure shows specialties at the top with four lines down: to organization_specialties ("switched on"), form_schemas, stage_templates and workflow_templates, all RESTRICT. form_schemas connects to form_schema_versions ("versions, RESTRICT"). stage_templates connects to stage_template_steps ("steps, CASCADE"). workflow_templates connects to workflow_template_versions ("versions, RESTRICT"). workflow_template_versions connects to workflow_states and to workflow_transitions. workflow_states connects twice to workflow_transitions, labelled "from state" and "to state". workflow_transitions and workflow_effects both connect to transition_effects ("runs" and "handler"). All lines except the stage steps are RESTRICT. The template boxes mark organization_id as "null = platform".

26.2 Engine tables

specialties and organization_specialties

specialties is a platform catalog of clinical specialties, each with a unique upper-case code, a name, is_active, and enabled_by_default (new organizations get it switched on; DENTAL does). organization_specialties records which specialties one organization works in, with is_enabled. Its primary key is the pair (organization, specialty). Rows are created lazily from enabled_by_default the first time an organization is read.

form_schemas and form_schema_versions — versioned order forms

A form schema is the stable identity of a form, such as CROWN or BRIDGE, within a specialty. If organization_id is empty, it is the platform default; an organization's own schema with the same code overrides the default for that organization. Partial unique indexes allow one platform schema and one per organization for each specialty and code.

A form schema version holds the content: schema_json (the field definitions), ui_json (layout, such as tooth-chart settings), promotions (which answers are copied into typed columns, for example into dental_item_details) and status (draft, published or retired) with published_at and retired_at.

Constraints that matter:

  • version_no is unique per form and above zero.
  • At most one draft and at most one published version per form (two partial unique indexes).
  • chk_form_schema_versions_published_at: a draft has no publish date, and every non-draft has one.

Correction to the catalog. The entity's code comment, repeated in the catalog, says a database trigger makes published versions immutable. No such trigger exists. The rule is enforced by the form schemas service, which allows content changes only on drafts.

stage_templates and stage_template_steps — try-in rounds

A stage template lists the try-in rounds a kind of work goes through, for example metal, then bisque, then final for a porcelain-fused-to-metal crown. It follows the same platform-or-organization pattern as forms. Each step has a seq (1-based, unique per template), a code (unique per template), a name, requires_patient_visit, requires_doctor_approval and default_lab_days (0–365). Lab orders copy step names into their own stage rows, so editing a template never changes work in progress.

workflow_templates, workflow_template_versions, workflow_states, workflow_transitions

A workflow template is a state machine for one kind of record: entity_type is order, item or stage. It follows the platform-or-organization pattern. A workflow template version holds the draft definition as JSON (definition_json) and a status of draft, published or retired; as with forms, at most one draft and one published version exist per template, and version_no is unique and above zero. Published versions never change; this is enforced by the service, not the database.

Publishing a version writes its rows once:

  • workflow_states: one row per state, with a code unique per version, a name, a category (initial, active, waiting, done or cancelled), is_terminal and sort_order.
  • workflow_transitions: one row per allowed move from one state to another under an action_code, unique per version, from-state, action and to-state. allowed_sides and allowed_roles say who may perform it (an empty role list means any role of an allowed side), required_fields lists data that must be present and requires_reason forces a reason.

workflow_effects and transition_effects

workflow_effects is a registry of effect handlers that exist in code, keyed by code. It is synced from the in-memory registry on every start. is_financial marks effects that validate money themselves; is_available is false when a handler was removed from code but old versions still mention it. transition_effects lists which effects a transition runs, in seq order (unique per transition), with optional JSON params; its primary key is the pair (transition, effect code). Effects run inside the transition's transaction.

26.3 Common tables

Figure 26.2 — The audit log, status history, number sequences and the unused chairs table.

The figure shows four main boxes. audit_logs receives dotted lines from organizations (organization_id) and users (actor_user_id). status_history receives dotted lines from organizations, users and labs (on_behalf_of_lab_id). number_sequences receives a dotted line from organizations. All dotted lines mean "no FK". chairs is the only box with a solid line, from locations, labelled CASCADE. audit_logs and status_history both show entity_type and an entity_id marked "polymorphic".

audit_logs — the generic audit trail

Status: [Implemented]. Used by about eighteen modules, including patients, appointments, staff, payroll, organizations, the engine and every lab module.

One row records who changed what. entity_type and entity_id name the changed record. subject_id names the record whose history this row joins when that is different, for example a patient for a change to the patient's vitals. action is create, update, void, delete, export or view_sensitive. changes holds { before, after } for the changed fields only. actor_user_id and actor_side (clinic, lab, platform or system) say who did it, and ip and request_id record where it came from. organization_id is empty for platform-level records, such as a lab edited by a super admin.

Append-only trigger. The hand-written migration 1792490000000-lab-management-foundation installs trg_audit_logs_append_only, which calls reject_append_only_mutation() before any UPDATE or DELETE and raises an error. Rows can only be inserted.

status_history — every status change

Status: [Implemented].

One row records one status change: from_state (empty for the creating transition), to_state, action_code, who did it (actor_user_id, actor_side), how (via: app, portal, magic_link, proxy or qr), an optional reason and metadata. on_behalf_of_lab_id is set when clinic staff updated something on the lab's behalf (via = proxy). States are free text, because workflow states are data, not code enums. The same migration installs trg_status_history_append_only, so rows cannot be updated or deleted.

number_sequences — human-readable numbers per organization

Status: [Implemented].

One row is a gapless counter for one organization and one sequence_key, with a prefix and next_value (CHECK: above zero). The primary key is the pair (organization, sequence key), supplied by the application. It is only touched through the numbering service inside a transaction, which increments the counter in a single statement. It produces numbers such as LAB-0001 for lab orders and SHP-0001 for shipments, and also numbers patient lab invoices, lab receipts, credit notes, lab refunds, vendor bills and vendor payments. Clinic invoice, receipt and refund numbers use a different mechanism, document_sequences (the Billing ledgers chapter, Chapter 21).

chairs — dental chairs

Status: [Not implemented]. Entity only.

The table would list the treatment chairs of a location: name, code, description and is_active. There is no module, service, controller or screen, and no module registers the entity, so the running application never creates the table in development. A production schema built with the command-line schema tools may contain it. An early link from appointments to chairs no longer exists.

26.4 Relationships explained

Engine:

  • Specialty → organization specialties, form schemas, stage templates, workflow templates. Each belongs to exactly one specialty; a specialty in use cannot be deleted (RESTRICT).
  • Organization → organization specialties. Deleting the organization deletes its specialty switches (CASCADE).
  • Organization → form schemas, stage templates, workflow templates. Each belongs to zero or one organization (empty = platform default). An organization with its own definitions cannot be deleted (RESTRICT).
  • Form schema → versions. Each version belongs to exactly one form; a form with versions cannot be deleted (RESTRICT).
  • Stage template → steps. Each step belongs to exactly one template; deleting the template deletes its steps (CASCADE). Lab stage rows that point at a step block that delete in practice (RESTRICT from order_item_stages).
  • Workflow template → versions. RESTRICT.
  • Workflow version → states and transitions. Each belongs to exactly one version (RESTRICT).
  • State → transitions. Each transition has exactly one from-state and one to-state (RESTRICT on both).
  • Transition → transition effects and effect → transition effects. Each transition effect belongs to exactly one transition and one effect (RESTRICT on both).
  • Links from the lab tables. Lab services point at form schemas, workflow templates and stage templates; lab orders, items and stages pin workflow versions; items and form responses pin form versions. All are RESTRICT (the Labs chapter, Chapter 25, lists them).

Common:

  • Location → chairs. Each chair belongs to one location; deleting the location deletes its chairs (CASCADE).
  • audit_logs and status_history have no foreign keys at all. entity_id and subject_id are polymorphic; organization_id, actor_user_id and on_behalf_of_lab_id are logical references. This is deliberate for an audit table: history must survive even if the record it describes is gone.
  • number_sequences.organization_id has no foreign key.
  • Actor columns in the engine (created_by, updated_by, published_by) hold a user id with no foreign key.

26.5 Tenant scope

  • Global, platform catalog: specialties, workflow_effects.
  • Platform or organization: form_schemas, stage_templates, workflow_templates (empty organization = platform default). Their child tables (form_schema_versions, stage_template_steps, workflow_template_versions, workflow_states, workflow_transitions, transition_effects) have no organization column and inherit the parent's scope.
  • Organization only: organization_specialties, audit_logs (empty for platform records), status_history, number_sequences.
  • Location only: chairs (the organization is reachable through locations).

Chapter 27 — Overlaps and ambiguities

This chapter collects the places where the Platform's data model is confusing, duplicated or weaker than it looks. It is written for the product owner, who will meet these questions when planning features, writing reports or reviewing a migration. Each item says what it is, why it matters, the risk, and a status label. The facts come from the entity catalog (backend/docs/data-model/ENTITY_CATALOG.md, sections 9 and 10) and were checked against the code; the other data-model chapters (Chapters 12 to 26) describe the tables themselves.

27.1 How to read this chapter

Each topic has the same four parts:

  • What it is. The tables or columns involved.
  • Why it matters. What goes wrong for a developer, a report writer or a user.
  • Risk. Low, medium or high, with the reason.
  • Status. One label. [Implemented] means both sides exist and work as designed; [Partial] means one side is incomplete; [Not implemented] means a planned link was never finished; [Unverified] means the code does not say which answer is right.

27.2 Two prescription tables

What it is. prescriptions (prescriptions module) is the current prescription record: draft and finalized states, medicines in their own table, change history, doctor signatures, templates and print layouts. patient_prescriptions (patients module) is the older, simpler record: one row with the medicines in a JSON array. The class comment of prescriptions says it "coexists with the legacy" table while consumers migrate.

Why it matters. The patient's Clinical tab shows both. The main card lists prescriptions from the new table, and a collapsible "Legacy quick-Rx history" section still reads the old table and still offers a form to add a legacy prescription. A report that counts prescriptions from only one table will be wrong.

Risk. Medium. Data is split, and new legacy rows can still be created.

Status. [Partial]. Migration to the new table is not finished; the legacy write path is still live.

27.3 Four "visit" concepts

Figure 27.1 — Appointments, queue entries, encounters and the patient visit summary, with treatments and charges.

The figure shows patients at the top, connected to appointments ("books"), queue_entries ("waits as"), patient_encounters and patient_visits ("summary per location"), all CASCADE. appointments connects optionally to queue_entries ("checked in as, CASCADE") and to patient_encounters ("booked visit, SET NULL"). queue_entries connects one-to-one to patient_encounters ("consulted in, CASCADE"). patient_encounters connects to treatments ("performed in, SET NULL") and, by a dotted line with no foreign key, to charges (encounter_id). patient_visits has no link to any of the other visit tables.

What it is.

  • appointments: a booking for a future time with a doctor.
  • queue_entries: a patient's place in one doctor's queue on one day. Created only at check-in or for a walk-in, never at booking.
  • patient_encounters: the clinical record of one consultation, created when the doctor starts it. Exactly one per queue entry; it points at the appointment for booked visits and has none for walk-ins.
  • patient_visits: a per-location summary for a patient (first and last visit date, total spent, preferred location).

Why it matters. "How many visits did we have?" has four possible answers. Appointments include no-shows and cancellations; queue entries include walk-ins and people who left; encounters are consultations that actually started. patient_visits gives no answer at all: in the code, the patients service only reads it (GET /patients/:id/visits), and nothing writes rows into it.

Risk. Medium. Reports and dashboards can disagree depending on which table they count. The visit summary will be empty for every patient.

Status. [Partial]. Appointments, queue entries and encounters are [Implemented]; patient_visits is read but never written.

27.4 Treatment-plan table families

Figure 27.2 — The tables whose names suggest "plan" or "prescription", and what they really hold.

The figure shows patients connected to patient_prescriptions ("legacy Rx"), prescriptions ("Rx"), patient_treatment_plans ("planned work") and treatments ("work done"), all CASCADE. patient_treatment_plans connects to treatment_plan_items (CASCADE). plan_templates connects to treatments ("based on, SET NULL"). treatment_plan_templates connects to prescriptions ("protocol used, SET NULL"), and patient_encounters connects to prescriptions (SET NULL). Notes on the template boxes say "Rx protocol" for treatment_plan_templates and "planned procedures" for plan_templates.

What it is.

  • patient_treatment_plans with treatment_plan_items: planned work for a patient.
  • treatments: work actually performed, optionally in an encounter.
  • plan_templates: predefined treatment plans ("Root canal treatment" with its usual steps), copied into a patient's plan.
  • treatment_plan_templates: despite the name, prescription protocols ("Root canal aftercare"), used by the prescription builder to pre-fill medicines and instructions.

Why it matters. The names invite mistakes. A developer asked to "add a step to the treatment plan template" could easily edit the prescription protocol table. The code comment on plan_templates itself warns against confusing the two.

Risk. Low for data, medium for development mistakes.

Status. [Implemented]. All four families work; the issue is naming. In prose the handbook uses plan template for plan_templates and calls treatment_plan_templates "prescription protocol templates".

27.5 Several audit tables

What it is. Change history lives in five places: audit_logs (generic, changed fields only), status_history (every status change of lab and workflow records), billing_audit_logs (billing's own log with full before and after snapshots), prescription_history (prescription changes) and queue_events (queue actions). The comment on billing_audit_logs says it exists because "the repo has no general audit module", which is no longer true.

Why it matters. "Who changed this invoice?" is answered by billing_audit_logs; "who changed this patient?" by audit_logs. A single audit screen or export must read all five.

Risk. Low. Each log is consistent within its area.

Status. [Implemented]. Consolidation is a design choice not yet made.

27.6 Two ledgers

What it is. ledger_entries is the patient statement: one-sided, in rupees. ledger_journals with ledger_journal_lines is a double-entry general ledger in paisa. Both are described in the Billing ledgers chapter (Chapter 21).

Why it matters. The general ledger is not a complete set of books. In the code, only lab money posts journals: patient lab invoices, lab payments, credit notes, lab refunds, commission on lab lines, vendor bills and vendor payments. Ordinary clinic invoices and payments, and expenses, do not post journals, and no report reads the general ledger.

Risk. Medium. Anyone who builds accounting reports from the journals will miss most clinic revenue.

Status. [Partial]. The patient statement is [Implemented]; the general ledger covers lab money only.

27.7 Two outboxes

What it is. outbox (queue module) carries realtime queue events to the Socket.IO relay. notification_outbox (notifications module) holds messages for people: in-app today, other channels later.

Why it matters. The names are similar but the purposes are separate. A developer adding a notification should never write to outbox, and a realtime screen update should never go through notification_outbox.

Risk. Low.

Status. [Implemented]. Both work as designed.

27.8 Two sequence mechanisms

What it is. document_sequences (billing) counts clinic invoices, receipts and refunds per organization, location, document type and year, giving numbers like <location code>-INV-<year>-00001. number_sequences (common) counts per organization and key, giving numbers like LAB-0001 and SHP-0001 for the lab module. The inventory module uses neither: it builds purchase-order numbers by reading the organization's last order.

Why it matters. Numbering rules differ by document: clinic documents restart every year at each location, lab documents run on per organization. The inventory approach reads the last number without a lock, so two orders created at the same moment can get the same number; and its purchase-order number is unique across the whole Platform while it is generated per organization, so a second organization's first purchase order collides with the first organization's (the Inventory chapter, Chapter 23, explains it).

Risk. Low for the two sequence tables; high for inventory purchase-order numbering.

Status. [Implemented] for the two sequence tables. The purchase-order numbering defect is recorded for the owner.

27.9 services versus lab_services

What it is. services (code class CatalogService) is the clinic's billable catalog: what the patient is charged for. lab_services is a lab's catalog: what the lab makes and charges the clinic for. service_mappings connects them. Lab tables call a services id clinic_treatment_id.

Why it matters. The class name, table name and column name all differ, which makes code search and SQL harder. The clinic price and the lab cost of the same crown live in different tables.

Risk. Low.

Status. [Implemented].

27.10 Logical references with uncertain targets

These columns hold an id but nothing in the code says for certain which table it belongs to:

  • dentist_id on patient_teeth_chart, patient_treatment_plans, patient_recalls and patient_feedback: an employee id or a user id. Only the request formats mention it, as a plain string.
  • doctor_signatures.employee_id: its code comment says it currently stores the signed-in user's id, despite the column name.
  • locations.manager_id: an employee or a user.
  • patient_consumptions.treatmentPlanId (inventory): probably a patient treatment plan.
  • notification_outbox.recipient_id (by recipient_type) and config_values.scope_id (by scope): polymorphic by design.
  • stock_movements.referenceId: polymorphic and stored as text, not as a UUID.

Why it matters. A join to the wrong table returns nothing or, worse, the wrong person. The employee-versus-user confusion is the most dangerous, because both tables use UUIDs and the mistake is silent.

Risk. Medium.

Status. [Unverified] for the dentist_id, manager_id and treatmentPlanId targets; the doctor_signatures case is confirmed by the code comment.

27.11 Foreign keys that look missing

What it is.

  • magic_links.shipment_id has no foreign key. Its comment says "no FK until that table exists here", but shipments now exists. No code creates shipment magic links.
  • lab_order_items.clinic_treatment_id has no foreign key, while service_mappings.clinic_treatment_id, pointing at the same services table, has one.
  • Almost every billing v2 table, and most lab tables, store organization_id and location_id without foreign keys, while older modules constrain them. No comment explains the choice.

Why it matters. Without a foreign key the database accepts ids that do not exist, and deletes are not blocked. Tenant isolation in these tables rests entirely on the application.

Risk. Medium. Low today because the application always fills these columns, but a bug or a manual SQL fix can create orphan rows.

Status. [Not implemented] for the shipment link; the others are as designed but undocumented.

27.12 "Append-only" that the database does not enforce

What it is. Class comments call ledger_entries, ledger_journals, ledger_journal_lines, payment_allocations, billing_audit_logs and notification_outbox append-only. Only three tables have a trigger that rejects changes: commission_entries (deletes and amount changes refused), audit_logs and status_history (all updates and deletes refused). A comment on form_schema_versions also claims a trigger, but none exists; the service enforces it.

Why it matters. For the unprotected tables, append-only is a promise of the application code only. A manual SQL statement or a future bug can change history without any error.

Risk. Medium for the financial tables.

Status. [Partial]. Enforced in the database for three tables, by the application for the rest.

27.13 Naming inconsistency

What it is. The ten registered inventory tables use camelCase column names (organizationId, currentStock, treatmentPlanId). Every other module, including the legacy inventory table, uses snake_case.

Why it matters. In SQL, camelCase names must be quoted ("organizationId"); unquoted names fail. Report writers who move between modules trip over it. In stock_movements the tenant columns are also text instead of UUID.

Risk. Low.

Status. [Implemented] as is; renaming would need a migration.

27.14 Employee phone and CNIC are unique across the whole Platform

What it is. employees is a person record shared by every clinic the person works for; the link to a clinic is the assignment. Its phone and cnic columns are unique across the entire Platform, not per organization.

Why it matters. If two clinics enter the same doctor separately, the second insert fails. The design intends the second clinic to reuse the existing person record, but the clinic may not know that record exists, and its contact details are shared with the other clinic.

Risk. Medium. Expect support questions when a doctor works at two unrelated clinics.

Status. [Implemented] by design.

27.15 Primary keys with no default

What it is. These tables have keys that the application must supply: document_sequences, number_sequences, organization_specialties, transition_effects (composite keys); location_billing_settings (location id), lab_billing_settings (organization id), dental_item_details and item_form_responses (item id), patient_comm_prefs (patient id); workflow_effects and notification_events (a code); and idempotency_keys.

Why it matters. Most of these are "one row per parent" tables, where using the parent's id as the key is the point: it makes a second row impossible. An insert that forgets the key fails at once, which is safe.

Risk. Low.

Status. [Implemented] by design.

27.16 Entities the running application does not create

What it is. chairs and the legacy inventory table have entity files, but no module registers them. The development database, built by the running application, does not contain them; a production database built by the command-line schema tool, which loads every entity file, may contain them.

Why it matters. Development and production schemas can differ by these two tables, which confuses schema comparisons.

Risk. Low.

Status. [Not implemented] for both tables.

Part 5 — Module chapters

Chapter 28 — Patients

The Patients module is the clinic's register of people it treats: who they are, how to reach them, and every clinical and administrative record attached to them. Front-desk staff use it to register and find patients; doctors and assistants use it to read and add clinical records; the owner uses it to import an old register, export data and review who changed what. Almost every other part of the Platform (appointments, the queue, the consultation workspace, prescriptions, billing, labs) points at a patient record from this module.

28.1 What this module is for

A patient is a person registered with one organization (one clinic business). The patient record belongs to the whole organization, not to one location: a patient registered at the Main location can be booked at the Second location without registering again. Each patient gets a patient number such as P-00042 that is unique inside the organization.

The module covers:

  • registration, editing, activation and deactivation, and permanent deletion;
  • the patient list with card and list views, search and filters;
  • bulk import from an Excel or CSV file, and export of the list to CSV;
  • the patient detail page with its tabs: Overview, Appointments, Visits, Treatments, Vitals & Dental, Teeth Chart, Clinical & Rx, Consents, Billing and Files;
  • clinical sub-records: dental info, teeth charts (FDI notation), vitals, consents with a drawn signature, uploaded documents, and the legacy quick prescription;
  • CRM-style sub-records (communications log, recalls, referrals, feedback, insurance), which exist in the backend but have no screen today;
  • a per-patient change history built from the audit log.

Who uses it (system roles, by default): the Receptionist registers, edits and finds patients at their location; the Doctor reads and adds clinical records for their own patients; the Assistant reads clinical records and edits teeth charts at their location; the Admin can do everything, including delete, export and change history; the Accountant has no patient-list access by default and sees patients only through billing screens.

Sidebar: the entry Patients (route /patients) sits in the "Clinic" section of the default sidebar and is shown to anyone holding patients.view. The detail page /patients/$patientId has no sidebar entry; it is reached from the list, from search pickers in other modules, or by link. The old route /patients/new only redirects to /patients, because registration happens in a dialog on the list page.

28.3 Features

28.3.1 Register a patient

Status: [Implemented]

What it does. Creates a new patient in the organization, gives them the next patient number and, optionally, books their first appointment straight away.

How the user does it.

  1. On /patients, press Create.
  2. Fill step "Basic Info": Full Name and Phone Number are required; for a minor, turn on the minor switch and enter the guardian.
  3. Press Next, fill "Clinic Info", and press Add Patient.
  4. On the "Book Appointment" step, pick a doctor and a time and press Book Appointment, or press Skip.

Behind the scenes — in simple terms. The Platform checks that no other patient in the clinic has the same phone number, counts the clinic's patients to make the next number, saves the patient with the current location as their home location, and writes a "created" entry in the audit log.

Behind the scenes — technically. POST /patients → PatientsService.create. It calls validatePhoneUnique (exact match of phone inside the organization), then generatePatientNumber (P- plus the count of the organization's patients plus one, padded to five digits). primaryLocationId defaults to the active location; createdBy is the caller's user id. The insert and the audit row (recordPatientChange, action create) run in one database transaction. While the user moves between steps, the web app keeps a draft of the form in the patient store so going back does not lose input. The appointment step calls the Appointments module (the Appointments chapter, Chapter 29, covers booking).

Rules and validations.

  • Full name: required, at most 150 characters. Phone: required, at most 20 characters; the form also checks 7–20 digits and the characters + - ( ) and space.
  • Phone must be unique inside the organization (server rule, exact text match).
  • Email must be a valid address; CNIC must look like 12345-0000000-0 (form rule); date of birth cannot be in the future (form rule).
  • A minor needs a guardian name (form rule).
  • Gender, blood group, marital status, language, communication preference and source must be values from fixed lists. Defaults: language Urdu, communication preference WhatsApp, source walk-in.
  • Tags are free text chosen in a multi-select that can create new tags.

Who can do it. patients.create (no scope; implies patients.view), feature patients.core. Default holders: Admin, Receptionist.

Data read and written. Reads patients; writes patients and audit_logs.

Effects on other modules. The new patient can be booked, checked in to the queue, billed and searched from every patient picker.

Error cases.

  • "A patient with this phone number already exists in this organization" (409) → another patient already has this exact phone.
  • "Full name is required" / "Phone number is required" (400) → missing fields.
  • The form's own messages (for example "Phone Number looks invalid (7–20 digits)") → shown at the top of the step before anything is sent.
  • "Failed to create patient" toast → any other server error.

Technical references: backend/src/patients/patients.service.ts · PatientsService.create, CreatePatientDto · web-app/src/features/patients/components/CreatePatientModal.tsx, PatientForm.tsx, AddAppointmentStep.tsx

28.3.2 Check a phone number before saving

Status: [Partial] — the endpoint and a web hook exist, but no screen calls them; the duplicate is caught only when the user saves.

What it does. Answers "does another patient in this clinic already have this phone number?" without saving anything.

How the user does it. No screen uses it. The registration form relies on the server's check at save time, which answers 409 for a duplicate phone.

Behind the scenes — in simple terms. The Platform looks for a patient with the same phone in the organization, optionally ignoring one patient (the one being edited), and answers yes or no.

Behind the scenes — technically. GET /patients/check-phone/:phone?excludeId= → PatientsService.checkPhoneExists returns { exists: boolean }. The web hook useCheckPhone and API function checkPhoneUnique are exported but not used by any component.

Rules and validations.

  • Exact text match on phone inside the organization; no normalisation.
  • The answer ignores the caller's patient scope, but only says yes or no.

Who can do it. patients.view (any scope), feature patients.core. Default holders: Admin, Doctor, Receptionist, Assistant.

Data read and written. Reads patients.

Effects on other modules. None.

Error cases. None specific.

Technical references: backend/src/patients/patients.controller.ts · checkPhone, checkPhoneExists · web-app/src/features/patients/hooks/useCheckPhone.ts

28.3.3 Browse, search and filter the patient list

Status: [Implemented]

What it does. Shows the patients the viewer is allowed to see, one page at a time, in a table or as cards, with search and filters.

How the user does it.

  1. Open Patients in the sidebar.
  2. Type in the search box to match name, phone or patient number.
  3. Narrow with Gender and Status; clear with the reset control or the "no results" state's clear button.
  4. Switch between table and card view with the view toggle; in table view change the page size or page.

Behind the scenes — in simple terms. The list only ever contains patients inside the viewer's reach: everyone in the organization, everyone connected to the current location, or only the doctor's own patients (those with an appointment or queue entry with that doctor).

Behind the scenes — technically. GET /patients → PatientsService.findAll → shared listQuery, which applies access.applyScope(qb, 'patients.view', patientScope('p.id')), then the filters, then sorting, then paging (page, limit, default 10, maximum 100). Search uses case-insensitive ILIKE on full_name, phone and patient_number.

Rules and validations.

  • The API also accepts bloodGroup, source, city, tag, isBlacklisted, isMinor, sortBy (createdAt, fullName, patientNumber) and sortOrder; the screen offers only search, gender and status.
  • Default order is newest registration first. Column sorting in table view re-orders the rows of the current page only.
  • Card view shows the current page only and has no paging controls.

Who can do it. patients.view with scope own, location or org, feature patients.core. Default holders: Admin (org), Receptionist (location), Assistant (location), Doctor (own).

Data read and written. Reads patients and, for scoped viewers, appointments, queue_entries and queue_sessions.

Effects on other modules. The same endpoint feeds the type-ahead patient pickers of other modules (usePatientSearch, two or more characters, 300 ms debounce, eight results).

Error cases. Error state with Retry → the list request failed.

Technical references: backend/src/patients/patients.service.ts · findAll, listQuery, PatientQueryDto · web-app/src/features/patients/pages/PatientsPage.tsx, PatientTable.tsx, PatientCard.tsx, FiltersBar.tsx

28.3.4 Open the patient detail page

Status: [Implemented]

What it does. Shows one patient's profile and the tabs of records the viewer may open.

How the user does it.

  1. Click a patient's name or the "View patient" eye button in the list.
  2. Pick a tab. Use the ← button to go back to where you came from.

Behind the scenes — in simple terms. Before answering, the Platform checks that the patient is inside the viewer's reach. A patient outside it is reported as "not found", exactly like a patient of another clinic, so the viewer cannot even learn that the patient exists.

Behind the scenes — technically. GET /patients/:id → PatientsService.findOne. The controller carries @PatientInScope('id'), so PatientScopeGuard runs isPatientInScope for every route with an :id parameter (every sub-record route too) and throws NotFoundException('Patient not found') when the patient is outside the patients.view scope. Tabs are chosen by visiblePatientTabs from the viewer's permissions and features.

Rules and validations.

  • A malformed id returns 400 (UUID check).
  • A tab appears only when the viewer holds the permission its data needs; for example Teeth Chart needs patients.clinical.view and the patients.teeth_chart feature, Files needs patients.documents.manage.

Who can do it. patients.view (scoped), feature patients.core; the route declares staticData.can: 'patients.view'.

Data read and written. Reads patients.

Effects on other modules. The header's dues badge reads the Billing module.

Error cases. "Failed to load patient details. Please try again." → patient missing, out of scope, or request failed.

Technical references: backend/src/patients/access/patient-scope.ts · PatientScopeGuard, PatientInScope · web-app/src/routes/patients/$patientId.index.tsx, features/patients/utils/patientTabs.ts

28.3.5 Edit patient details

Status: [Implemented]

What it does. Changes any demographic, contact, medical quick-access or clinic field of a patient.

How the user does it.

  1. In the list, press the "Edit patient" pencil, or on the detail Overview tab press Edit Details.
  2. Change fields in the same two-step form, shown in a side sheet.
  3. Press Update Details.

Behind the scenes — in simple terms. If the phone changed, the Platform re-checks that no other patient has it. It then saves the changes and records exactly which fields changed, from what to what.

Behind the scenes — technically. PUT /patients/:id → PatientsService.update. A snapshot of the row is taken first; Object.assign applies the DTO; saveAudited saves the row and the audit row (update, with a field diff) in one transaction. An update that changes nothing writes no audit row.

Rules and validations.

  • All fields optional; same limits as registration.
  • Phone uniqueness is checked only when the phone actually changes, ignoring this patient.
  • The DTO also accepts isActive, isBlacklisted and blacklistReason; the form does not send the blacklist fields.

Who can do it. patients.edit, feature patients.core. Default holders: Admin, Receptionist.

Data read and written. patients, audit_logs.

Effects on other modules. Name, phone and allergies changes appear immediately in appointments, queue, consultation and billing screens, which read the patient row.

Error cases. 409 phone duplicate (same message as registration); "Patient not found" (404).

Technical references: backend/src/patients/patients.service.ts · update, UpdatePatientDto · web-app/src/features/patients/components/EditPatientSheet.tsx

28.3.6 Activate or deactivate a patient

Status: [Implemented]

What it does. Marks a patient inactive (hidden from "Active" filters, but every record kept) or active again. It is the recommended alternative to deletion.

How the user does it.

  1. In the list (table or card), flip the switch in the patient's action area. Its tooltip reads "Deactivate patient" or "Activate patient".

Behind the scenes — in simple terms. The Platform flips the active flag and writes a status-change entry saying who moved the patient from active to inactive or back.

Behind the scenes — technically. PATCH /patients/:id/status with { isActive } → PatientsService.setActive. When the value already matches, nothing is written. Otherwise the save and AuditService.recordStatus (table status_history, action code activate or deactivate, subject = the patient) run in one transaction.

Rules and validations.

  • Only the isActive boolean is accepted.
  • Inactive patients are not blocked anywhere else: they can still be booked, checked in and billed. The flag is informational and a list filter.

Who can do it. patients.edit, feature patients.core. Default holders: Admin, Receptionist.

Data read and written. patients, status_history.

Effects on other modules. The dashboard's patient count asks for active patients only.

Error cases. "Could not update patient status" toast → request failed.

Technical references: backend/src/patients/patients.service.ts · setActive, UpdatePatientStatusDto · web-app/src/features/patients/hooks/useSetPatientStatus.ts

28.3.7 Blacklist a patient

Status: [Partial] — stored, filterable and displayed, but no screen can set it; only an API client can.

What it does. Flags a patient the clinic does not want to serve, with a reason.

How the user does it. No screen sets the flag. When it is set, the Overview tab's "Alerts & Tags" card shows "Blacklisted Patient" and "Reason: …" ("Not specified" when empty).

Behind the scenes — in simple terms. It is a yes/no flag plus a reason text on the patient row. Nothing in booking, the queue or billing reads it.

Behind the scenes — technically. Set through PUT /patients/:id (the patient edit endpoint) with isBlacklisted and blacklistReason, audited as a field change. Listable with GET /patients?isBlacklisted=true.

Rules and validations.

  • No rule blocks a blacklisted patient from being booked, queued or billed.

Who can do it. patients.edit, feature patients.core. Default holders: Admin, Receptionist.

Data read and written. patients (is_blacklisted, blacklist_reason), audit_logs.

Effects on other modules. None.

Error cases. As for editing.

Technical references: backend/src/patients/entities/patient.entity.ts · isBlacklisted, blacklistReason · web-app/src/features/patients/components/tabs/OverviewTab.tsx

28.3.8 Delete a patient permanently

Status: [Partial] — works for patients without billing or lab records; for a patient with charges, invoices, payments, refunds or lab records the database refuses and the user sees a generic failure.

What it does. Removes the patient and every record that hangs off them, for good.

How the user does it.

  1. In the list, press the red bin ("Delete patient permanently").
  2. Read the dialog "Delete patient permanently?", which says the patient and all records will be deleted and suggests deactivating instead.
  3. Press Delete permanently.

Behind the scenes — in simple terms. Before deleting, the Platform counts how many linked records of each kind will disappear and stores the patient's last state and those counts in the audit log, so the deletion itself stays on record. Then it deletes the row, and the database deletes the dependent records.

Behind the scenes — technically. DELETE /patients/:id → PatientsService.remove, in one transaction: cascadeCounts reads the Postgres catalog for every foreign key that cascades from patients and counts rows per table; recordPatientChange writes an audit row with action delete, before = snapshot plus linkedRecords; then a hard DELETE. Cascading tables include appointments, queue entries, encounters, treatments, prescriptions, inventory consumption, patient credits and every patient_* sub-record. Tables charges, invoices, payments, refunds, lab_orders, lab_invoices, lab_payments and lab_credits reference patients with ON DELETE RESTRICT, so the delete fails when any of them has a row, and the whole transaction (including the audit row) rolls back.

Rules and validations.

  • Always behind a confirmation dialog.
  • Hard delete: the entity has a deleted_at column but the service does not use soft delete.

Who can do it. patients.delete (high-risk permission), feature patients.core. Default holder: Admin.

Data read and written. Every table that cascades from patients; audit_logs.

Effects on other modules. The patient disappears from appointments, the queue history, consultation history and prescriptions. Patient numbering is count-based, so after a deletion the next new patient can be given a number that already exists, and that save then fails.

Error cases.

  • "Could not delete patient" toast → the server failed, typically because of billing or lab records (the server answers with the generic "Something went wrong").
  • "Patient not found" (404).

Technical references: backend/src/patients/patients.service.ts · remove, cascadeCounts · web-app/src/features/patients/pages/PatientsPage.tsx (ConfirmDialog)

28.3.9 Import patients from a spreadsheet

Status: [Implemented]

What it does. Brings an existing patient register (for example from an old system or an Excel sheet) into the Platform: read the file, match its columns to patient fields, check every row without saving, then create the valid rows.

How the user does it.

  1. On /patients, press Import. Optionally press Download sample template to get a CSV with the recognised headers (Full Name, Phone, CNIC, Gender, Date of Birth, Age, Email, Address, City, Blood Group, Allergies, Medical History, Notes, Old File No).
  2. Upload one .xlsx or .csv file.
  3. In Map columns, check the suggested "Import as" field for each column; set unwanted columns to be ignored. Full name (or first name) and Phone must be mapped.
  4. Press Check N rows. Review the counts and the "Rows that will not be imported" table. Choose Skip the row or Create anyway for duplicates.
  5. Press Import N patients. Wait for the progress bar.
  6. On Summary, press Download error report if any row failed, then Done.

Behind the scenes — in simple terms. The file is read in memory and never stored. Each row is cleaned up the way a careful receptionist would: extra phone numbers move into notes, an age becomes an estimated birth date, CNICs are reformatted, common spellings of blood groups and genders are understood. Every row is checked against the same rules as manual registration and against existing patients (same phone or CNIC). Each row is then created on its own, so one bad row never undoes the others. Every imported patient is tagged imported.

Behind the scenes — technically. Figure 28.7 shows the flow.

Figure 28.7 — Sequence of a patient import, from file upload to summary.

The diagram has six participants: Receptionist, Web app, API, PatientImportService, PatientsService and PostgreSQL. (1) The receptionist chooses a file. (2) The web app sends it to POST /patients/import/parse. (3) The API returns headers, rows and a suggested column mapping; nothing is stored. (4) The receptionist confirms the mapping. (5) The web app sends all mapped rows to POST /patients/import with dryRun: true. (6) The API hands them to PatientImportService, which (7) reads the phone and CNIC of every existing patient in the organization and (8) returns, per row, would_create, duplicate or error. (9) The receptionist picks the duplicate rule and presses Import. A loop then runs once per batch of 500 rows: (10) the web app posts the batch with dryRun: false; (11) the service marks the organization as "import running" in this server process; an inner loop runs per valid row, where (12) the service calls the normal patient create and (13) PatientsService inserts the patient and its audit row in one transaction; (14) the batch result comes back per row as created, duplicate or error. (15) The web app shows the summary and offers the error-report CSV.

Parsing uses parseImportFile (first non-empty worksheet of an .xlsx, or RFC-4180 CSV; the first non-empty row is the header; blank headers become "Column N"; repeated headers get "(2)", "(3)"). suggestMapping matches header names, including common local spellings, to the fields in IMPORT_FIELDS. validateImportRow runs mapImportRow and then the CreatePatientDto validators. Duplicate detection normalises phones to digits with a leading zero (so +92…, 0092… and 0… match) and CNICs to digits. "Today" for date-of-birth checks is the location's date (ClockService).

Rules and validations.

  • File: .xlsx (checked by its zip signature) or .csv/.txt; at most 10 MB; at most 5,000 data rows. Old .xls files are rejected with a "Save as .xlsx" hint.
  • A dry run accepts up to 5,000 rows in one request; a real import at most 1,000 per request (the web app sends 500).
  • Only one real import per organization at a time in one server process.
  • Mapping fields: full name, first name, last name, phone, WhatsApp, CNIC, gender, date of birth, age, email, address, city, blood group, marital status, occupation, allergies, medical history, notes, old file number, guardian name and phone, emergency contact name and phone, referred by.
  • First phone number becomes the patient's phone; further numbers go to internal notes as "Other phone: …".
  • An age (for example "35", "35 years", "6 months") becomes 1 January of the estimated birth year, with a note "Date of birth estimated from age …". Dates accept day-first formats, ISO, month names and Excel serial numbers. A birth date in the future or before 1900 is an error.
  • "Old File No" goes into internal notes as "Old file no: …" (the patient has no legacy-number column).
  • Source becomes referral when "referred by" is filled, otherwise other.
  • Duplicates: same phone or same CNIC as an existing patient or a previous row of the same file. With Skip the row the row is reported as a duplicate. With Create anyway, a same-CNIC row is created, but a same-phone row is always an error because phones are unique per clinic.

Who can do it. patients.create, feature patients.core. Default holders: Admin, Receptionist.

Data read and written. Reads patients; writes patients and audit_logs (one create entry per imported patient).

Effects on other modules. Imported patients behave exactly like hand-registered ones.

Error cases.

  • "No file provided" → upload without a file.
  • "Unsupported file. Upload an Excel (.xlsx) or CSV file — for old .xls files use "Save as" .xlsx first." → wrong type.
  • "Could not read the Excel file. Is it a valid .xlsx?", "The workbook has no sheets", "The file is empty", "The file has no patient rows", "The file has more than 5,000 patient rows. Split it into smaller files." → unreadable or oversized file.
  • "Send at most 1000 rows per import request" → oversized real-import request.
  • "Another patient import is running for this clinic. Try again when it finishes." (409) → parallel import.
  • Per-row reasons such as "Phone number "…" looks invalid (7–20 digits)", "CNIC "…" must have 13 digits (e.g. 12345-0000000-0)", "Date of birth cannot be in the future", "Same phone number as P-00012 (…)".
  • "The server could not import this batch" → a batch request failed; all its rows are reported as errors and the import continues with the next batch.

Technical references: backend/src/patients/import/patient-import.service.ts, patient-import.ts · PatientImportService.import, parseImportFile, mapImportRow, findDuplicate · web-app/src/features/patients/components/ImportPatientsSheet.tsx, hooks/usePatientImport.ts, utils/patientImport.ts

28.3.10 Export the patient list

Status: [Implemented]

What it does. Downloads the patients matching the current search and filters as a CSV file that opens correctly in Excel, including Urdu names.

How the user does it.

  1. On /patients, set the search and filters you want.
  2. Press Export. A toast says "Export downloaded", or "Export downloaded (first 10,000 patients only)" when the result was cut.

Behind the scenes — in simple terms. The export uses the same reach and filters as the list but no paging, stops at 10,000 patients, and is always written to the audit log because patient data is leaving the system.

Behind the scenes — technically. GET /patients/export → PatientsService.exportCsv (same listQuery, take(10001) to detect truncation). The controller writes an audit row with entity_type = 'patient_export', action export, and after = { rows, truncated, filters }, then streams the CSV with headers Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="patients-YYYY-MM-DD.csv", X-Export-Truncated: true|false (exposed to the browser) and Cache-Control: no-store.

Rules and validations.

  • Columns: Patient number, Name, Phone, Email, Gender, Date of birth, Blood group, City, Source, Active, Registered on.
  • At most 10,000 rows (EXPORT_MAX_ROWS).
  • Cells that a spreadsheet would run as a formula get a leading apostrophe; phone-like values such as +92… are left as they are.
  • The file starts with a UTF-8 byte-order mark.
  • The date in the file name and the "Registered on" column are UTC dates, not the location's date.
  • The button is disabled when the list is empty.

Who can do it. patients.export (high-risk; implies patients.view), feature patients.core. Default holder: Admin. The rows are limited by the caller's patients.view scope.

Data read and written. Reads patients; writes audit_logs.

Effects on other modules. None.

28.3.14 View a patient's change history

Status: [Implemented]

What it does. Shows who created, changed, activated, deactivated or deleted the patient and any of their records, field by field.

How the user does it.

  1. On the patient detail header, press the "Change history" button.
  2. Read the timeline in the side panel.

Behind the scenes — in simple terms. Every write in this module also writes an audit entry in the same transaction, tagged with the patient as its subject, so one lookup reads the patient's whole history. File links (documents, X-rays, signatures, insurance cards, profile picture) are never copied into the log. When a reader lacks the right to open a kind of record, they still see that the event happened but not the values.

Behind the scenes — technically. GET /patients/:id/audit-trail → PatientsService.getAuditTrail → AuditService.subjectTimeline (merges audit_logs and status_history where subject_id = patient, newest first, at most 200 entries) → redactPatientTimeline. Values are removed for dental info, teeth charts, vitals, treatment plans, plan items, legacy prescriptions and consents unless the reader holds patients.clinical.view, and for documents unless they hold patients.documents.manage; medical history and allergies are removed from patient-row changes for readers without patients.clinical.view. What is logged:

Record entity_type Logged on
Patient patient create, update (diff), delete (last state and linked-record counts); activate/deactivate in status_history
Dental info patient_dental_info create, update
Teeth chart, vitals, document, consent, communication, referral, feedback, legacy prescription patient_teeth_chart, patient_vitals, patient_document, patient_consent, patient_communication, patient_referral, patient_feedback, patient_prescription create
Treatment plan, plan item, recall, insurance patient_treatment_plan, treatment_plan_item, patient_recall, patient_insurance create, update
Patient export patient_export every export (row count, truncated flag, filters); not tied to a patient subject

The table lists each kind of patient record, the entity_type value its audit rows carry, and which actions produce a row. Updates that change nothing are not logged. Identity and bookkeeping columns (ids, timestamps, created-by) are left out of every snapshot because the audit row already records who and when.

Rules and validations.

  • The button and endpoint need admin.audit.view in addition to the patient being in the caller's scope.

Who can do it. admin.audit.view (feature core, always on). Default holder: Admin.

Data read and written. Reads audit_logs, status_history.

Effects on other modules. The Audit logging chapter (Chapter 60) describes the shared audit tables.

Error cases. Error state with retry in the panel.

Technical references: backend/src/patients/patient-audit.ts · PATIENT_AUDIT_ENTITY, recordPatientChange, redactPatientTimeline · web-app/src/features/patients/components/PatientAuditSheet.tsx
