44.3 Features

44.3.1 See notifications in the header bell

Status: [Implemented]

What it does. Shows the signed-in user's in-app notifications, with an unread count that refreshes by itself.

How the user does it.

  1. Look at the bell in the header. A badge shows the unread count.
  2. Click the bell to open the popover.
  3. Click an item to open the linked page.

Behind the scenes — in simple terms. Each person has their own inbox. It spans every clinic the person works at, because it is tied to the user and not to a location. The badge asks the server for the count every 30 seconds and when the browser window regains focus. There is no live push.

Behind the scenes — technically. GET /me/notifications?page&limit&unreadOnly (limit 1–50, default 20) and GET /me/notifications/unread-count in MyNotificationsController, which is @ContextFree(): no organization or location headers are needed, and lab users have none. UserNotificationsService.list reads user_notifications for the user, newest first. The web hook useUnreadNotificationCount polls with refetchInterval 30 000 ms; the popover loads useMyNotifications({ limit: 20 }) only while open.

Rules and validations.

  • Always scoped to the signed-in user; there is no way to read another user's inbox.
  • The list is paged; the bell shows only the first 20.

Who can do it. Any signed-in user; no permission key and no feature key.

Data read and written. Reads user_notifications.

Effects on other modules. None. Links in items point to pages such as /lab-orders/<id>.

Error cases. A 401 when no user is resolved; the popover shows "Couldn’t load notifications." on any load failure.

Technical references: backend/src/notifications/controllers/my-notifications.controller.ts · MyNotificationsController, UserNotificationsService · web-app/src/features/notifications/components/NotificationBell.tsx, hooks/useMyNotifications.ts

44.3.2 Mark notifications as read

Status: [Implemented]

What it does. Marks one notification, or all of them, as read.

How the user does it.

  1. Click an item (marks it read and follows its link), or click Mark all read.

Behind the scenes — in simple terms. Reading sets a time stamp on the inbox row. Nothing is ever deleted from the inbox, and there is no "mark as unread".

Behind the scenes — technically. POST /me/notifications/:id/read and POST /me/notifications/read-all (declared first so the route does not clash). markRead loads the row by id and user and sets read_at if it is empty; it is idempotent. markAllRead updates every row of the user where read_at IS NULL and returns { updated }. The web mutations invalidate the inbox queries on completion.

Rules and validations. :id must be a UUID. Only the owner's rows are touched.

Who can do it. Any signed-in user.

Data read and written. Writes user_notifications.read_at.

Effects on other modules. None.

Error cases. NOTIFICATION_NOT_FOUND (404) when the id does not exist for this user.

Technical references: UserNotificationsService.markRead, markAllRead · web-app/src/features/notifications/hooks/useMyNotifications.ts

44.3.3 Raise a notification event (how messages are created)

Status: [Implemented]

What it does. Any module can notify people about a business event. The module decides who is told, on which channel, with what wording and when, and records the result for every recipient and channel.

How the user does it. Users do not do this directly. It happens as a side effect of actions such as submitting a lab order or recording a lab payment (see 44.6).

Behind the scenes — in simple terms. For each person concerned and each channel their audience uses, the module asks six questions in a fixed order and the first match decides:

  1. Is this a mandatory event for an internal audience, on the in-app channel? Then send, whatever the settings say.
  2. Is the audience's master switch off? Then skip.
  3. Is the rule for this event, audience and channel off? Then skip.
  4. Has the patient opted out of this channel? Then skip.
  5. Is it inside quiet hours (not in-app)? Then hold until quiet hours end.
  6. Otherwise send.

A row is written for every outcome, so the message log can explain why something was not sent. Defaults when the clinic has changed nothing: internal audiences (doctor, coordinator, lab) are on with in-app on; the patient audience and every rule for it are off.

Behind the scenes — technically. NotificationService.enqueue(manager, input) runs inside the caller's transaction. It loads the event, de-duplicates recipients by type and id, rejects an audience the event does not allow (NOTIFICATION_AUDIENCE_INVALID), reads audience settings, rules, templates, contact details and patient preferences, and calls the pure function decide() for each recipient and channel in channelsFor(). A template is chosen by rule, then by channel and language (clinic override before platform default; language from the recipient, then the patient preference, then English), and renderTemplate fills {placeholders}; unknown placeholders become empty. Rows are inserted into notification_outbox in one statement, then pg_notify('notification_outbox') is issued in the same transaction, so listeners wake only on commit. A recipient with no phone or email on an external channel gets a failed row with reason no_address. Because the work is inside the caller's transaction, a rollback removes the messages too.

Rules and validations.

  • Unknown event code: NOTIFICATION_EVENT_UNKNOWN (422); a typo fails the business action instead of silently dropping messages.
  • Mandatory in-app messages ignore master switches and rules.
  • Quiet hours never hold in-app messages.
  • The same person listed twice (or under two audiences) gets one row per channel.

Who can do it. Internal service call; no permission.

Data read and written. Reads notification_events, notification_audience_settings, notification_rules, notification_templates, patient_comm_prefs, users, patients, organizations; writes notification_outbox.

Effects on other modules. 44.6 lists the emitters.

Error cases. NOTIFICATION_EVENT_UNKNOWN, NOTIFICATION_AUDIENCE_INVALID, PATIENT_NOT_FOUND (404). All abort the caller's transaction.

Technical references: backend/src/notifications/services/notification.service.ts · NotificationService.enqueue · decision/notification-decision.ts · decide, quietHoursEnd · templates/template-render.ts

44.3.4 Deliver messages in the background

Status: [Implemented] (in-app channel only)

What it does. A worker sends committed outbox rows, retries failures and releases rows held for quiet hours.

How the user does it. Nothing; it is automatic. The user sees the result in the bell, and the clinic admin sees it in the message log.

Behind the scenes — in simple terms. The worker wakes the moment a database message arrives, and also checks every two seconds in case it missed one. It takes a batch of due messages, sends each one and records the outcome. If a send fails it waits and tries again, up to five times, then marks the message failed.

Behind the scenes — technically. NotificationRelayService runs only where background jobs run (NotificationsRuntimeModule.forRole; never on a second API process). It opens a dedicated LISTEN notification_outbox connection and a 2 000 ms setInterval; if the listen connection fails it logs a warning and polls only. Each tick calls NotificationDispatcher.drain(), which coalesces concurrent calls. claim() is one UPDATE … WHERE id IN (SELECT … status IN ('queued','held_quiet_hours') AND scheduled_for <= now() ORDER BY scheduled_for LIMIT 50 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED) RETURNING … that also increments attempts and pushes scheduled_for forward by a 5-minute lease, so a crashed worker's rows reappear. The provider is called with no transaction open. The result is written back only when attempts is unchanged. Failures wait 30 s, 2 min, 10 min, then 1 h; a PermanentSendError or the fifth attempt gives failed. Delivery is at-least-once. Providers are chosen per channel by ChannelProviderRegistry: InAppChannelProvider for in-app, and DevLogChannelProvider for WhatsApp, SMS and email, which only writes a log line and reports success. A PayloadFinalizers hook lets an event fill in data that must never be stored, used by the lab magic-link event.

Rules and validations. Batch size 50; at most 5 attempts; in-app copies are unique per outbox row (ON CONFLICT (outbox_id) DO NOTHING), so a retry never shows twice. An in-app message to a non-user recipient fails permanently.

Who can do it. Automatic; job role only.

Data read and written. Reads and updates notification_outbox; inserts user_notifications.

Effects on other modules. None. If the worker is not running, no message is delivered, although rows are still recorded.

Error cases. Failures are stored in last_error and shown in the message log. A lost listen connection is logged once and polling continues.

Technical references: backend/src/notifications/delivery/notification-relay.service.ts · NotificationRelayService · notification-dispatcher.service.ts · NotificationDispatcher · in-app.provider.ts · dev-log.provider.ts · channel-provider.registry.ts · notifications-runtime.module.ts

Figure 44.6 — A lab member accepts an order and the ordering doctor sees it behind the bell.

The diagram has seven participants: Lab member, API, NotificationService, PostgreSQL, Notification relay (worker), In-app provider and Doctor web app. The Lab member asks the API to accept a lab order. In the same transaction the API calls NotificationService, which reads settings, rules and templates, inserts outbox rows and issues a database notify. The API then commits. The commit wakes the relay (or its two-second poll), which claims due rows with a skip-locked update, hands each row to the In-app provider, which inserts one inbox row per outbox row, and the relay marks the outbox row sent. Separately, the Doctor web app asks the API for the unread count every 30 seconds and shows it on the bell.

44.3.5 Choose who is notified (master switches and rules)

Status: [Implemented]

What it does. The clinic admin switches an audience on or off and turns individual event rules on or off.

How the user does it.

  1. Open Settings → Notifications, tab Team & labs.
  2. Use the switch on an audience card to turn the whole audience on or off.
  3. In the Events table, use the switch in the audience and channel column of an event.

Behind the scenes — in simple terms. A switch the admin never touched uses the default (internal on, patient off). Mandatory events keep their in-app switch locked on. Only in-app switches appear, because the other channels are not offered to any audience.

Behind the scenes — technically. GET /notification-settings returns audiences, events with their rules (defaults filled in, isDefault, locked), channelsByAudience and languages. PATCH /notification-settings/audiences/:audience (body isEnabled, quietStart, quietEnd, timezone) upserts notification_audience_settings under a pessimistic_write row lock. PUT /notification-settings/rules takes 1–500 {eventCode, audience, channel, isEnabled} changes and upserts notification_rules, skipping unchanged ones and returning {changed}. Both write an audit entry in the same transaction (notification_audience_setting, notification_rule).

Rules and validations.

  • The event must exist, include the audience, and the audience must be reachable on the channel (NOTIFICATION_EVENT_UNKNOWN, NOTIFICATION_AUDIENCE_INVALID, NOTIFICATION_CHANNEL_INVALID).
  • Switching a locked mandatory in-app rule off is refused with NOTIFICATION_RULE_LOCKED; switching it on is accepted and ignored.
  • Audience must be one of patient, doctor, coordinator, lab.

Who can do it. notifications.settings.manage (feature core, no scope); Admin by default. No feature key.

Data read and written. notification_events, notification_audience_settings, notification_rules, audit_logs.

Effects on other modules. Changes apply to the next event raised by any module.

Error cases. The codes above, all HTTP 422; 403 without the permission.

Technical references: backend/src/notifications/controllers/notification-settings.controller.ts · NotificationSettingsService.overview, updateAudience, updateRules · web-app/src/features/notifications/pages/NotificationSettingsPage.tsx, components/AudienceSwitchCard.tsx, EventRulesTable.tsx, RuleSwitch.tsx

44.3.6 Set quiet hours

Status: [Partial]

What it does. Lets an audience have a daily window in which messages are held. The setting is saved and applied by the decision step, but it has no visible effect today, because quiet hours never hold in-app messages and in-app is the only channel in use.

How the user does it.

  1. On an audience card, click Quiet hours.
  2. Switch on "Use quiet hours", set the start and "Until" times, and optionally a timezone.
  3. Save.

Behind the scenes — in simple terms. The window may cross midnight (22:00 to 08:00). Without a timezone, the location's own timezone is used. A held message is released when the window ends.

Behind the scenes — technically. Same endpoint as 44.3.5. quietHoursEnd(now, quiet) compares local HH:MM and returns the end instant, or null outside the window; start equal to end means no window. A held row has status held_quiet_hours and scheduled_for set to the end.

Rules and validations. Times are 24-hour HH:MM. Start and end are required together (NOTIFICATION_QUIET_HOURS_INVALID), they must differ, and a non-empty timezone must be a valid IANA zone. Without a location, UTC is used.

Who can do it. notifications.settings.manage.

Data read and written. notification_audience_settings.

Effects on other modules. None today.

Error cases. NOTIFICATION_QUIET_HOURS_INVALID (422): one time missing, equal times, or unknown timezone.

Technical references: NotificationSettingsService.updateAudience · decision/notification-decision.ts · web-app/src/features/notifications/components/QuietHoursSheet.tsx, hooks/useQuietHoursForm.ts

44.3.7 Edit message wording in several languages

Status: [Implemented]

What it does. Lets the clinic replace the platform text of an event, per channel and language (English, Urdu, Roman Urdu).

How the user does it.

  1. In the Events table, click the edit-wording icon on a row.
  2. Pick a channel and a language.
  3. Edit the title and message, using placeholders such as {clinic_name}.
  4. Save, or choose Reset to return to the platform text.

Behind the scenes — in simple terms. The platform keeps default wording for each event. A clinic's own wording overrides it for that clinic only. The page shows the placeholders the event allows. Resetting deletes the clinic's own text.

Behind the scenes — technically. GET /notification-settings/templates?eventCode returns platform rows (organization null) and the clinic's (isOverride). PUT /notification-settings/templates upserts by organization, event, channel and language under a row lock, and stores the placeholders used. DELETE /notification-settings/templates/:id clears notification_rules.template_id values that point to it, deletes the row and audits a void. Platform defaults are seeded on boot, insert-if-missing, under an advisory lock.

Rules and validations. Body required, at most 1 000 characters; subject at most 200; template reference at most 200. Every {placeholder} must be a common one (clinic_name, recipient_name) or one of the event's variables (NOTIFICATION_TEMPLATE_INVALID lists the unknown ones). The channel must be one the event's audiences can use.

Who can do it. notifications.settings.manage.

Data read and written. notification_templates, notification_rules, audit_logs.

Effects on other modules. Changes the text of future messages only; existing inbox rows keep the text they were created with.

Error cases. NOTIFICATION_TEMPLATE_INVALID, NOTIFICATION_TEMPLATE_NOT_FOUND (404 on reset), NOTIFICATION_CHANNEL_INVALID, NOTIFICATION_EVENT_UNKNOWN.

Technical references: NotificationSettingsService.templates, upsertTemplate, resetTemplate · templates/template-render.ts · seeds/notification-seed.service.ts · web-app/src/features/notifications/components/TemplateSheet.tsx, hooks/useTemplateForm.ts

44.3.8 Review the message log

Status: [Implemented]

What it does. Shows every notification the clinic generated, with status, reason and error.

How the user does it.

  1. Open Settings → Notifications → Message log.
  2. Search by recipient name, address or text, and filter by status or channel.
  3. Page through results.

Behind the scenes — in simple terms. Skipped and held messages are listed too, so an admin can see why someone was not told.

Behind the scenes — technically. GET /notification-settings/log?page&limit&status&eventCode&channel&audience&search (limit 1–100, default 20) over notification_outbox for the active organization, newest first. Search matches recipient name, address or body inside the JSON payload. Rows expose status, reason, attempts, last_error, sent_at and the cause entity.

Rules and validations. Status, channel and audience must be valid enum values.

Who can do it. notifications.settings.manage.

Data read and written. Reads notification_outbox.

Effects on other modules. None.

44.3.9 Record a patient's messaging opt-outs and language

Status: [Partial]

What it does. Stores whether a patient has opted out of WhatsApp, SMS or email and their preferred message language. The backend works and the decision step honours it. No screen is reachable: the card that would show it is commented out in the patient page while notifications are in-app only.

How the user does it. Not available in the web app. The component PatientMessagesCard exists but is not rendered.

Behind the scenes — in simple terms. If a patient opts out of a channel, messages on that channel are recorded as skipped. The first time any opt-out is switched on, the time is stored.

44.3.10 Notify through a workflow transition

Status: [Partial]

What it does. A workflow transition can carry a notify effect that raises an event inside the transition's transaction. The effect and the recipient registry are built, but the shipped lab code paths raise their events directly through the service, and the repository contains no transition definition that uses the effect.

How the user does it. A workflow author adds the effect with the event code (and optionally a narrower list of audiences) in the Config Studio.

Behind the scenes — in simple terms. The engine does not know any table. Each module registers how to find the doctor, lab and patient of its own record type.

Behind the scenes — technically. NotifyEffect (code notify) validates params.event and params.audiences, looks up the resolver for request.entityType in NotificationRecipientsRegistry, and calls enqueue with the resolved recipients. A missing resolver or malformed params raises WORKFLOW_MISCONFIGURED. The lab-order workflow registers its resolver.

Rules and validations. Unknown event codes fail the transition.

Who can do it. Whoever may perform the transition.

Data read and written. notification_outbox.

Effects on other modules. The Workflow engine chapter (Chapter 43) describes effects.

Error cases. WORKFLOW_MISCONFIGURED; NOTIFICATION_EVENT_UNKNOWN.

44.3.11 Send to patients by WhatsApp, SMS or email

Status: [Not implemented]

What it does. Nothing reaches a patient. Patients have no in-app inbox, and the audience-to-channel table gives the patient audience no channels (WhatsApp and SMS are commented out). No patient row is ever queued. The WhatsApp, SMS and email code path exists only as a development stand-in that writes a log line. The seeded events addressed to patients (such as "Payment receipt") are recorded in the catalog, but produce no patient message.

How the user does it. Not available. The Patients tab on the settings page is commented out.

Behind the scenes — technically. CHANNELS_BY_AUDIENCE[patient] is empty; DevLogChannelProvider covers the three channels but would only log. No real provider is registered. The WhatsApp template ID field in the wording sheet is stored but never used.

Rules and validations. None active.

Who can do it. Not applicable.

Data read and written. None.

Effects on other modules. Lab events that list the patient audience produce no patient message.

44.4 Entities and data model

Figure 44.7 — The notification tables and the tables around them.

The diagram shows seven notification tables and three neighbours. notification_events (key code, audiences, is_mandatory_internal, variables) is the catalog. notification_rules (organization, event, audience, channel, is_enabled, optional template) holds one on/off decision per event, audience and channel. notification_templates holds wording per event, channel and language; organization_id is null for platform defaults. notification_audience_settings holds one row per organization and audience with the master switch and quiet hours. notification_outbox records every message decision per recipient and channel. user_notifications is the inbox copy. patient_comm_prefs holds a patient's opt-outs and language. organizations, users and patients are the owners.

The relationships in words:

  • Audience settings and rules belong to one organization; deleting the organization deletes them (ON DELETE CASCADE). A rule is unique per organization, event, audience and channel; a setting is unique per organization and audience.
  • Each rule and each template points to exactly one event; an event cannot be deleted while they exist (RESTRICT).
  • A rule may point to one template for custom wording. Deleting the template sets the rule's pointer to NULL.
  • A template belongs to an organization or to nobody (platform default). Deleting the organization deletes its templates.
  • Each outbox row belongs to one organization and one event, both RESTRICT. Its recipient is a user, a patient or a lab, identified by recipient_type and recipient_id. These are logical links with no foreign key.
  • An outbox row has at most one inbox row (outbox_id is unique, RESTRICT). Each inbox row belongs to one user; deleting the user deletes their inbox.
  • Each patient has at most one preferences row; deleting the patient deletes it.

Key outbox columns: audience, recipient_type, channel, status, scheduled_for, attempts (5 at most), provider_message_id, last_error, sent_at, entity_type and entity_id (what caused it) and a payload JSON (title, body, link, language, address, reason). A partial index covers rows with status queued or held. Identifiers are time-ordered UUID v7. Settings, rules, templates and preferences use a version column.

44.5 Status lifecycles

Figure 44.8 — Lifecycle of a notification_outbox row.

An outbox row starts in one of five states, chosen by the decision step at enqueue time. queued means it is due for the worker. held_quiet_hours means it must wait for the end of quiet hours (scheduled_for is set to that moment). skipped_disabled means the audience or the rule was off. skipped_opt_out means the patient opted out. failed at creation means the recipient had no phone number or email address. A skipped or failed row is final. A held row becomes eligible when its time arrives, and the worker claims it just as it claims a queued row. From queued, a successful send moves the row to sent. A transient error keeps it queued with a later scheduled_for (30 s, 2 min, 10 min, 1 h). A permanent error, or the fifth attempt, moves it to failed. The status delivered exists in the enum and in the web labels, but no code sets it, so it is never reached.

Figure 44.9 — Read state of a user_notifications row.

An inbox row is created unread when the in-app provider delivers an outbox row. It becomes read, by setting read_at, either when one notification is marked read or when all are marked read. There is no way back to unread and no deletion.

44.6 Connections to other modules

All current emitters are in the lab modules. The 21 seeded events and who raises them:

Event Audiences Raised by
order.submitted lab (mandatory) lab-orders, order submit
order.accepted doctor, coordinator lab-access, order actions
order.rejected, order.clarification_requested, order.expected_date_changed doctor, coordinator (mandatory) lab-access, order actions
order.magic_link lab lab-access, magic links
item.ready doctor, coordinator, patient lab-production, lab work
stage.sent_to_clinic doctor, coordinator lab-production, shipments
stage.approved, stage.correction lab lab-production, clinic production
shipment.received lab lab-production, shipments
shipment.lost lab, doctor (mandatory) lab-production, shipments
remake.requested lab (mandatory) lab-production, workflow
remake.agreed lab (mandatory) lab-production, clinic production
order.completed doctor, patient lab-billing, when an order reaches completed
payment.receipt patient lab-billing, lab payments
payment.outstanding_reminder patient lab-billing, lab invoices, on request
order.overdue, shipment.dispatched, tryin.appointment_due, appointment.rescheduled_lab_delay various no emitter found

The table groups the events by emitter. Every audience listed as patient produces no message today (44.3.11). The events with no emitter exist only in the catalog. Billing for clinic treatments (the Billing chapter, Chapter 34) raises no notification at all: the two "payment" events belong to lab patient invoices. Lab members receive messages as users in the audience lab, except the magic-link event, which is addressed to the lab itself. The Dental lab chapter (Chapter 40) and the Lab portal chapter (Chapter 41) describe the screens that trigger them. The Notification mechanics chapter (Chapter 59) covers the cross-cutting design. Notification settings changes are audited (the Audit logging chapter, Chapter 60). The Patients chapter (Chapter 28) owns the patient page where the messaging card is hidden.

44.7 Limitations and known gaps

  • Only the in-app channel works. WhatsApp, SMS and email are not delivered, and the patient audience has no channel.
  • Appointment reminders do not exist.
  • Four seeded events have no emitter; billing for clinic treatments emits nothing.
  • The status delivered is never set.
  • The patient opt-out screen is hidden, so the opt-out backend cannot be used from the web app.
  • Quiet hours are saved but cannot hold any message today.
  • The inbox updates by 30-second polling, not by live push, and the bell shows only the latest 20.
  • No sidebar entry; the settings page is reached only from Settings.
  • Feature keys comms.in_app and comms.whatsapp do not control anything.
  • Delivery needs the worker process. Without it, messages stay queued.
  • The inbox has no delete and no mark-as-unread.

44.8 Owner's FAQ

Can I message patients about appointments? No. No patient channel is active and there is no reminder event.

A doctor says they never got a lab notification. Where do I look? Open Settings → Notifications → Message log, search for the doctor, and read the status and reason. Check that the doctor's audience is switched on and that the doctor has a staff login linked to the employee record.

Can I switch off a notification? Optional events yes, using the event table. Events marked Mandatory (for example a rejected order) cannot be switched off in-app.

Who can change notification settings? Users with notifications.settings.manage, which is the Admin role by default, and the owner.

What happens if a business action fails after a message was queued? The message disappears with the rolled-back transaction, because it is written in the same transaction.

Will a message be sent twice? Delivery is at-least-once, but the inbox copy is unique per outbox row, so the user sees it once.

Can I change the wording? Yes, per event, channel and language, using only the placeholders the editor allows. Reset returns the platform text.

Where are messages stored? In notification_outbox (the record of every decision) and user_notifications (the inbox).

Is it live? The bell updates every 30 seconds and on window focus, not instantly.

Chapter 45 — Subscriptions and Onboarding

This chapter describes how a new clinic joins the Platform and how its right to keep using the Platform is tracked. It covers self-signup, email verification, the one-time setup wizard, the 14-day trial, plan limits, the read-only mode that starts after a subscription runs out, and the super admin screens that record manual payments. It is written for the product owner, who needs to know what a clinic sees, what the backend enforces and where the gaps are.

45.1 What this module is for

A subscription is the clinic's permission to use the Platform for a period of time under a plan. Plans are defined in code, not in a table. Nothing charges the clinic automatically: the clinic pays by bank transfer, JazzCash or similar, and a super admin records the payment by hand, which extends the period.

Onboarding is the path from "I found the Platform" to "my clinic is set up". A visitor creates an account and a clinic in one step, starts a 14-day trial on the Professional plan, and then completes a three-step setup wizard.

Who uses it:

  • Visitor, then owner: registers, verifies the email address, completes the wizard and watches the trial.
  • Owner: opens "Plan & billing" to see the plan, usage and payment history. Only the owner (or a super admin) can use the setup and plan screens. Other staff see only the warning banners.
  • Super admin: lists every clinic's subscription, changes plan, dates and limits, records payments and edits the payment instructions text.

Where it appears: the super admin sidebar item Subscriptions (key nav.subscriptions, route /subscriptions, super admin only). Owners reach Plan & billing from Settings (route /settings/subscription), where the link is shown to owners only. /register, /verify-email and /setup have no sidebar entry.

Permissions and feature keys: none. These endpoints are @AnyMember() with an owner check in code, @Public(), or @RequireSuperAdmin(). There is no feature key.

45.3 Features

45.3.1 Sign up and create a clinic

Status: [Implemented]

What it does. Creates the owner's login, the clinic (organization), its first location and the ownership link in one step, starts a 14-day trial and signs the owner in.

How the user does it.

  1. Open /register.
  2. Fill in clinic name, full name, email, phone (optional) and password.
  3. Submit. The app signs the owner in and opens the setup wizard.

Behind the scenes — in simple terms. The clinic is ready to use at once. It starts on the Professional plan for 14 days, with PKR and the Asia/Karachi timezone as starting values, and is marked "onboarding pending" until the wizard is finished. If clinic creation fails, the new login is removed so no orphan account is left behind.

Behind the scenes — technically. POST /auth/register (@Public, rate limit 5 per hour) runs AuthService.register: UserService.createLocalUser, then ClinicSetupService.createClinicForOwner in one transaction. The transaction creates the organization (slug from the clinic name, with a random suffix on collision; plan TRIAL_PLAN = professional; trial_ends_at = now + TRIAL_DAYS (14); onboarding_pending = true), a location with code MAIN and is_main_branch, its settings row and the primary ownership row. After the commit, FeatureFlagsService.seedFlagsForOrg and AccessTemplatesService.seedForOrg seed feature switches and the five system roles; a failure there is only logged. A verification email is then sent and the user is signed in through login() with a 30-day session.

Rules and validations. Email must be valid; name and clinic name are required (at most 255); password at least 6 characters; phone at most 20.

Who can do it. Anyone, no account needed (a public route, also listed in PUBLIC_ROUTES).

Data read and written. Writes users, organizations, locations, location_settings, organization_ownership, and, after commit, feature-flag and role tables.

Effects on other modules. The new clinic gets the default features and roles (Chapters 10 and 11).

Error cases. A duplicate email is rejected by user creation; more than 5 attempts per hour is rate limited; any clinic-creation error returns the error and deletes the new user.

Technical references: backend/src/auth/auth.service.ts · AuthService.register · backend/src/subscriptions/clinic-setup.service.ts · ClinicSetupService.createClinicForOwner · web-app/src/routes/register.tsx, web-app/src/features/auth/components/RegisterForm.tsx

Figure 45.8 — From sign-up to a verified, set-up clinic.

The diagram has six participants: Owner, Web app, API, ClinicSetupService, PostgreSQL and SMTP mail. The Owner fills the "Create your clinic" form and the Web app posts to the API. The API creates the user, then asks ClinicSetupService to create the clinic, which writes the organization, the MAIN location, its settings and the ownership in one transaction and, after the commit, seeds feature flags and system roles. The API sends the verification link by email (a failure is only logged) and returns a signed-in 30-day session. The Web app moves the Owner to /setup. The Owner completes the Clinic step and the Location and tax step, which the Web app saves with two PATCH calls, then finishes on the Your team step, which posts to /account/setup/complete and clears the pending flag. Separately, the Owner opens the link from the email; the Web app posts the token to the API, which stores the verification time and clears the token.

45.3.2 Verify the email address and resend the link

Status: [Partial]

What it does. Sends a link to the new owner's email and confirms the address when the link is opened. Verification is informational: nothing is blocked while the email is unverified.

How the user does it.

  1. After signing up, read the banner "Please verify your email".
  2. Open the link in the email, which lands on /verify-email.
  3. If the link is lost or expired, click Resend link in the banner.

Behind the scenes — in simple terms. The email contains a one-time random token. The server stores only a fingerprint of it, valid for 48 hours. A new link replaces the old one. The banner shows while a token is still waiting.

Behind the scenes — technically. sendVerificationEmail creates 32 random bytes, stores the SHA-256 hash in users.email_verification_token with email_verification_expires = now + 48 h, and calls MailService.sendEmailVerification, which builds <frontend URL>/verify-email?token=… and sends through SMTP (environment variables SMTP_USER, SMTP_PASS and FRONTEND_URL). POST /auth/verify-email (@Public, 10 per 15 minutes) hashes the token, finds an unexpired match, sets email_verified_at and clears the token. POST /auth/resend-verification (signed in, @ContextFree, 3 per hour) sends a fresh link, or answers "Email already verified" when no token is pending. The user DTO exposes emailVerificationPending (token present), which drives the banner.

Rules and validations. Token valid for 48 hours; single use. Partial because no feature or screen is gated by email_verified_at, and a failed email send is only logged, so the user sees success.

Who can do it. Anyone with the link (verify); any signed-in user (resend).

Data read and written. users (email_verification_token, email_verification_expires, email_verified_at).

Effects on other modules. None; sign-in does not require verification.

Error cases. "This verification link is invalid or has expired" (validation error) when the token is unknown or expired; 429 when rate limited; toast "Could not send the email. Try again." when resend fails.

Technical references: backend/src/auth/auth.service.ts · verifyEmail, resendVerification · backend/src/common/services/mail.service.ts · MailService · web-app/src/routes/verify-email.tsx, web-app/src/features/account/pages/VerifyEmailPage.tsx, components/AccountBanner.tsx

45.3.3 Complete the setup wizard

Status: [Implemented]

What it does. Collects the clinic's real details in three steps and then clears the "onboarding pending" flag.

How the user does it.

  1. After signing up, the app opens /setup. Until it is finished, an owner who opens any other page is sent back to /setup.
  2. Step Clinic: name, clinic types, phone, email, timezone, currency. Save and continue.
  3. Step Location & tax: location name, address, city, phone, email and the sales tax percentage. Save and continue.
  4. Step Your team: read the hints, then finish. The app refreshes the session and opens the home page.

Behind the scenes — in simple terms. The first two steps save immediately. The finish button only flips the flag; it does not check the earlier steps were saved. Saving the clinic step copies the timezone and currency to every location of the clinic, because a new clinic's branches follow the clinic.

Behind the scenes — technically. GET /account/setup returns the main location (first active by is_main_branch DESC, created_at ASC). PATCH /account/setup/clinic (SetupClinicDto: name, phone, email, website, specialtyTags from CLINIC_SPECIALTIES, timezone, currency upper-cased) runs saveClinic in a transaction, updating the organization and every location. PATCH /account/setup/location runs saveLocation in a transaction, updating the main location and its settings, with taxRate 0–100. POST /account/setup/complete sets onboarding_pending to false. All four are @AnyMember() and call assertOwner. Setup writes are on the always-writable path list, so an expired clinic can still finish setup.

Rules and validations.

  • Owner or super admin only.
  • Email must be valid; tax 0–100; clinic types must come from the fixed list; timezone is free text and is not checked against the IANA list.
  • Currency is upper-cased.

Who can do it. The owner or a super admin; no permission key, no feature key.

Data read and written. Reads and writes organizations, locations, location_settings; reads organization_ownership.

Effects on other modules. Timezone and currency drive clinic times and money display everywhere (Chapter 62). Tax rate is added to patient invoices (Chapter 34). Clinic types decide which tools show.

Error cases. 403 "Only the clinic owner can do this"; validation errors per field; toast "Could not save. Try again."

Technical references: backend/src/subscriptions/account.controller.ts · AccountController · clinic-setup.service.ts · ClinicSetupService.saveClinic, saveLocation, complete · web-app/src/routes/setup.tsx, web-app/src/features/account/pages/SetupWizardPage.tsx, hooks/useSetupForms.ts

45.3.4 Trial, plans and plan limits

Status: [Implemented]

What it does. Gives each managed clinic a plan with limits on locations and logins, and refuses to exceed them.

How the user does it. The owner opens Settings → Plan & billing to see the plan, the usage bars and the plan catalog. Reaching a limit shows the error when adding a location or a login.

Behind the scenes — in simple terms. Four plans exist. A clinic with no trial date and no paid date is called unmanaged: it has no limits and never expires (older clinics and clinics created by a super admin). A limit set on the clinic itself wins over the plan's limit.

Plan Price per month (PKR) Locations Logins
Free 0 1 2
Starter 4 999 1 5
Professional 9 999 3 15
Enterprise custom unlimited unlimited

The table lists the plan catalog from code. Prices are only what the clinic sees; nothing bills them. A "login" is an owner plus any employee with portal access.

Behind the scenes — technically. PLANS in plans.ts. effectiveLimits(org) returns org.maxLocations ?? plan.maxLocations and likewise for users, and none for unmanaged clinics. assertCanAddLocation and assertCanAddUser compare against usage() (active locations; owners plus active staff with a user_id) and throw PlanLimitException (code PLAN_LIMIT). GET /account returns the summary, usage and, for owners, the plans, payment instructions and payments. Location creation calls the check for non-super-admins; login creation calls it from the user service.

Rules and validations. Limits are skipped for super admins and unmanaged clinics.

Who can do it. Any member reads the summary; owners also get plans and payments. Writes happen when locations or logins are added.

Data read and written. Reads organizations, locations, employee_org_location_assignments, organization_ownership, subscription_payments, config_values.

Effects on other modules. Locations (Chapter 9) and Employees (Chapter 37) are blocked at the limit.

Error cases. PLAN_LIMIT (HTTP 403): "Your Professional plan allows 3 locations. Upgrade your plan to add more." or "… allows 15 logins. …".

Technical references: backend/src/subscriptions/plans.ts · PLANS, TRIAL_PLAN, TRIAL_DAYS · subscription-state.ts · effectiveLimits · subscriptions.service.ts · SubscriptionsService.usage, assertCanAddLocation, assertCanAddUser · web-app/src/routes/settings_.subscription.tsx, web-app/src/features/account/pages/SubscriptionPage.tsx

45.3.5 Read-only mode after expiry

Status: [Implemented]

What it does. When a clinic's period and its grace days have passed, every write is refused until a payment is recorded. Reading still works, so the clinic keeps its data.

How the user does it. Staff see the red banner and a rejected save. The owner pays and the super admin records it (45.3.7).

Behind the scenes — in simple terms. The period end is the later of the trial end and the paid-until date. After that there are 3 grace days with a warning, then the clinic becomes read-only. The decision is cached for 30 seconds per server process, so a renewal can take up to 30 seconds to be seen.

Behind the scenes — technically. SubscriptionGuard is the last global guard. It lets GET, HEAD and OPTIONS pass; skips @Public routes and super admins; lets paths starting with /auth/, /account, /me/ and /admin/subscriptions through; resolves the organization from the access context or the x-organization-id header; and calls SubscriptionsService.isReadOnly, a 30 s cache over subscriptionState(). When read-only it throws HTTP 402 with code SUBSCRIPTION_EXPIRED. Requests with no organization pass.

Rules and validations. GRACE_DAYS = 3. Unmanaged clinics are never read-only.

Who can do it. Applies to every user except super admins.

Data read and written. Reads organizations (trial_ends_at, paid_until).

Effects on other modules. Every module's write endpoints are blocked, including the queue and billing. Realtime reads are unaffected.

Error cases. HTTP 402 SUBSCRIPTION_EXPIRED: "Your subscription has expired — the clinic is read-only until it is renewed."

Technical references: backend/src/subscriptions/subscription.guard.ts · SubscriptionGuard · subscriptions.service.ts · isReadOnly · web-app/src/features/account/components/AccountBanner.tsx

45.3.6 See subscription status and warnings

Status: [Implemented]

What it does. Shows owners and staff where the subscription stands and warns before it runs out.

How the user does it. The banner appears automatically. Owners open Plan & billing for detail.

Behind the scenes — in simple terms. The status is never stored. It is worked out every time from the two dates and the current time.

Behind the scenes — technically. subscriptionState(org, now) returns status, periodEndsAt, readOnlyFrom, daysLeft and readOnly. Rules: no dates means unmanaged; paid_until in the future means active; else trial_ends_at in the future means trialing; else before period end plus 3 days means grace; else expired. AccountBanner reads GET /account and shows the matching message; owners see trial and renewal messages, everyone sees grace and expiry.

Rules and validations. The status rules are the ones in the technical paragraph.

Who can do it. Any signed-in member sees the banner for their clinic.

Data read and written. Reads organizations.

Effects on other modules. None.

Error cases. The banner is simply absent if the account request fails.

Technical references: backend/src/subscriptions/subscription-state.ts · subscriptionState · web-app/src/features/account/components/AccountBanner.tsx, hooks/useAccount.ts

45.3.7 Record a manual payment (super admin)

Status: [Implemented]

What it does. Records a payment the clinic made outside the Platform and extends the paid period.

How the user does it.

  1. As a super admin, open Subscriptions in the sidebar.
  2. Click Manage subscription on the clinic's row.
  3. On the Record payment tab, pick the plan, months paid, amount, method, date, reference and notes.
  4. Save. A toast says "Payment recorded — the plan is extended".

Behind the scenes — in simple terms. The new period starts where the current trial or paid period ends, so paying early loses no days. Recording a payment also sets the clinic's plan to the plan paid for, so paying for Starter during a Professional trial lowers the limits at once.

Behind the scenes — technically. POST /admin/subscriptions/:orgId/payments (RecordSubscriptionPaymentDto) runs SubscriptionsService.recordPayment in a transaction: locks the organization row, computes nextPaidPeriod(org, months, now), inserts a subscription_payments row with period_start and period_end, sets paid_until to the period end and subscription_plan to the payment's plan, writes audit entries and clears the read-only cache.

Rules and validations. Plan in the enum; months 1–36; amount at least 0 with 2 decimals; method one of bank_transfer, jazzcash, easypaisa, cash, cheque, other; reference at most 120; notes at most 1 000; date optional.

Who can do it. Super admin only (@RequireSuperAdmin() on the controller). No feature key.

Data read and written. Writes subscription_payments, organizations, audit_logs.

Effects on other modules. Lifts read-only mode; changes the plan limits.

Error cases. 404 "Organization not found"; 400 validation errors; 403 for non-super-admins.

Technical references: backend/src/subscriptions/admin-subscriptions.controller.ts · AdminSubscriptionsController.recordPayment · subscriptions.service.ts · recordPayment · entities/subscription-payment.entity.ts · web-app/src/routes/subscriptions.tsx, web-app/src/features/account/components/ManageSubscriptionSheet.tsx

45.3.8 Change a clinic's plan, dates or limits (super admin)

Status: [Implemented]

What it does. Lets a super admin set the plan, trial end, paid-until date and per-clinic location and login limits directly.

How the user does it.

  1. Open Subscriptions, click Manage subscription on a row, choose the Plan & limits tab.
  2. Change fields and save. A toast says "Subscription updated".

Behind the scenes — in simple terms. Moving the trial date extends a trial. Clearing both dates makes the clinic unmanaged (no limits, no expiry).

Behind the scenes — technically. PATCH /admin/subscriptions/:orgId (UpdateSubscriptionDto) runs update under a pessimistic_write lock, records an audit entry with before and after values (organization_subscription) and clears the cache. GET /admin/subscriptions lists clinics (including inactive ones) with derived state, and GET /admin/subscriptions/:orgId returns one clinic with its payments.

Rules and validations. Dates are ISO strings or null; limits are integers of at least 1 or null.

Who can do it. Super admin only.

Data read and written. organizations, audit_logs; reads subscription_payments.

Effects on other modules. Same as 45.3.4 and 45.3.5.

Error cases. 404 for an unknown clinic; 400 on invalid values.

Technical references: AdminSubscriptionsController.list, get, update · SubscriptionsService.update · web-app/src/features/account/pages/AdminSubscriptionsPage.tsx, hooks/useAdminSubscriptionForms.ts

45.3.9 Edit the payment instructions (super admin)

Status: [Implemented]

What it does. Sets the text every clinic owner sees under "How to pay".

How the user does it. On the Subscriptions page, edit the "Payment instructions" card and save ("Payment instructions saved").

Behind the scenes — in simple terms. One text for the whole Platform, with a built-in default asking the clinic to pay by bank transfer or JazzCash and share the receipt with support.

Behind the scenes — technically. GET and PUT /admin/subscriptions/payment-instructions (PaymentInstructionsDto, at most 2 000 characters) through the settings registry key subscription.payment_instructions at platform scope. The route is declared before :orgId.

Rules and validations. At most 2 000 characters; platform scope only; not lockable.

Who can do it. Super admin only.

Data read and written. config_values.

Effects on other modules. None.

Error cases. Toast "Could not save. Try again."

Technical references: backend/src/subscriptions/subscription.settings.ts · SUBSCRIPTION_SETTINGS · SubscriptionsService.setPaymentInstructions

45.3.10 Create a clinic from the Organizations screen (older path)

Status: [Partial]

What it does. A super admin can create or edit an organization on the Organizations screen. The result is an unmanaged clinic with no owner, no location and no trial. The plan selector on that screen is broken: it sends uppercase values the API rejects.

How the user does it. Super admin, Organizations screen, create or edit dialog.

Behind the scenes — technically. The form offers FREE, BASIC, PREMIUM and ENTERPRISE and sends them as the subscriptionPlan. The DTO validates against the SubscriptionPlan enum, whose values are lowercase free, starter, professional and enterprise. So every uppercase value fails validation, and BASIC and PREMIUM are not plans at all. This was verified by reading both files; the app was not run. The plan is optional in the DTO, so a request that omits it would pass. Plan changes made here are not audited, unlike changes through the Subscriptions screen.

Rules and validations. @IsEnum(SubscriptionPlan) on create and update.

Who can do it. Super admin.

Data read and written. organizations.

Effects on other modules. None.

Error cases. HTTP 400 with a message that subscriptionPlan must be one of the enum values.

Technical references: backend/src/organizations/dto/organization.dto.ts · subscriptionPlan · web-app/src/features/organizations/OrganizationManagementView.tsx · backend/docs/modules/01-organizations-locations.md

45.4 Entities and data model

Figure 45.9 — The tables behind subscriptions and sign-up.

The diagram shows seven tables. users carries the email verification columns (email_verification_token, email_verified_at). organizations carries the subscription columns: subscription_plan, trial_ends_at, paid_until, max_locations (and a login limit) and onboarding_pending. organization_ownership links a user to an organization. locations has a code and an is_main_branch flag. location_settings holds the tax rate. subscription_payments records each manual payment. employee_org_location_assignments is read to count logins.

The relationships in words:

  • Each ownership row links one user to one organization; deleting either deletes the row (ON DELETE CASCADE). A clinic created through signup has one primary owner.
  • Each location belongs to one organization (CASCADE). Signup creates the first one with code MAIN.
  • Each location has at most one settings row.
  • Each payment belongs to one organization; deleting the organization deletes its payments (CASCADE). The organization has many payments over time.
  • Login usage is counted from owners plus active assignments that have a user; this is a read, not a link.

Key subscription_payments columns: plan, months, amount (numeric, 2 decimals), method, reference, paid_at, period_start, period_end, notes and recorded_by. Plan definitions are not stored; they live in plans.ts. The subscription status is not stored either.

45.5 Status lifecycles

Figure 45.10 — Derived subscription status.

A clinic is unmanaged when created by a super admin (no dates), and trialing when created by signup. Trialing becomes active when a payment is recorded, or grace when the trial end passes. Active becomes grace when paid_until passes. Grace lasts 3 days and then becomes expired; a recorded payment returns it to active. Expired is read-only, and a recorded payment returns it to active. A super admin can move an unmanaged clinic to active (payment) or trialing (set a future trial end), and can send an active or expired clinic back to unmanaged by clearing both dates. A future trial end also moves an expired clinic back to trialing. Status is computed on read, so these changes happen as time passes, not through a job.

Figure 45.11 — The onboarding_pending flag.

A signup creates the organization as pending. POST /account/setup/complete sets it to done. An organization created by a super admin starts as done. There is no way back to pending.

45.6 Connections to other modules

  • Authentication (Chapter 56) owns register, verify and resend, and the 30-day session after signup.
  • Organizations and locations (Chapter 9) and Features (Chapter 10): signup seeds feature switches and the five system roles (Chapter 11). Plan limits block adding locations and logins.
  • Employees (Chapter 37): adding a login counts against the login limit.
  • Billing (Chapter 34): the tax rate saved in the wizard applies to patient invoices.
  • Request lifecycle (Chapter 5) lists the five global guards; the subscription guard is the last.
  • Audit logging (Chapter 60): plan changes and payments are audited.
  • Time, money and numbering (Chapter 62): timezone and currency from the wizard.

45.7 Limitations and known gaps

  • Nothing charges clinics. Payments are recorded by hand, and there is no reminder email for renewals.
  • Email verification is not required for anything; a failed send is only logged.
  • A free-text timezone is accepted in the wizard without checking it against the IANA list.
  • The wizard's finish button does not check the earlier steps were saved.
  • Saving the clinic step overwrites timezone and currency on every location.
  • Recording a payment overwrites the plan, which can lower the limits.
  • The location limit is skipped when a super admin acts; unmanaged clinics have no limits.
  • Read-only state is cached for 30 seconds per server process.
  • The Organizations screen sends plan values the API rejects (45.3.10), and changes through it are not audited.

45.8 Owner's FAQ

What does a new clinic get? A 14-day trial on Professional (3 locations, 15 logins), one location called MAIN, default features and the five system roles.

What happens when the trial ends? The clinic has 3 grace days with a warning banner, then becomes read-only. Reads work, all saves are refused with SUBSCRIPTION_EXPIRED.

How does a clinic pay? Outside the Platform, by the method in the instructions text. A super admin then records the payment, which extends the period and lifts read-only mode.

Can an expired clinic still finish setup? Yes. Sign-in, /account (including setup), /me/ and /admin/subscriptions paths stay writable.

Can a clinic add a fourth branch on Professional? No. It gets PLAN_LIMIT unless a super admin raises its location limit.

Do users have to verify their email? No. The banner nags, but nothing is blocked.

Where is the status stored? Nowhere. It is derived from trial_ends_at and paid_until.

Can a super admin give a clinic unlimited access? Yes, by clearing both dates (unmanaged) or by setting Enterprise limits.

What if the verification email never arrives? The owner clicks Resend link (3 per hour). If SMTP is not configured, sending fails silently on the server and only a log line records it.

Part 6 — End-to-end workflows

Chapter 46 — Workflow: Onboarding a New Clinic

This chapter follows one new clinic from nothing to a clinic that is ready to receive patients. There are two ways in: the owner signs up alone, or a super admin creates the organization by hand. It is written for the product owner, who needs to know which steps are automatic, which need a super admin, and where the two paths differ. Each step names the module, its status and the chapter that explains it in full.

46.1 Who is involved

  • Owner: the person who runs the clinic business. On the self-signup path this person creates the clinic. On the other path an owner login is created for them.
  • Super admin: the Platform operator. Creates organizations by hand, entitles features, records payments and can act inside any clinic.
  • Example Clinic: the fictional organization used in this chapter, with a Main location.
  • Sample staff: employees added at the end (Chapter 47 covers staff onboarding).

46.2 The steps

Figure 46.1 shows both paths and the shared steps that follow them.

Figure 46.1 — Two ways to create a clinic, then the shared set-up steps.

The diagram has six participants from left to right: Owner, Super admin, Web app, API, PostgreSQL and SMTP mail. It has 22 numbered messages. A box labelled "alt" holds the two paths. In Path A (messages 1 to 7) the Owner fills the "Create your clinic" form, the Web app posts to POST /auth/register, and the API writes the user, the organization, the MAIN location, the ownership row, the feature rows, the system roles and a 14-day trial to PostgreSQL. The API sends a verification link through SMTP mail (a failure is only logged) and returns a signed-in 30-day session. The Owner then goes through the three-step setup wizard, and the Web app saves it with two PATCH calls and one POST that completes setup. In Path B (messages 8 to 15) the Super admin creates the organization from the Organizations screen; the API stores the organization, its feature rows and system roles but no owner, no location and no dates. The Super admin then creates a location, selects the organization and location, and creates a user of type Owner in User Admin, which writes the user and an ownership row. After the box, both paths continue: the Super admin entitles features (messages 16 to 18), the Owner switches features on (19 and 20), and the Owner sets up roles, locations, theme, navigation and employees (21 and 22).

Step 1a — Self-signup (Path A)

Module: Subscriptions and Onboarding. Status: [Implemented]. The visitor opens /register, enters clinic name, full name, email, an optional phone and a password. The Platform creates the owner login, the organization, one location with code MAIN, the ownership link, a 14-day trial on the Professional plan, the feature rows and the five system roles, then signs the owner in. Chapter 45 describes this in full: a visitor registers, and a trial starts at once.

Step 1b — Verify the email address

Module: Subscriptions and Onboarding. Status: [Partial]. The owner receives a link that is valid for 48 hours and opens /verify-email. Verification is informational: nothing is blocked while the address is unverified, and a failed email send is only logged. Chapter 45 and the Authentication chapter (Chapter 56) cover it.

Step 1c — Setup wizard

Module: Subscriptions and Onboarding. Status: [Implemented]. An owner whose setup is pending is sent to /setup from any other page. Step "Clinic" collects name, clinic types, phone, email, timezone and currency. Step "Location & tax" collects the main location's details and the sales tax percentage. Step "Your team" only explains that staff are added later; its finish button clears the pending flag without checking that the first two steps were saved. Saving the clinic step copies timezone and currency to every location of the clinic (Chapter 45).

Step 2 — Super admin creates the organization (Path B)

Module: Organizations and locations. Status: [Partial]. POST /organizations works, and it seeds the feature rows and the five system roles. The Organizations screen's form offers plan, clinic type, timezone and currency values that the API rejects, so a form filled with those fields fails with HTTP 400 (found by reading both files, not by running the app). The result is an unmanaged clinic: no owner, no location, no trial and no plan limits (Chapter 9 and Chapter 45).

Step 3 — Give the clinic a location and an owner (Path B)

Module: Organizations and locations, and User Admin. Status: [Partial]. A super admin adds a location from the Locations screen by choosing the organization. There is no field on the organization screen to name an owner. The code creates an owner login through User Admin with the account type "Owner", which uses the active organization from the request header. A super admin therefore has to select that organization and a location before creating the owner. This sequence is deduced from the code and was not run. Chapter 8 explains ownership; Chapter 56 explains User Admin.

Step 4 — Entitle features

Module: Features. Status: [Implemented]. A super admin opens "Manage features" for the clinic. Every feature has an Entitled switch, an optional trial end date and an Enabled switch; "Entitle module" acts on a whole module. The seeding at clinic creation sets entitled and enabled equal to each feature's default. Several features that clinics rely on are off by default and need this step: among them billing.invoices, billing.commissions, inventory.core, dental.lab_orders, reports.financial and reports.clinical. Without billing.invoices, completing a consultation creates no charges (Chapter 31). Chapter 10 covers the three switches.

Step 5 — Owner enables features

Module: Features. Status: [Implemented]. The owner opens Features (/admin/features) and switches on the features in the plan. A locked feature, which is not entitled or whose trial ended, cannot be switched on. Turning a feature off shows an impact list of the permissions and roles affected, and a location can switch a feature off for itself only (Chapter 10).

Step 6 — Roles

Module: Roles and permissions. Status: [Implemented]. The five system roles (Admin, Doctor, Receptionist, Assistant, Accountant) already exist. The owner may clone one or build a custom role at Roles & permissions (/admin/roles) with None, Basic or Full per module. System roles are read-only (Chapter 11).

Step 7 — Locations

Module: Organizations and locations. Status: [Implemented]. The owner adds further branches from Locations. The plan's location limit applies (Professional allows 3) and an expired subscription refuses the write. The edit screen for locations sends fields the API refuses, so changing a location afterwards may fail [Partial] (Chapter 9).

Step 8 — Theme and navigation

Module: Customization. Status: [Implemented]. At /admin/theme the owner sets the display name (default "Clinic Portal"), logos, favicon, brand colour (default a blue), sidebar style and default light, dark or system mode. A location may override the name and logos. At /admin/navigation the owner arranges the sidebar for the whole clinic. Both need their own permission (admin.theme.manage, admin.nav.manage). Changing the sidebar layout raises the access version; the theme save does not appear to (Chapter 58 covers customization; Chapter 54 describes how access changes spread).

Step 9 — Staff

Module: Employees. Status: [Implemented]. The owner or an Admin adds employees with roles and logins. Chapter 47 follows that workflow.

46.3 What can go wrong

  • Duplicate email at sign-up. User creation rejects it. If clinic creation fails after the user is created, the new user is deleted so no orphan account remains.
  • Rate limit. Registration is limited to 5 per hour, verification to 10 per 15 minutes and resend to 3 per hour.
  • Feature set after signup is smaller than expected. Features that are off by default must be entitled by a super admin. Clinics that have not been entitled for billing see no automatic charges.
  • Seeding failure. After the clinic is committed, seeding the feature rows and roles can fail; the failure is only logged, so a clinic can exist with no roles (Chapter 45).
  • Plan limit. Adding a fourth location on Professional gives PLAN_LIMIT.
  • Super admin path cannot be finished in one screen. Owner creation needs an organization context, which needs a location first.
  • Expired trial. After the trial and 3 grace days the clinic is read-only; setup and account paths stay writable (Chapter 53).

46.4 Data left behind

  • users: the owner login, with the email verification columns.
  • organizations: plan, trial_ends_at, onboarding_pending, access_version.
  • organization_ownership: one primary owner on Path A; one non-primary owner on Path B.
  • locations and location_settings: at least one location with the tax rate.
  • org_feature_flags (entitled and enabled per feature) and employment_roles (the five system roles).
  • config_values: theme settings. nav_layouts: the sidebar layout, if the owner saved one.
  • audit_logs: feature entitlement changes and nav layout changes.
  • Employees and assignments after Step 9.

Chapter 47 — Workflow: Onboarding a Staff Member

This chapter follows one new staff member, Dr. Example One, from the first employee record to the first sign-in. It is written for the product owner, who needs to know how a person, a role, a login, working hours and pay terms fit together, and what the Platform cannot do. The workflow touches Employees, Roles, User Admin, Authentication and Commissions.

47.1 Who is involved

  • Admin (or the owner): holds employees.manage, admin.users.manage and compensation.manage. Only the Admin system role holds them by default.
  • Dr. Example One: the new employee. Becomes a staff login once a user account is linked.
  • Example Clinic, Main location.

47.2 The steps

Figure 47.1 shows the whole flow.

Figure 47.1 — From the Add Employee form to the first sign-in.

The diagram has five participants: Admin, Staff member, Web app, API and PostgreSQL, and 20 messages. The Admin fills the Add Employee form and the Web app calls POST /employees. The API first refuses the request if the phone number exists anywhere on the Platform, then inserts the employee, an EMP- code, the assignment with its role and the first compensation plan version. PostgreSQL raises the organization's access version after the commit, and the API answers "Employee created". Next the Admin opens User Admin and creates a staff login (POST /user with type employee); the API checks the login limit, creates the user and links it to every active assignment with portal access on. The Admin saves the weekly schedule (POST /employees/:employeeId/schedule, seven rows for this location) and, if needed, a new compensation plan version (POST /assignments/:assignmentId/compensation-plans). Finally the Staff member signs in, the Web app calls POST /auth/login and, when asked, POST /auth/select-location, and then GET /me/access, which returns permissions, features and the home page.

Step 1 — Employee record, assignment and role

Module: Employees. Status: [Implemented]. On Employees, Add Employee asks for Full Name, Phone, Designation, Role, Employment Type and Joining Date. The server rejects a phone that already exists on the Platform (the employee record is shared across clinics). It generates the employee code (EMP-001 style, counting the organization's assignments), inserts the assignment at the active location with the chosen role, and adds the first compensation plan version starting on the joining date: salaried with the entered salary, unless a commission plan was chosen (Chapter 37, Chapter 35). The role decides what the person may do at that location; a login alone grants nothing.

Step 2 — Staff login

Module: Employees and User Admin. Status: [Implemented]. There are two routes. The Portal Access switch on the employee form creates a login with an email and a password of at least 6 characters, linked only to the active location's assignment. User Admin → Create User → Staff (existing employee) needs a password of at least 8 characters, checks the plan's login limit and links the login to all the person's active assignments in the organization. Only the second route checks the limit (Chapter 37). The user receives no verification email when created by an administrator (Chapter 56).

Step 3 — Weekly schedule

Module: Employees. Status: [Implemented]. On the Schedule tab the Admin switches days on or off, sets start and end times and a slot length of 15, 30, 45 or 60 minutes, and saves seven rows. Booking checks these hours: a doctor with no working block that day cannot be booked (Chapter 29). The Save button is visible to people without employees.manage, but the server refuses them. Availability overrides and approved leave are stored but do not affect booking [Partial] (Chapter 37).

Step 4 — Compensation plan

Module: Commissions. Status: [Implemented]. On the Compensation tab the Admin picks Salaried, Commission or Both and an effective date. A new version closes the old one on the previous day. Commission is allowed only for roles that can conduct consultations, and the feature billing.commissions must be on. A second change on the same day replaces the first only if no charge used it (Chapter 35).

Step 5 — First sign-in

Module: Authentication and Access control. Status: [Implemented]. The staff member signs in with the email and password. If they have one location, it becomes active at once; otherwise the app shows the location picker. GET /me/access returns what they can do and the role's home page, for example /queue/doctor for a Doctor (Chapter 8, Chapter 11, Chapter 56).

What is not possible: a second location

Module: Employees. Status: [Not implemented]. There is no endpoint that assigns an existing employee to another location or organization. CreateAssignmentDto exists but nothing uses it. Add Employee at a second location fails because the phone number is already taken. A doctor who works at two locations therefore cannot be set up through the Platform (Chapter 37).

47.3 What can go wrong

  • Duplicate phone gives 409 "An employee with this phone number already exists". A duplicate CNIC is caught only by a database index and returns a generic 500 error.
  • Duplicate login email gives 409.
  • Commission plan refused: 403 COMMISSIONS_DISABLED when the feature is off, 422 COMMISSION_ROLE_CANNOT_CONSULT for a non-consulting role.
  • Login limit reached gives PLAN_LIMIT on the User Admin route.
  • Wrong or missing role: the person signs in but sees a restricted sidebar or the no-access page.
  • Read-only mode: every step is refused with 402.
  • The person is saved before the login and the assignment, outside the final transaction, so a failure part-way can leave a person record with no assignment.

47.4 Data left behind

  • employees (person), employee_org_location_assignments (role, location, user_id, has_portal_access).
  • users (login), employee_schedules (seven rows per location).
  • compensation_plans and commission_rules.
  • organizations.access_version raised by the assignment save.

Chapter 48 — Workflow: The Patient Journey

This chapter follows Sample Patient A through one visit at Example Clinic, from registration to a printed receipt. It is written for the product owner. It follows the order the code really uses, which differs from a naive reading in two places: the invoice is created when payment is collected, and a lab case is a separate flow that is billed separately.

48.1 Who is involved

  • Receptionist R1: registers, books, checks in and collects payment.
  • Dr. Example One: calls the patient, consults, prescribes, completes the visit.
  • Sample Patient A: the patient.
  • Accountant and Admin: may also collect payments and correct invoices.

48.2 The steps

Figure 48.1 — One visit from registration to receipt.

The diagram has seven participants: Receptionist R1, Dr. Example One, Web app, API, QueueOrchestrator, PaymentsService and PostgreSQL, and 24 messages. R1 creates the patient (POST /patients) and the API stores the patient with the next P- number and an audit row. R1 books an appointment (POST /appointments); it is saved as scheduled and the database blocks a doctor overlap. On arrival R1 clicks "Check in and get token" (PATCH /appointments/:id/check-in), the API hands over to QueueOrchestrator, which writes the session, the token, a queue entry in state waiting and sets the appointment to checked in. Dr. Example One calls the next patient and presses "Patient is here, start" (PATCH /queue/entries/:id/start-consultation); the entry becomes in consultation and the encounter is created. The doctor records notes and treatments, signs the prescription (POST /encounters/:id/treatments, POST /prescriptions, POST /prescriptions/:id/finalize) and presses "Complete visit" (PATCH /queue/entries/:id/complete); in one transaction the entry and appointment become completed and the consultation and treatment charges are created with the commission snapshot. R1 then opens the billing desk, presses Bill and Receive (POST /payments); PaymentsService runs one transaction that issues the invoice, records the receipt, allocates the money, writes commission entries and the ledger row. The API returns the receipt and invoice numbers and R1 prints them.

Step 1 — Registration

Module: Patients. Status: [Implemented]. Create on /patients takes Full Name and Phone. The phone must be unique inside the organization. The server assigns P- plus a five-digit number and writes an audit row. The check-before-save endpoint exists, but no screen calls it [Partial] (Chapter 28).

Step 2 — Appointment

Module: Appointments. Status: [Implemented]. The booking checks the doctor works at that location, that the slot fits a working block, that the doctor has no overlapping booking and the daily limit. A booking has no token yet. A walk-in skips this step (Chapter 29).

Step 3 — Check-in

Module: Appointments and Queue. Status: [Implemented]. Check-in is allowed only on the booking's own day and up to the location's maximum lateness (45 minutes by default). It opens the doctor's queue session if needed and issues a token such as A-007. A patient who is too late is offered "Convert to walk-in" (Chapter 29, Chapter 30).

Step 4 — Queue

Module: Queue. Status: [Implemented]. The doctor starts the queue, then Call next picks the next patient by the smart or first-come rules. Reception and the TV display update live (Chapter 30).

Step 5 — Consultation

Module: Consultation. Status: [Implemented]. Starting the consultation creates the encounter, the clinical record of this visit, in the same transaction. The workspace shows the patient summary and allergy strip, and auto-saves notes (Chapter 31).

Step 6 — Treatment

Module: Consultation. Status: [Implemented]. The doctor taps procedure chips from the service catalog. Each becomes a treatment. The doctor never sees prices. A treatment typed by name has no price and is later priced by reception (Chapter 31).

Step 7 — Prescription

Module: Prescriptions. Status: [Implemented]. In the workspace panel the doctor adds medicines and presses "Sign & print". The prescription is optional and has no effect on billing (Chapter 32).

Step 8 — Lab case (separate flow)

Module: Dental Lab. Status: [Not implemented] from the consultation workspace. The workspace has no lab-order button, and a lab order has no link to an encounter in the data model (Chapter 31). A lab order is actually created from the sidebar: Lab orders → New lab order, where the user picks the patient, the lab, the ordering doctor and the items, then presses Submit to lab. The API accepts an optional appointment and treatment on the order, but the order form in the web app does not appear to send them [Unverified]. Chapter 49 follows the lab case. Lab work is billed by its own invoice, not by the clinic's charges.

Step 9 — Automatic charges

Module: Billing. Status: [Implemented] with a condition. When the doctor completes the visit, the Platform creates one consultation charge and one charge per treatment, priced from the service catalog with any doctor-specific price. This runs only when the feature billing.invoices is enabled; that feature is off by default (Chapter 31, Chapter 34). A charge with no price is marked "needs pricing" and blocks invoicing until someone sets a price. Each charge stores a snapshot of the doctor's commission terms (Chapter 35).

Step 10 — Payment and invoice

Module: Billing. Status: [Implemented]. On the Billing desk, "ready to bill" lists patients with unbilled charges. Collect payment previews the split and then saves. The invoice is issued at this moment, taking the next INV number, with the location's sales tax added on top. Surplus money becomes the patient's advance. A patient who leaves without paying can still be invoiced with Issue invoice from the patient's Billing tab (Chapter 34).

Step 11 — Receipt

Module: Billing. Status: [Implemented]. The payment takes the next REC number. The result screen prints the receipt and the invoice in A4 or 80 mm thermal layout. There is no server-generated PDF receipt [Not implemented] (Chapter 34).

48.3 What can go wrong

  • Duplicate phone on registration gives 409.
  • Booking conflicts: DOCTOR_DOUBLE_BOOKED, DAILY_LIMIT_REACHED, outside working hours.
  • Check-in too late (LATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED), wrong day (NOT_TODAY), queue closed (SESSION_NOT_OPEN).
  • A stale queue screen gives 409 VERSION_CONFLICT.
  • With billing.invoices off, completion succeeds and no charge appears.
  • A charge needing a price blocks the invoice ("Set a price for ...").
  • Payment errors: missing reference for an account that requires one, allocation above balance.
  • In read-only mode every write gives 402.

48.4 Data left behind

patients, audit_logs, appointments, queue_sessions, queue_entries, queue_events, outbox, idempotency_keys, patient_encounters, treatments, prescriptions and children, charges, billing_audit_logs, invoices, payments, payment_allocations, document_sequences, ledger_entries, commission_entries.

Chapter 49 — Workflow: A Dental Lab Case

This chapter follows one lab case, a zirconia crown for Sample Patient A, from the order to the delivered work, and then follows the money: what the patient is billed, what the clinic owes the lab and what the doctor earns. It is written for the product owner. The case involves three modules (Dental Lab, Lab Finance, Commissions) and two sides: the clinic and the lab, which is not a tenant of the Platform. The lab feature dental.lab_orders is off by default; a super admin entitles it and the owner switches it on.

49.1 Who is involved

  • Dr. Example One: creates and submits the order, decides try-ins, approves and delivers.
  • Receptionist R1: receives shipments at the front desk.
  • Accountant: bills the patient for lab work, approves vendor bills, pays the lab.
  • Example Dental Lab: the lab. Its people are lab members (lab admin, lab technician) who use the lab portal, or a contact who acts through a magic link.
  • Admin: may act on behalf of a lab that does not answer.

49.2 The steps

Figure 49.1 — Order to delivery, then the money.

The diagram has seven participants: Dr. Example One, Example Dental Lab, Receptionist R1, Accountant, Web app, API and PostgreSQL, and 23 messages. The doctor submits the order (POST /lab-orders, then POST /lab-orders/:id/submit); the API freezes the prices, assigns a LAB number, stores revision 1 and a magic link row. The doctor copies the link and pastes it into a chat. The lab accepts, through the link (POST /lab-link/:token/accept) or the portal (POST /lab-portal/orders/:id/accept), and the API marks the items accepted, creates the stages and drafts a vendor bill. The lab then works through the portal: start, finish and QC (POST /lab-portal/production/items/:itemId/start and the following actions) and dispatches a shipment (POST /lab-portal/production/shipments).
