The front desk receives it by scanning the QR code (POST /lab-shipments/:id/receive). The doctor records the try-in and approves or asks for correction (.../stages/:stageId/tryin and /decision). After the final shipment is received, the doctor approves and marks the work delivered (.../items/:itemId/approve and /deliver), which starts a 12-month warranty and completes the order. The Accountant bills the patient (POST /lab-billing/invoices and /issue), approves the vendor bill and pays the lab (POST /lab-payables/bills/:id/approve, POST /lab-payables/payments).

Step 1 — Create and submit the order

Module: Dental Lab. Status: [Implemented]. Lab orders → New lab order: choose patient, lab, ordering doctor, priority and date needed; add items (service, options, quantity, teeth, form answers); Submit to lab. The lab must be an active lab link of the clinic. At submit the Platform checks the forms, freezes the lab and patient prices of every line, assigns a number such as LAB-0001 and queues a message for the lab members. Every line needs a lab price and a mapped clinic treatment on the submit day (Chapter 40).

Step 2 — Reach the lab

Module: Dental Lab. Status: [Partial]. Three routes exist. The lab portal gives members the order in their own inbox [Implemented] (Chapter 41 covers the portal). A magic link opens one order without a login and allows view, accept, reject and ask a question only. Send link to lab queues a message, but the only registered provider for WhatsApp, SMS and email writes the message to the server log, so nothing reaches the lab; Copy link returns the link once and the doctor pastes it into a chat by hand (Chapter 40, Chapter 44). A coordinator holding both lab.orders.create and lab.links.manage can record the lab's answer on its behalf [Implemented].

Step 3 — Lab accepts

Module: Dental Lab and Lab Finance. Status: [Implemented]. Accept needs an expected date. Items move to accepted, the stage rows are copied from the item's stage template, and a draft vendor bill is created or updated at the frozen lab cost (Chapter 42).

Step 4 — Production stages

Module: Lab Portal. Status: [Implemented]. Production actions (start, assign a technician, finish, QC, dispatch a shipment) are lab portal endpoints for members. A lab that has only a magic link and no portal login cannot perform them, and the clinic's proxy actions cover only accept, reject, clarification and expected date. The clinic follows progress on the order's Production panel (Chapter 40).

Step 5 — Try-in

Module: Dental Lab. Status: [Implemented]. For items with try-in stages the doctor presses Record try-in after the patient visit, then Approve or Needs correction with notes. A correction closes the round and opens the same stage as the next round. No appointment is created or reminded automatically; the event for a due try-in is never emitted (Chapter 40).

Step 6 — Shipment and receive

Module: Dental Lab. Status: [Implemented]. The front desk opens the incoming shipment or scans its QR code, sets condition and quantity per line and presses Receive. A parcel that never arrives can be marked lost with a reason.

Step 7 — Approve and deliver

Module: Dental Lab. Status: [Implemented]. The doctor presses Approve work, then Fitted, mark delivered, which starts a 12-month warranty. Rejecting received work opens a remake request that the lab may dispute. When all items are approved or delivered the order is completed.

Step 8 — Money: patient lab invoice

Module: Lab Finance. Status: [Implemented]. This is not the clinic's normal invoice: lab work is billed through its own tables and numbers (LINV). The Accountant opens the submitted order and presses Bill N item(s), which starts an estimate; Issue invoice gives it a number and due date. The lines copy the patient prices frozen at submit. This can be done any time after the order is submitted, not only after delivery. Payments, advances and credit notes follow (Chapter 42).

Step 9 — Money: vendor bill and payment to the lab

Module: Lab Finance. Status: [Partial]. The draft vendor bill appears under Lab payables → Bills. The Accountant presses Approve, setting the lab's invoice number, due date and tax, which books the debt. Pay lab records a payment and splits it over approved bills. Editing the bill header and adding manual lines exist only in the API (Chapter 42).

Step 10 — Money: lab-line commission

Module: Commissions. Status: [Implemented] (backend only by design). When the lab invoice is issued, each line stores the doctor's plan and rate. As the patient pays, the doctor earns commission on the money collected minus the lab's cost, so the doctor is paid on the clinic's margin. Reversals and credit notes give it back. It needs billing.commissions on and feeds My earnings and payroll like any other commission (Chapter 35).

49.3 What can go wrong

  • Submit fails when a line has no lab price, no mapped treatment, a per-tooth service without teeth or answers that fail the form (LAB_ORDER_INVALID, LAB_PRICE_MISSING).
  • The lab link is not active: LAB_NOT_LINKED.
  • A magic link dies after 24 hours by default, on revoke, when the order closes or when the lab is suspended.
  • A lab that never answers: use the proxy actions.
  • Parcels may arrive damaged, short or not at all.
  • A rejected final piece needs a remake; who pays is decided in the remake request.
  • Double billing is blocked: an item can be on only one live lab invoice.
  • A bill of 0 cannot be approved; approval is refused if the draft changed since it was read.
  • Four seeded notification events are never emitted, including overdue orders.

49.4 Data left behind

lab_orders, lab_order_items, order_revisions, magic_links, order_item_stages, shipments, item_warranties, status_history, audit_logs, notification_outbox, vendor_bills, vendor_bill_lines, vendor_payments and allocations, lab_invoices, lab_invoice_lines, commission_entries with a lab invoice line, and journal rows in ledger_journals.

Chapter 50 — Workflow: Closing the Clinic Day

This chapter describes how a clinic day ends at Example Clinic: the doctor closes the queue, late bookings become no-shows, reception reviews the day's collection, the accountant closes the counter, and the Platform's overnight jobs run. It is written for the product owner. Some of the work is done by people and some by background jobs in the worker process (Appendix E lists all jobs). Job times use the server clock, not each clinic's timezone.

50.1 Who is involved

  • Dr. Example One: closes the queue.
  • Receptionist R1: reads the day's collection.
  • Accountant: closes the counter. Admin may also do this.
  • Worker process: the one process that runs scheduled jobs.

50.2 The steps

Figure 50.1 — People first, then the jobs that run on their own.

The diagram has seven participants: Dr. Example One, Receptionist R1, Accountant, Web app, API, Worker jobs and PostgreSQL, and 15 messages. The doctor closes the day and decides cancel or transfer for each waiting patient (PATCH /queue/sessions/:id/close); the API cancels or transfers them and closes the session. In parallel, the worker marks late bookings as no-shows every 60 seconds and closes empty sessions of past days every 5 minutes. Receptionist R1 opens Payments and picks the day (GET /payments/daily-collection) and the API returns receipts, refunds and net per account. The Accountant closes the counter with a counted amount per account (POST /billing/cash-close) and the API stores the close and its lines with an audit row. The worker then runs four overnight jobs: expire prepaid credits at 01:00, billing invariant check at 02:30, queue cleanup at 03:15 and inventory alert count at 08:00.

Step 1 — Queue day-end

Module: Queue. Status: [Implemented]. In My Queue, Close day is disabled while a patient is with the doctor. The "Close today's queue" dialog lists every remaining patient (waiting, skipped or at a test) with Cancel as the default or "Transfer to Dr. ..." for waiting patients only. Confirming cancels or moves them and closes the session. Cancelling a booked patient closes the appointment as cancelled. Everything succeeds or nothing does (Chapter 30).

Step 2 — Automatic day-end

Module: Queue. Status: [Implemented]. Every 5 minutes the worker closes sessions of a past service day if they are empty. A session that still has patients is only logged as an alert and is never cancelled automatically, so someone must decide. The "past day" is judged by each location's timezone and day cut-off, not by the server date.

Step 3 — No-show marking

Module: Appointments and Queue. Status: [Implemented]. Staff can press No show on a scheduled or confirmed booking (appointments.cancel). Otherwise the worker does it every 60 seconds once start time plus maximum lateness (45 minutes by default) has passed. The job writes with plain SQL, so there is no queue event, no audit row and no realtime message. A no-show no longer shows Check in in the web app, so a late patient usually has to be added as an ordinary walk-in (Chapter 29).

Step 4 — Daily collection

Module: Billing. Status: [Implemented]. On Payments, the day picker (future days not allowed) shows receipts by their payment date and refunds by their refund date per payment account, with the net in hand (Chapter 34).

Step 5 — Cash close

Module: Billing. Status: [Implemented]. Close counter computes for each payment account the expected money since the previous close, asks for the counted amount on accounts marked "Count physically at cash close", and requires a note when there is a difference. A close is a permanent record with a printable slip and a red "Flagged" badge when the difference exceeds the alert amount. Closing never blocks taking payments, and a close cannot be edited or deleted. It needs billing.cash_close (Admin, Accountant).

Step 6 — Overnight jobs

Module: Several. Times are server time (Appendix E).

Time Job Status
01:00 Patient credit expiry: marks credits past their expiry date as expired [Implemented] (credit packages have no screen, so little to expire in practice)
02:30 Billing invariant check: re-checks ten money rules and logs any break [Implemented], log only
03:15 Queue cleanup: deletes idempotency keys older than 24 hours and published outbox rows older than 7 days [Implemented]
08:00 Inventory alerts: counts low and expiring items per location [Partial], server log only

The table lists the four daily jobs with what each does and its status. The credit job reads the server date rather than the location's, so a credit can expire a few hours early or late for a clinic in another timezone. Nobody is notified by the invariant check or the inventory alert; an operator must read the logs (Chapter 34, Chapter 39).

50.3 What can go wrong

  • Closing the queue while someone is with the doctor: 409 DOCTOR_BUSY.
  • A remaining patient without a decision: 422 INVALID_TRANSITION.
  • A skipped or at-test patient cannot be transferred, only cancelled or brought back.
  • Counter close: 422 when a count or a note is missing, or when the close period is stale.
  • Overnight times differ from clinic local time when the server is in another timezone.
  • Jobs run only in a worker (or all-in-one) process; if no worker runs, none of the jobs run. Exactly one worker must run.
  • The invariant check only logs; a violation is not repaired or announced.

50.4 Data left behind

queue_sessions (closed), queue_entries, queue_events and outbox (for closes done by users), appointments (cancelled or no-show), cash_closes, cash_close_lines, billing_audit_logs, patient_credits (expired), and server log lines for the invariant check and the inventory alerts.

Chapter 51 — Workflow: Month-End Payroll

This chapter follows payroll for one month at Example Clinic, from the automatic run on the 1st to the payment record. It is written for the product owner. Payroll combines two things: the base salary from each employee's compensation plan and the doctor commission earned but not yet paid out. The Platform records the payout; it does not move money.

51.1 Who is involved

  • Scheduler (the worker process): runs the job.
  • Admin: holds payroll.manage (feature hr.payroll, on by default). No other system role holds it.
  • Dr. Example One: an employee with a salary and commission.

51.2 The steps

Figure 51.1 — The automatic run, the optional manual run and the payment.

The diagram has six participants: Scheduler, Admin, Web app, API, PayrollService and PostgreSQL, and 16 messages. At 05:00 on the 1st the Scheduler calls the month-end run on PayrollService, which loads the active locations. For each assignment it reads the base salary from the plan in force on the last day of the month, locks the unsettled commission entries up to month end, and inserts a pending payroll record and a pending settlement. The Admin opens Payroll for the month (GET /payroll) and sees records with base, commission and total. If the job missed a location, the Admin presses Generate Payroll (POST /payroll/generate) and existing records are skipped. The Admin presses Mark as Paid with a method and reference (PATCH /payroll/:id/mark-paid); the service sets the record and the settlement to paid. The last message shows the CSV export and payslip PDF endpoints, which no button calls.

Step 1 — Automatic generation

Module: Payroll. Status: [Implemented]. The cron expression is 0 5 1 * * with no timezone option, so it fires at 05:00 on the 1st in the server's timezone. A code comment says 00:05; the code wins. The month is taken from the server's own date (the previous month), not from each location's timezone. The job covers every active location of every organization, each in its own transaction, so one failing location does not stop the others. It does not check that the organization is active or that hr.payroll is on. It runs without a request, so the subscription read-only guard, which acts on web requests, does not apply to it (deduced from the guard being an HTTP guard) (Chapter 38, Appendix E).

Step 2 — Base plus commission

Module: Payroll and Commissions. Status: [Implemented]. For each active assignment: skip if a record already exists for that employee, location and month; otherwise base salary = the plan version in force on the month's last day (else the first day); commission = the sum of unsettled commission entries created before the end of the month's last clinic day. A net-negative sum is not settled and waits for a later month. Total = base + commission. An employee with neither is listed as "no salary" and gets no record (Chapter 38, Chapter 35).

Step 3 — Settlement lock

Module: Commissions. Status: [Implemented]. The entries are row-locked and tied to a settlement so they cannot be paid twice. Entries are never edited; a reversal after settlement lands as a negative entry in a later month's settlement (Chapter 35).

Step 4 — Manual generation

Module: Payroll. Status: [Implemented]. Generate Payroll on /payroll takes a month and year, refuses future months and generates for the whole active location, even when pressed from an employee tab. It is safe to run after the automatic job.

Step 5 — Review and edit

Module: Payroll. Status: [Implemented]. Records start as pending. Edit, delete and create-by-hand exist. A record that paid out commission cannot be deleted. Deleting an unpaid record releases its commission back to the pool. Putting a record on hold has an endpoint but no button; the edit dialog's status field can set it [Partial].

Step 6 — Mark paid

Module: Payroll. Status: [Implemented]. Mark as Paid needs a method (cash, bank transfer or cheque) and optional reference and notes. The record becomes paid with time and payer, and the settlement becomes paid in the same transaction. No money moves and nothing is posted to the general ledger or expenses. Setting status to paid through the edit dialog does not pay the settlement, which is a trap: a later delete would release the commission.

Step 7 — Payslip and export

Module: Payroll. Status: [Partial]. GET /payroll/:id/payslip-pdf returns an A4 PDF (Latin text only) and GET /payroll/export?month&year returns a CSV. Neither has a button in the web app, so they can be called only through the API. Deductions are always 0.00, net equals gross, and the designation column is empty.

51.3 What can go wrong

  • Server timezone differs from the clinic's, so "the 1st at 05:00" falls at another local time, and the month boundary can shift near midnight.
  • No worker process is running: nothing is generated.
  • A location error is logged and skipped; no in-app notification tells anyone.
  • Future month: 400 "Cannot generate payroll for future months".
  • "Payroll already marked as paid" on a second payment.
  • Paying through the edit dialog leaves the commission unpaid.
  • No deductions, tax, overtime or unpaid-leave handling exist [Not implemented].
  • Payroll changes are not written to the general audit log.

51.4 Data left behind

payroll_records (pending, then paid with paid_at, method, reference), commission_settlements (period, total, payroll record id, status), commission_entries.settlement_id. Records made by the job have no created_by.

Chapter 52 — Workflow: Correcting an Invoice and Refunding Money

This chapter follows what the Accountant does when an issued invoice turns out to be wrong: preview and save an edit that creates a new revision, cancel an unpaid invoice, refund money, or undo a payment first. It is written for the product owner, who needs to know what stays on record and how doctor commission follows each change. Invoices are never deleted; every change adds to the history.

52.1 Who is involved

  • Accountant (or Admin): holds billing.invoice.edit, billing.invoice.void and billing.refund.issue. The last two are marked high risk.
  • Sample Patient A: the patient whose invoice is corrected.
  • Dr. Example One: the doctor whose commission adjusts.

52.2 The steps

Figure 52.1 — Edit with preview, then refund or cancel.

The diagram has five participants: Accountant, Web app, API, CommissionService and PostgreSQL, and 18 messages. The Accountant opens the invoice, presses Edit, changes lines and types a reason; the Web app calls POST /invoices/:id/edit/preview, the API applies the edit inside a transaction and rolls it back, and returns the preview. The Accountant presses Save changes (POST /invoices/:id/edit with the expected revision); the API raises the revision, releases allocations, posts an adjustment to the ledger and writes an audit row, then asks CommissionService to record the signed commission entries. An "alt" box has three outcomes. To give freed money back, the Accountant presses Refund or Save and refund (POST /invoices/:id/refund) and the API writes the refund, its sources, a ledger row and an audit row. To cancel an unpaid invoice, the Accountant presses Cancel with a reason (POST /invoices/:id/cancel), and the invoice becomes cancelled with its charges back to not invoiced. To cancel a paid invoice, an API client must first unapply the payment (POST /payments/:id/unapply), which writes negative allocations and reverses commission.

Step 1 — Preview the edit

Module: Billing. Status: [Implemented]. On the invoice detail, Edit lets the Accountant change quantities, prices and discounts, void lines, add unbilled charges or add a manual line, with a reason of 5 to 300 characters. The preview really runs the edit in a transaction and discards it, so the numbers match what saving will do (Chapter 34).

Step 2 — Save a revision

Module: Billing. Status: [Implemented]. Saving raises the revision number; the invoice number never changes. If a line's payable shrinks, the allocation above the new amount is released, newest first, and moves to the patient's advance. Older revisions can be printed from audit snapshots. If two people edit at once, the second gets BILLING_INVOICE_REVISION_CONFLICT. Voiding a line needs billing.invoice.void; changing a catalog price needs billing.price.override.

Step 3 — Commission follows

Module: Commissions. Status: [Implemented] (backend only). On every edit the Platform recomputes the doctor's commission target per charge and inserts only the difference as a signed entry. A voided charge brings its commission to zero. Entries already settled in payroll are never changed; the correction lands in the next settlement (Chapter 35).

Step 4 — Cancel an unpaid invoice

Module: Billing. Status: [Implemented]. Cancel needs a reason and is shown only when nothing is paid. The invoice keeps its totals and prints with a CANCELLED watermark, the number stays used, the charges return to Ready to bill, and the patient's statement gets a credit. Cancelled is final.

Step 5 — Unapply a payment (backend only)

Module: Billing. Status: [Partial]. POST /payments/:paymentId/unapply takes back all or part of a payment's allocations and sends the money to advance. It adds negative rows and deletes nothing, and the receipt stays. No screen calls it, so cancelling an invoice that has payments cannot be done from the web app (BILLING_INVOICE_HAS_PAYMENTS: "Unapply its payments before cancelling this invoice").

Step 6 — Refund

Module: Billing. Status: [Implemented]. A refund always comes out of the patient's advance. An advance refund returns unused money from the patient's Billing tab. An invoice refund returns money released from an invoice, optionally in the same step as the edit that released it. The accountant chooses the account under "Paid out from"; it is not forced to be the account that received the payment. Sources are chosen automatically: payments released from that invoice first, latest first, then other advance, newest first. A refund takes the next RFD number, needs a reason of 5 to 300 characters, and cannot be undone. Cash close subtracts refunds per account (Chapter 34, Chapter 50).

52.3 What can go wrong

  • BILLING_INVOICE_REVISION_CONFLICT: someone else changed the invoice; reload.
  • BILLING_INVOICE_CANCELLED: a cancelled invoice is read-only.
  • BILLING_REFUND_EXCEEDS_ADVANCE and BILLING_REFUND_EXCEEDS_INVOICE_REFUNDABLE: the amount is above what can be returned.
  • BILLING_REFERENCE_REQUIRED for an account that needs a reference.
  • BILLING_UNAPPLY_EXCEEDS_ALLOCATION: more than was applied.
  • Wrong refunds cannot be reversed; the only remedy is a new payment.
  • Read-only mode refuses all of these with 402.

52.4 Data left behind

invoices (revision, status), charges, payment_allocations (including negative and release rows), payments, refunds, refund_sources, ledger_entries (INVOICE_ADJUSTED, INVOICE_CANCELLED, REFUND), billing_audit_logs (EDITED, CANCELLED, REFUNDED, UNAPPLIED with snapshots), commission_entries (signed differences), document_sequences.

Chapter 53 — Workflow: Subscription Expiry and Recovery

This chapter follows Example Clinic when its trial runs out and the clinic is brought back by a manual payment. It is written for the product owner. The Platform never charges anyone: the clinic pays outside the Platform and a super admin records the payment, which extends the period. The subscription status is never stored; it is worked out from two dates every time it is read.

53.1 Who is involved

  • Owner: sees the banners and pays.
  • Other staff: see warning banners and rejected saves.
  • Super admin: records the payment and may change plan, dates and limits.

53.2 The steps

Figure 53.1 — Trial, grace, read-only, payment, back to active.

The diagram has five participants: Owner, Super admin, Web app, API and SubscriptionGuard (drawn as one box), and PostgreSQL, and 17 messages plus two notes. During the trial the Owner opens a page, the Web app calls GET /account, and the API answers status trialing with the banner "Free trial, N days left". A first note says that after the trial end passes there are 3 grace days in which writes still work and a banner warns everyone; a save in that period is accepted. A second note says that once the trial end plus 3 days has passed, the status is expired. A save then returns 402 SUBSCRIPTION_EXPIRED, while reads still work. The Owner pays outside the Platform and sends the reference to the Super admin, who opens Subscriptions, Manage subscription, Record payment (POST /admin/subscriptions/:orgId/payments). The API locks the organization, writes the payment row, sets paid_until and the plan and writes an audit entry, then clears the read-only cache of its own process. The Owner saves again and the write is accepted; other server processes may take up to 30 seconds to notice.

Step 1 — Trial

Module: Subscriptions and Onboarding. Status: [Implemented]. Self-signup gives 14 days on the Professional plan (3 locations, 15 logins). Owners see "Free trial, N days left" with a See plans link. A clinic with no trial date and no paid date is "unmanaged": no limits, never expires (Chapter 45).

Step 2 — Grace period

Module: Subscriptions and Onboarding. Status: [Implemented]. The period end is the later of the trial end and the paid-until date. For 3 days after it (GRACE_DAYS) the clinic works normally; everyone sees a warning that the clinic turns read-only in N days. A plan close to its end shows owners "Your plan renews in N days".

Step 3 — Read-only mode (402)

Module: Subscriptions and Onboarding. Status: [Implemented]. After the grace days, the last global guard refuses every write with HTTP 402 and code SUBSCRIPTION_EXPIRED. Reads (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS) pass, public routes pass, super admins pass, and paths starting with /auth/, /account, /me/ and /admin/subscriptions stay writable. The banner says "Subscription expired. The clinic is read-only" to owners and "read-only until the owner renews the plan" to others. Everything is affected, including the queue and billing. Jobs in the worker are not requests, so they keep running; this is deduced from the guard being an HTTP guard [Unverified].

Step 4 — Pay outside the Platform

Module: Subscriptions and Onboarding. Status: [Implemented]. The owner opens Settings → Plan & billing and reads the "How to pay" text, which the super admin edits on the Subscriptions page (up to 2,000 characters). Methods recorded are bank transfer, JazzCash, EasyPaisa, cash, cheque and other.

Step 5 — Super admin records the payment

Module: Subscriptions and Onboarding. Status: [Implemented]. On Subscriptions, Manage subscription → Record payment takes plan, months (1 to 36), amount, method, date, reference and notes. The new period starts where the current trial or paid period ends, or now if that is over, so early payment loses no days. The plan on the clinic becomes the plan paid for, so paying for Starter during a Professional trial lowers the limits at once.

Step 6 — Active again

Module: Subscriptions and Onboarding. Status: [Implemented]. With paid_until in the future the status is active and writes resume. The decision is cached for 30 seconds per server process, so a renewal can take up to 30 seconds to be seen by a process other than the one that took the payment. A super admin can also set a future trial end or clear both dates to make the clinic unmanaged from the Plan & limits tab.

53.3 What can go wrong

  • The owner never sees a renewal reminder email; none is sent.
  • The grace period is only 3 days.
  • Recording a payment overwrites the plan and can lower the limits.
  • Staff cannot read the cause of a rejected save unless the banner is visible; the API message is "Your subscription has expired. The clinic is read-only until it is renewed."
  • The Organizations screen's plan selector sends values the API rejects, so use the Subscriptions screen for plan changes (Chapter 45).
  • Nothing charges the clinic, so a payment the super admin forgets to record keeps the clinic read-only.

53.4 Data left behind

subscription_payments (plan, months, amount, method, reference, period start and end, recorded_by), organizations (paid_until, subscription_plan, limits), audit_logs (before and after values). The status itself is not stored.

Chapter 54 — Workflow: How an Access Change Reaches Every Screen

This chapter follows what happens after an owner edits a role, a feature switch or the sidebar layout: how the change reaches the server's caches and the staff members' open browser tabs without anyone signing out. It is written for the product owner. The key idea is the access version, a counter on the organization that goes up by one on every change to who can do what.

54.1 Who is involved

  • Owner (or an Admin with admin.roles.manage): makes the change.
  • Staff member: has the Platform open in a browser tab.
  • API and worker processes: keep a cache of each user's access.

54.2 The steps

Figure 54.1 — From Save changes to a re-drawn sidebar.

The diagram has seven participants: Owner, Web app, API, PostgreSQL, Redis, Realtime gateway and Staff browser tab, and 12 messages plus one note. The Owner presses Save changes on the role (PATCH /admin/roles/:id). The API updates employment_roles and commits, then raises access_version by one after the commit. It publishes "access changed" with the organization and version to Redis, and every API and worker process drops its cached contexts. The API tells the realtime gateway to emit access.changed to the room for the organization, and the gateway sends it to the Staff browser tab with the new version. The tab calls GET /me/access; the API reads the version, resolves a fresh context and returns new permissions, features, navigation and home page, and the sidebar and buttons re-render. The note says that if the socket is down, the tab refetches on window focus once its data is 30 seconds old, and the backend still enforces the new version within 15 seconds.

Step 1 — The owner edits

Module: Roles and permissions, Features, Customization. Status: [Implemented]. Three kinds of edit start the chain: a role at Roles & permissions, a feature switch at Features or the entitlement page, and the clinic sidebar layout at Navigation. Granting a high-risk permission asks for a reason (Chapter 11, Chapter 10).

Step 2 — The version goes up

Module: Access control. Status: [Implemented]. organizations.access_version increases after any committed change to employment roles, assignments (role, location, active flag, portal access, login), organization feature flags or ownership. A database event subscriber does this automatically once per transaction, after the commit. Location feature overrides and nav layout changes bump it explicitly; saving the same nav layout again does not. The theme save has no bump in the code, so theme changes do not trigger this chain (Chapter 57).

Step 3 — Server caches drop

Module: Access control. Status: [Implemented]. The new version goes over Redis to every API and worker process, which drop cached contexts and feature sets. The resolver's cache is keyed on user, organization, location and access version, holds up to 10,000 entries and lasts 5 minutes; the version itself is trusted for 15 seconds without a bus message. If Redis is down, other processes catch up within 15 seconds. Because the key includes the version, a stale entry is never matched after a bump.

Step 4 — The browser is told

Module: Realtime. Status: [Implemented]. The gateway emits access.changed to the organization's room. The web app joins that room through the same socket used for the queue. A message whose version is not newer than the one the tab already has is ignored. After a reconnect the tab refetches in case messages were missed.

Step 5 — The tab refetches and redraws

Module: Access control (web app). Status: [Implemented]. The tab invalidates its access query, loads GET /me/access and redraws the sidebar, buttons and home page from can(...). Route permission checks happen when the user navigates. If the room is refused or the socket is down, the fallback is refetch on window focus with a 30-second freshness window (Chapter 57).

Step 6 — Enforcement is already updated

Module: Access control (backend). Status: [Implemented]. The backend never trusts the screen. The access guard resolves access again on each request using the current version, so a removed permission is refused as soon as the version bump is visible to that process, even if the tab has not redrawn. A missing key means no access (fail-closed).

54.3 What can go wrong

  • Redis is down: other server processes may take up to 15 seconds; tabs rely on window focus.
  • Socket blocked or offline: the tab keeps old buttons until focus or the next reload, but the server still refuses actions.
  • Raw SQL edits to roles do not bump the version unless done explicitly.
  • A bump failure after commit is logged and the change itself stays saved, so caches may age out only on their own timers.
  • Escalation protection: granting more than the editor holds is refused (ESCALATION).
  • Super admin acting in the clinic is recorded as a platform action.

54.4 Data left behind

organizations.access_version, employment_roles (or org_feature_flags, location_feature_overrides, nav_layouts), audit_logs entries for the edit, and short-lived in-memory caches that hold no lasting data.

Chapter 55 — Workflow: From Purchase Order to Consumption

This chapter follows a box of gloves from a purchase order to stock, then to use on a patient and to a low-stock alert. It is written for the product owner. The honest summary is that the chain is only partly connected: the pieces exist in the backend, several have no screen, two steps carry a database risk that could not be tested, and the final alert reaches nobody. Each link in the chain carries its own label.

55.1 Who is involved

  • Admin: the only system role with inventory write permissions (inventory.po.manage, inventory.stock.adjust). The Assistant role can only view.
  • Worker process: runs the alert job.
  • Features: inventory.core and inventory.alerts, both off by default.

55.2 The steps

Figure 55.1 — The inventory chain and where it breaks.

The diagram has eight participants: Admin, Web app, API, PurchaseOrderService, applyMovement, PostgreSQL, Alert job and Server log, and 16 messages. The Admin opens /inventory by typing the address and creates a purchase order (POST /purchase-orders); the service stores the order number, lines, totals and status draft, with the Unverified note that the creator column points to employees. The Admin marks it ordered (PATCH /purchase-orders/:id/status), then receives items with batch and expiry (POST /purchase-orders/:id/receive). The service calls applyMovement with PURCHASE_IN per line, which writes a stock movement row and updates the item's stock, nearest expiry and cost price, again marked Unverified. A call to POST /patient-consumptions has no screen; it lowers stock per line and saves the consumption. At 08:00 the alert job counts low and expiring items and writes only a warning line to the server log.

Link 1 — Reach the page

Module: Inventory. Status: [Partial]. The page /inventory works and needs inventory.view, but there is no sidebar entry and no screen links to it. Users must type the address. The feature inventory.core must be entitled and enabled first (Chapter 39).

Link 2 — Purchase order

Module: Inventory. Status: [Unverified]. Screens and logic exist: Create PO with supplier, lines, quantity, unit price and tax; the server numbers it like PO-2026-00001 and computes totals; status goes Draft then Ordered (Mark as Ordered), and only a draft can be cancelled. The risk: creation stores the signed-in user's id in purchase_orders.createdBy, which has a foreign key to employees. A user id and an employee id are different records, so the insert is expected to fail. Reading the entity and the controller confirms that the user id is passed to that column; it was not run. PO numbers are also unique across the whole database but counted per organization, so a second organization's first order of a year can collide (deduced from code). Purchase orders are not linked to expenses or lab payables (Chapter 39).

Link 3 — Receive goods

Module: Inventory. Status: [Unverified]. Receive Items on an Ordered or Partially received PO takes quantities, batch and expiry per line; over-receiving is refused; the status becomes Partially received or Received. Each line adds a "purchase in" stock movement through the single applyMovement path, sets the item's cost price to the line price and moves the item's expiry date earlier if the batch expires sooner. It carries the same kind of foreign-key risk as the purchase order, through stock_movements.performedBy.

Link 4 — Stock movement and manual adjustment

Module: Inventory. Status: [Unverified]. Every quantity change is a row in stock_movements with previous and new stock; stock cannot go below zero. The Adjust stock dialog offers manual adjustment, wastage, return to supplier and transfers (notes required for wastage and manual). A transfer is recorded at one location only; nothing is added at the other. The item row is read without a row lock, so two simultaneous adjustments could start from the same number.

Link 5 — Patient consumption

Module: Inventory. Status: [Not implemented] in the web app. POST /patient-consumptions exists and prices each line at the item's current cost, then lowers stock in one transaction, but the component that would call it (ConsumptionRecorder) is placed on no screen, including the consultation workspace. Consumption templates (kits) can be created but nothing uses them. Consumed materials are not billed and do not show on the encounter (Chapter 39, Chapter 31).

Link 6 — Low-stock alert

Module: Inventory. Status: [Partial]. At 08:00 server time, for every location where both features are on, the job counts low-stock items and items expiring within 30 days and writes one warning line to the server log. No user is notified, no inbox entry is created and nothing appears on a screen; a code comment says notifications are planned (Chapter 44, Appendix E).

55.3 What can go wrong

  • The first purchase order, receive or adjustment may fail with a database foreign-key error, which would stop the whole chain [Unverified].
  • The page is not discoverable without a sidebar entry.
  • "Insufficient stock" when an outgoing movement would go below zero.
  • "Cannot receive more than ordered".
  • Alerts are visible only to whoever reads server logs.
  • Stock movement history is the only audit trail; no separate log exists.
  • With inventory.core off, nothing in the module is permitted.

55.4 Data left behind

purchase_orders, purchase_order_items, stock_movements, inventory_items (stock, expiry, cost), patient_consumptions and patient_consumption_items (API only), and server log lines from the alert job. No billing, ledger or notification rows are written by any step.

Part 7 — Cross-cutting concerns

Chapter 56 — Authentication and sessions

This chapter explains how a person proves who they are to the Platform and stays signed in: registering a clinic, signing in, choosing an organization and location, the short-lived access token and the long-lived session cookie, managing sessions, password flows, rate limiting and the staff-login administration screen. It is written for the product owner, who needs to know exactly how long a sign-in lasts, what a user can revoke and which protections exist today. What a signed-in person may then do is a different question, answered by Chapter 11 (roles and permissions) and Chapter 57 (access control in depth).

56.1 The model in one paragraph

Status: [Implemented]

A user is a login: an email address, a password hash and an account status (active, suspended or deleted). A user is not the same as an employee, who is the person record that the Employees module keeps (Chapter 37). A staff login links one user to one employee. Signing in creates a session row in the database and gives the browser two things. The first is an access token, valid for 15 minutes, which the web app keeps in memory only and sends as a Bearer header. The second is a session cookie named refresh_token, which is httpOnly (scripts cannot read it) and carries the session id and a long random secret. When the access token expires, the web app calls POST /auth/refresh; the cookie proves the session is still valid and a new access token is issued. Nothing about the login is stored in the browser's local storage.

Technical references: backend/src/auth/auth.service.ts · AuthService · backend/src/session/session.service.ts · SessionService · backend/src/auth/jwt.service.ts · web-app/src/store/useAuthStore.ts

56.2 Screens

The sign-in related screens are public pages (/login, /register, /forgot-password, /reset-password, /verify-email), the location selector (/select-location), the signed-in pages for sessions and security (/sessions and the Security and Sessions sections of Settings), and the staff-login administration page (/users).

Figure 56.1 — Login page (screenshot pending).

The login page shows the clinic's own name and logo when the browser knows which clinic it last used (Chapter 58 explains the public theme). It has an email field, a password field with a show and hide button, a "Keep me signed in for 30 days" check box, a "Forgot password?" link, a sign-in button and a link to the sign-up page. The sign-up page asks for clinic name, the owner's name, email, an optional phone number and a password, with a five-segment strength meter (Weak, Fair, Good, Strong, Very strong) that is advice only and does not block the form.

Figure 56.2 — Location selector (screenshot pending).

The selector is a two-step screen. Step one lists the organizations the user can enter; choosing one with a single location selects that location and continues at once. Step two lists the organization's locations as cards; the user picks one and continues. If an organization has no location, the screen says that a location must be created to continue.

Figure 56.3 — Active sessions (screenshot pending).

The sessions list (page title "Active Sessions", also available as the Sessions section of Settings) shows one row per active session with browser, operating system, device, IP address, the time it started and the time it was last active. The current session is marked. Every other row has a Revoke button, the current row has Sign out, and a Sign out all others button sits at the top.

Figure 56.4 — User management (screenshot pending).

The user administration page (/users, title "User Management", subtitle "Manage system access across roles and organizations") lists users by type and has a Create User button. The create form asks for name, email, password, role type (Super Admin, Owner or Staff), and, for a staff user, which employee the login is for. Each row can be edited (including its status) or deleted.

56.3 Features

56.3.1 Register a clinic (self-signup)

Status: [Implemented]

What it does. Lets a new clinic owner create the login and the clinic in one step. The Platform creates the user, a new organization with a main location and a 14-day trial (Chapter 45 covers subscriptions and onboarding), sends a verification email and signs the owner straight in.

How the user does it.

  1. Open the sign-up page and enter clinic name, name, email, optional phone and a password.
  2. Submit. The owner lands in the application, kept signed in for 30 days.
  3. Later, click the link in the verification email.

Behind the scenes — technically. POST /auth/register is public and rate limited. AuthService.register creates the user, calls the clinic set-up service to create the organization, and sends the verification email. If clinic creation fails, the new user row is deleted so no empty login remains. It then runs the normal login flow with "keep me signed in" on.

Rules and validations.

  • Email must be a valid address; name and clinic name are required (at most 255 characters); phone at most 20 characters; password at least 6 characters.
  • An email that already exists is refused.
  • The verification email failing to send is logged but does not stop registration.

Who can do it. Anyone; the route is public.

Data read and written. users, organizations, locations, owner link, subscription rows, user_sessions, security_logs.

Error cases. 429 when more than 5 sign-ups come from one address in an hour; 400 for invalid fields or a duplicate email.

Technical references: backend/src/auth/auth.controller.ts · register · backend/src/subscriptions/clinic-setup.service.ts · web-app/src/features/auth/components/RegisterForm.tsx

56.3.2 Verify an email address

Status: [Implemented]

What it does. Confirms that the owner controls the email address. Verification is informational: an unverified user can still sign in and work. The web app shows a "verify your email" banner until verification is done.

How the user does it. Click the link in the email, which opens /verify-email?token=…. The page shows "Verifying your email…" and then a success or failure message. A signed-in user whose address is still unverified can ask for a fresh link.

Behind the scenes — technically. The email carries a random 32-byte token; the database stores only its SHA-256 hash, valid for 48 hours. POST /auth/verify-email (public, 10 attempts per 15 minutes) hashes the supplied token, finds an unexpired match and sets email_verified_at. POST /auth/resend-verification (signed in, 3 per hour) issues a new token; if the user has no pending token it answers "Email already verified". Sending depends on SMTP settings in the server environment (SMTP_USER, SMTP_PASS).

Rules and validations. An invalid or expired token gives 400 "This verification link is invalid or has expired". Users created by an administrator through user administration are not sent a verification email.

Who can do it. Anyone holding the token; resend needs a signed-in user.

Data read and written. users (email_verification_token, email_verification_expires, email_verified_at).

Technical references: AuthService.verifyEmail · AuthService.resendVerification · backend/src/common/services/mail.service.ts · web-app/src/features/account/pages/VerifyEmailPage.tsx

56.3.3 Sign in

Status: [Implemented]

What it does. Checks the email and password, creates a session and returns the information the web app needs to continue: the user, an access token, the organizations and locations the user may enter, and flags saying whether an organization or location still has to be chosen.

How the user does it. Enter email and password, optionally tick "Keep me signed in for 30 days", and click sign in.

Behind the scenes — in simple terms. The server looks up the user, compares the password against the stored hash, refuses suspended or deleted accounts, records a new session, and works out where the person is allowed to go. The session lasts one day, or 30 days if the box was ticked. Only five sessions can be active at once; a sixth sign-in quietly revokes the oldest.

Behind the scenes — technically. POST /auth/login (public; 5 attempts per 15 minutes per address and route). UserService.validateUser compares with bcrypt (12 rounds). SessionService.createSession stores a bcrypt hash of a 64-byte random refresh secret, the user agent, parsed browser, operating system and device, and the client IP. AuthorizationService.resolveUserAccess returns the accessible organizations. The response also lists any lab memberships, so a user who works only for a lab is sent to the lab portal (Chapter 41). The cookie is httpOnly, sameSite=lax, secure in production, with a maximum age equal to the session's remaining lifetime.

Rules and validations.

  • Email valid; password at least 6 characters.
  • A wrong email or password gives a plain 401 with no hint about which was wrong.
  • A suspended account gets 403 "Your account has been suspended. Please contact support."; a deleted account gets 403 "This account has been deleted."
  • A session's expiry is fixed at sign-in and is never extended by refreshing.

Who can do it. Anyone with an account.

Data read and written. users, user_sessions, employee_org_location_assignments, owner links, organizations, locations, security_logs (a success row).

Effects on other modules. The login result seeds the web app's auth store, which every later request reads for its tenant headers (Chapter 8).

Error cases. 401 wrong credentials; 403 suspended or deleted; 429 too many attempts (message "Too many requests. Please try again later.", with a retryAfter value in seconds).

Technical references: AuthService.login · SessionService.createSession · AuthorizationService.resolveUserAccess · web-app/src/features/auth/components/LoginForm.tsx

56.3.4 Choose and switch organization and location

Status: [Implemented]

What it does. Decides which clinic and branch a person is working in. Every later request carries that choice in two headers.

How the user does it. After sign-in the selector appears when a choice is needed. Later, the location switcher in the page header changes the active location.

Behind the scenes — in simple terms. A single organization with a single location is chosen automatically. A super admin always picks an organization first. Otherwise the person picks, and the Platform remembers the last choice for next time.

Behind the scenes — technically. The login response sets requiresOrgSelection and requiresLocationSelection. POST /auth/select-location and POST /auth/switch-location (both signed in, context free) validate access with AuthorizationService.validateAccess and save last_accessed_organization_id and last_accessed_location_id on the user. Switching also returns the legacy permission flags for the new location (deprecated; the web app reads GET /me/access). Chapter 8 describes the choice flow and what each type of user may enter in full.

Figure 56.5 — Sequence of a sign-in, the optional location choice and the first access fetch.

The diagram has three participants besides the User: the Web app, the API and PostgreSQL. (1) The user enters email, password and the optional keep-me-signed-in choice. (2) The web app calls POST /auth/login. (3) The API finds the user and compares the password hash. (4) It creates the session row and enforces the limit of five active sessions. (5) It resolves the organizations and locations. (6) It answers with the access token, the session cookie and the selection flags. An "alt" box then shows two paths. If the user has one organization with one location, the web app stores them as active. Otherwise the web app shows the selector, the user chooses, the web app calls POST /auth/select-location, the API validates access and saves the last accessed choice, and returns the two active ids. After the box, the web app calls GET /me/access with the tenant headers and receives permissions, features and the home page, and opens the home page. A note says that a later 401 answer triggers POST /auth/refresh with the cookie.

Rules and validations. Both organization id and location id are required UUIDs. A request for a location the user may not enter gets 403 "You do not have access to this location".

Who can do it. Any signed-in user.

Data read and written. users.last_accessed_*.

Error cases. 403 no access; the web app shows the toast "Failed to select location".

Technical references: AuthService.selectLocation · AuthService.switchLocation · web-app/src/features/auth/components/LocationSelector.tsx · web-app/src/components/layout/LocationSwitcher.tsx · web-app/src/routes/__root.tsx

56.3.5 Stay signed in: access token, refresh cookie and silent refresh

Status: [Implemented]

What it does. Keeps a person signed in across page reloads and across the 15-minute life of the access token, without storing credentials in the browser.

Behind the scenes — in simple terms. The access token is a short pass kept only in the page's memory. When the page is reloaded the memory is empty, so the web app quietly asks the server for a new pass using the cookie. When a pass expires in the middle of work, the same quiet request happens and the failed request is repeated.

Behind the scenes — technically.

  • The access token is a JWT signed with the server's access secret, expiring in 15 minutes, holding the user id, email, global role and session id. There is no JWT refresh token; the refresh secret is a random value whose bcrypt hash lives on the session row.
  • On every app start the root route calls POST /auth/refresh once ("silent refresh"). On success the auth store is filled; on failure the user is treated as signed out.
  • POST /auth/refresh (public) reads the cookie, validates the session (not revoked, not expired, secret matches), re-checks the account status, rotates the refresh secret (the old one stops working) and returns a new access token and the full login payload. The cookie's expiry is the original session expiry, not a fresh window.
  • When any API call returns 401, the axios interceptor refreshes and retries once (Chapter 61 shows the sequence).
  • The auth store is memory only; it never uses local storage.

Rules and validations. A missing, revoked or expired session gives 403 "Invalid or expired session" and the cookie is cleared. A session whose user turned suspended or deleted is revoked on the spot.

Who can do it. Any browser holding a valid cookie.

Data read and written. user_sessions (refresh_token_hash, last_active_at).

Technical references: AuthService.refreshTokens · SessionService.rotateRefreshToken · JwtTokenService · backend/src/session/session-lifetime.ts · web-app/src/lib/api.ts

56.3.6 Sign out, list and revoke sessions

Status: [Implemented]

Figure 56.6 — Status lifecycle of a session.

The diagram shows a session starting at a dot and entering active when the user logs in or registers. A loop on active is labelled refresh: a refresh rotates the secret but keeps the same session and the same expiry. Active moves to revoked in three ways: the user logs out or revokes a session (single, all others or all), the user changes or resets the password, or the user is deleted. Active moves to expired when expires_at passes, which is one day or 30 days after sign-in. Revoked and expired are both final states. (A sixth sign-in also revokes the oldest session; the diagram leaves that case out to stay readable.)

What it does. Lets a user end the current session, see every active session with device details, and end any of them.

How the user does it. Open Settings, Sessions (or /sessions). Click Revoke on a row, Sign out on the current row, or Sign out all others. The toasts are "Session revoked", "Signed out successfully" and "All other sessions revoked".

Behind the scenes — technically.

Action Endpoint Notes
Sign out this session POST /auth/logout Public; reads the cookie, revokes that session, clears the cookie, writes a security log row
List active sessions GET /auth/sessions Newest activity first; marks the current one
Revoke one session DELETE /auth/sessions/:id Only the caller's own sessions; otherwise 404
Revoke all others POST /auth/sessions/revoke-all Keeps the current session
Sign out everywhere POST /auth/logout-all Revokes all sessions including the current one, clears the cookie

The table lists the five session endpoints. Revoking is a flag (is_revoked) on the row; rows are kept. There is no clean-up job for old session rows.

Rules and validations. A revoked session cannot refresh. An access token that was already issued stays valid until it expires, at most 15 minutes, because requests are checked by the token only.

Who can do it. Any signed-in user, on their own sessions.

Data read and written. user_sessions, security_logs.

Error cases. 404 "Session not found" for an id that is not the caller's.

Technical references: backend/src/auth/auth.controller.ts · SessionService · web-app/src/features/auth/components/SessionManagement.tsx · web-app/src/routes/sessions.tsx

56.3.7 Passwords: change, forgot and reset

Status: [Implemented] for change, forgot and reset. Add password is [Partial]: the endpoint exists but no screen calls it, because it is meant for accounts created through the disabled OAuth sign-in.

What it does. Lets a user change a known password, or recover from a forgotten one through an emailed link.

How the user does it.

  • Change: Settings, Security, enter the current and new password. All other sessions are revoked, as the page says.
  • Forgot: on the login page click "Forgot password?", enter the email and click "Send reset link". The page always says to check the inbox.
  • Reset: open the link in the email, enter a new password.

Behind the scenes — technically.

  • POST /auth/change-password (signed in) checks the current password with bcrypt, hashes the new one (12 rounds), and by default revokes every other session, keeping the current one.
  • POST /auth/forgot-password (public, 3 per hour) always answers "If the email exists, a reset link will be sent", whether or not the address exists. For a real user it stores the SHA-256 hash of a random token, valid for 15 minutes, and emails the link.
  • PATCH /auth/reset-password (public) hashes the supplied token, finds an unexpired match, sets the new password, clears the token and revokes all sessions of that user.
  • POST /auth/add-password (signed in) sets a password only when the account has none; otherwise 400 "Account already has a password".
  • All three paths write security log rows (change, reset requested, reset succeeded).

Rules and validations. Password rules are in section 56.5. A wrong current password gives 401 "Current password is incorrect". An invalid or expired reset token gives 400 "Invalid or expired token". Reset has no rate limit of its own; the token is single use and short lived.

Who can do it. Anyone for forgot and reset; signed-in users for change.

Data read and written. users (password, password_reset_token, password_reset_expires), user_sessions, security_logs.

Technical references: AuthService.changePassword · AuthService.forgotPassword · AuthService.resetPassword · AuthService.addPassword · web-app/src/features/auth/components/ForgotPasswordForm.tsx · ResetPasswordForm.tsx · web-app/src/features/settings/pages/SettingsPage.tsx

56.3.8 Rate limiting

Status: [Implemented], with a limit: the counters live in the memory of one API process.

What it does. Slows down guessing and abuse on the public and sensitive authentication routes.

Behind the scenes — technically. RateLimiterGuard counts requests per client address and route in a fixed window and answers 429 with retryAfter when the count is exceeded. The address comes from the first value of the forwarding header when present, otherwise the connection address.

Endpoint Allowed Window
POST /auth/login 5 15 minutes
POST /auth/register 5 1 hour
POST /auth/verify-email 10 15 minutes
POST /auth/resend-verification 3 1 hour
POST /auth/forgot-password 3 1 hour

The table lists the five throttled endpoints with their allowed attempts per window. Other routes, including refresh, reset-password and all clinical routes, have no limiter. A separate small throttle (120 requests per minute per address by default) protects the public lab magic-link routes (Chapter 41). Because the counters are in process memory, they reset when the process restarts and are not shared between API processes, so with several API processes the effective limit is higher. The code notes that a shared store such as Redis would fix this.

Who can do it. Not applicable; it applies to everyone.

Technical references: backend/src/auth/guards/rate-limiter.guard.ts · RateLimiterGuard · RateLimit · backend/src/lab-access/magic-links/magic-link-throttle.guard.ts

56.3.9 Security log

Status: [Partial]

What it does. Keeps a record of authentication events in the table security_logs: user, event type, IP address, user agent, session, success flag and a small metadata object.

What is written today. Successful sign-in, sign-out, sign-out everywhere, password change, password reset requested, password reset succeeded, and a failed sign-in only for suspended or deleted accounts. The event list in the code also names email verification, session, token, OAuth, account and suspicious-activity events, but nothing writes them yet. A wrong password does not produce a row.

What is missing. No endpoint or screen reads the security log, and no job deletes old rows, so it is a write-only record that can be queried in the database only.

Technical references: backend/src/auth/security-log.service.ts · SecurityLogService · backend/src/auth/enum/SecurityEventType.ts · backend/src/auth/entities/SecurityLog.ts

56.3.10 User administration and staff logins

Status: [Implemented]

What it does. Lets a super admin, an owner, or a user with the permission admin.users.manage create, edit, suspend and delete logins. The most common case is giving an existing employee a login.

How the user does it.

  1. Open User Admin (/users) and click Create User.
  2. Choose the type. For Staff, pick the employee from the list of staff who have no login yet.
  3. Enter name, email and a password of at least 8 characters, and save.

Behind the scenes — technically.

Action Endpoint
Profile of the caller GET /user/me
List users by type (super_admin, owner, employee), paged GET /user
Staff without a login GET /user/staff-candidates
Create a user POST /user
Edit a user (including status and password) PATCH /user/:id
Delete a user DELETE /user/:id

The table lists the user endpoints. The controller is context free and checks access itself: a super admin may act with or without an organization; anyone else must send an organization header and hold admin.users.manage at their location.

A staff login (type employee) runs in one transaction that locks the employee's active assignments in the organization. It refuses an employee who already has a login (409 "This employee already has a login") and an email already in use. It creates the user, then links the user to all of the employee's active assignments and switches portal access on for them. The login grants no permission by itself: what the person can do comes from the role of each assignment (Chapter 11). Changing assignments bumps the organization's access version, so the change reaches open tabs (Chapter 57).

Rules and validations.

  • Only a super admin can create or edit a super admin. Only an owner can add, edit or delete another owner.
  • A non-super-admin manager may touch only users of their own organization, never a super admin, and cannot elevate a user to super admin.
  • Creating a user checks the plan's login limit for the organization (error code PLAN_LIMIT); super admins may exceed it.
  • Delete is a soft delete: the status becomes deleted, a deletion time is set and every session of the user is revoked.
  • Passwords created here need 8 characters, which is stricter than the 6 required elsewhere.

Who can do it. Super admin, owner, or admin.users.manage (high-risk; the Admin system role holds it).

Data read and written. users, organization_ownership, employee_org_location_assignments.

Error cases. 403 for the manager-scope rules in this list; 409 existing login; 400 duplicate email.

Technical references: backend/src/user/user.controller.ts · UserService.createUser · createStaffLogin · staffCandidates · web-app/src/features/users/ · web-app/src/routes/users.tsx

56.3.11 Sign-in with Google or GitHub

Status: [Not implemented]

The code for Google and GitHub sign-in exists but is disabled: neither the controller nor the two strategies are registered in the authentication module, so the /auth/google and /auth/github routes do not exist. The user table has a provider field and an oauth_providers table, and the service has an OAuth login method, but none of it can be reached. To switch it on, a developer would register the three classes, read callback addresses from the environment and add the routes to the public route list. The Platform therefore supports email and password only.

Technical references: backend/src/auth/oauth.controller.ts · backend/src/auth/auth.module.ts · AuthService.handleOAuthLogin

56.3.12 The first super admin

Status: [Partial]

There is no screen, command or seed that creates a super admin. The usual path is to register an account and then set users.global_role to super_admin directly in the database (Chapter 7, section 7.5, gives the steps). After that, other super admins can be created from User Admin. A super admin signs in, chooses any active organization, and may open the setup pages (Organizations, Locations, Lab Directory, Config Studio, Subscriptions) even before choosing a location.

Technical references: backend/src/common/enums/global-role.enum.ts · web-app/src/routes/__root.tsx · SUPER_ADMIN_SETUP_PATHS

56.4 Entities

The tables involved are users, user_sessions, security_logs and the unused oauth_providers; Chapter 13 describes them column by column. In short: each session belongs to exactly one user and is deleted if the user row is deleted; a security log row points to a user but is kept (the link is set to null) if the user is removed; a user is linked to organizations as an owner through the ownership table and to employees through assignments.

56.5 Password rules

Status: [Implemented]

Where Minimum length
Register, login, change password, reset password 6 characters
Create user in User Admin 8 characters

The table shows the lengths the API enforces. There is no rule about letters, digits or symbols, no list of banned passwords and no expiry. The sign-up and reset pages show a strength meter, but it only advises. Passwords are stored as bcrypt hashes with 12 rounds and are never returned by the API.

56.6 Limitations and known gaps

  • Revoking a session does not cancel an access token that was already issued; it works until it expires, at most 15 minutes.
  • Rate-limit counters are per process and lost on restart.
  • The security log has no reader and no clean-up; failed password attempts are not recorded.
  • No two-factor authentication, no password strength enforcement and no lockout of an account after repeated failures.
  • Session rows are never deleted, only flagged.

56.7 Owner's FAQ

How long does a sign-in last? One day by default and 30 days when "Keep me signed in for 30 days" is ticked. The length is fixed at sign-in; using the application does not extend it.

If an employee leaves, how do I cut off access at once? Set the user's status to suspended or delete the user in User Admin. Deleting revokes every session; a suspended user is refused at the next refresh. An access token already issued may still work for up to 15 minutes.

Can one person have several logins on different devices? Yes, up to five active sessions. A sixth sign-in revokes the oldest.

What happens if someone forgets their password? They use "Forgot password?". The link lasts 15 minutes and a successful reset signs the user out of every device.

Can staff sign in with Google? No. That feature is built but disabled.

Where do I see failed sign-in attempts? Nowhere in the application today. Only the throttle protects the login route.

Chapter 57 — Access control in depth

This chapter follows the Platform's access control from the first guard that sees a request to the last button hidden in the browser. It is written for the product owner, who needs to know where a permission is checked, how quickly a change reaches users and which protections do not exist. Chapter 11 explains the permission catalog, the system roles and the roles screen; this chapter does not repeat them and goes deeper into the mechanics. Customization screens (features, roles, sidebar, theme) are in Chapter 58.

57.1 The idea in one minute

Status: [Implemented]

Access control answers four separate questions, in this order: Is this a real, signed-in user? Is this user allowed to work in this organization and location? Is the feature switched on for this clinic? Does the user's role hold the permission this action needs? A fifth check asks whether the clinic's subscription still allows writing. Each question is a global guard that runs before the controller. After the guards, two more mechanisms narrow what a person sees inside a permitted action: row scope (only own, location or organization rows) and field hiding (prices removed from a response). The browser repeats the same questions only to decide what to show; the server never trusts the browser.

Technical references: backend/src/app.module.ts · backend/src/access/ · web-app/src/features/access/

57.2 The five guards in order

Status: [Implemented]

Five global guards run on every HTTP request, in a fixed order, and the first refusal stops the request (Chapter 5, section 5.4, lists them with their skip rules).

Figure 57.1 — The five global guards in the order they run, with the refusal each can give.

The flowchart reads from top to bottom. A Request enters guard 1, JwtAuthGuard, which asks whether the token is valid; if not, the answer is 401 and the request is refused. Guard 2, TenantContextGuard, asks whether the organization and location in the headers are allowed for this user; if not, the answer is 400 (headers missing) or 403. Guard 3, FeatureFlagGuard, asks whether the required feature is active; if not, 403. Guard 4, AccessGuard, asks whether the permission is held; if not, 403 with the code NO_PERMISSION. Guard 5, SubscriptionGuard, asks whether a write is allowed; if the subscription has expired the answer is 402. A request that passes all five reaches the handler, where row scope and field hiding apply. Every refusal leads to the same "Refused" box.

The details that matter to an owner:

  • Guard 1 and public routes. JwtAuthGuard skips only the routes in a fixed public list (sign-in, register, refresh, password routes, email verification, logout, the public theme, the waiting-room display state and the lab magic links). Marking a handler @Public() is not enough on its own; the route must also be in that list.
  • Guard 2 and super admins. A super admin passes without headers. @RequireSuperAdmin() routes are checked here: anyone else gets 403 "Super admin access required". @ContextFree() routes skip the tenant check, and the handler then checks access itself. The guard has no path-prefix exceptions. A user passes for an organization if they own it, or if they have an active assignment at that exact location with portal access on.
  • Guard 3 only runs for tagged routes. @RequireFeature('key') is needed only on routes that use @AnyMember(), because a permission already implies its feature (the access context drops permissions of inactive features).
  • Guard 4 attaches the access context. Whenever the request names an organization, it puts the resolved access context on the request for the handler, even on routes with no permission marker.
  • Guard 5 is read-only mode. It refuses writes with 402 SUBSCRIPTION_EXPIRED for a clinic whose subscription has lapsed. Reads, super admins and the paths for signing in, the account, /me/ and subscription administration stay open.

Technical references: backend/src/auth/guards/jwt.guard.ts · backend/src/auth/guards/tenant-context.guard.ts · backend/src/feature-flags/guards/feature-flag.guard.ts · backend/src/access/access.guard.ts · backend/src/subscriptions/subscription.guard.ts

57.3 The decorators

Status: [Implemented]

Decorator Where What it means Enforced by
@Can('a', 'b') handler or controller Every listed permission is required; class-level and handler-level lists are merged AccessGuard
@AnyMember() handler or controller Any active member of the location (owners and super admins too) AccessGuard
@Public() handler or controller No sign-in required (plus the public route list) all guards skip
@ContextFree() handler or controller No tenant headers needed; the handler checks access itself TenantContextGuard skips
@RequireSuperAdmin() handler or controller Platform operator only TenantContextGuard
@RequireFeature('key') handler or controller The feature must be active; class and handler lists are merged FeatureFlagGuard
@Access() handler parameter Injects the AccessContext of the request decorator
@VisibleIf('perm') property of a response class The field is removed from the response unless the caller holds the permission global interceptor

The table lists the eight decorators with their placement and meaning. The first five say who may call a handler. @RequireFeature adds a feature condition. @Access() and @VisibleIf are tools for handlers and response classes.

The coverage test. The test access-coverage.spec.ts loads every controller and fails if any handler lacks one of the markers @Can, @AnyMember, @Public, @RequireSuperAdmin, @ContextFree or an explicit @UseGuards(...), or if any handler still uses the removed role decorator. Controllers under the path prefixes for authentication, sessions and health, and the hello endpoint, are exempt. This test is the safety net, because at runtime a handler with no marker passes the access guard.

Technical references: backend/src/access/decorators/access.decorators.ts · backend/src/common/decorators/ · backend/src/access/access-coverage.spec.ts

57.4 The access context

Status: [Implemented]

For each request that names an organization, AccessResolver builds an AccessContext: user id, organization, location, access version, super-admin flag, owner flag, member flag, employee id, active features, granted permissions (feature-filtered, with implied permissions expanded), the role and its home page. Owners and super admins receive every permission at its widest scope. Staff receive the permissions of the role on their assignment at the active location, and only if portal access is on for that assignment. A role that is inactive or belongs to another organization gives nothing. A missing key means no access.

The context offers a small set of questions that code uses instead of role names:

  • can(permission) and canAll([...]): is it granted.
  • scope(permission): own, location or org, or nothing. An unscoped grant reads as org.
  • applyScope(queryBuilder, permission, columns): adds the row filter to a database query. With own it adds a condition on the caller's employee id (or a custom condition). With location it adds a condition on the active location. With org it adds nothing, because the organization filter is the caller's. With no grant, or when the caller has no employee record or no location to match, it adds a condition that matches no rows. If a developer forgets to name the column, it throws an error rather than silently showing nothing.
  • decide(permission, { value, min, max, approvalFlow }): returns allow, deny or "needs approval". Inside the range the answer is allow; outside it, allow only when the caller holds the escalation permission (today: preset discounts are escalated by the custom-discount permission), otherwise needs approval when the clinic runs an approval flow, else deny.

Field hiding. A response class can mark a property @VisibleIf('patients.price.view'). A global interceptor removes that property from every instance in the response when the caller lacks the permission, and removes every guarded field when there is no access context. It works only on class instances, not on plain object literals.

Technical references: backend/src/access/access.resolver.ts · backend/src/access/access-context.ts · AccessContext · backend/src/access/visible-if/visible-if.ts · backend/src/patients/access/patient-scope.ts

57.5 What the web app receives: GET /me/access

Status: [Implemented]

GET /me/access is a context-free route that checks membership itself. It needs the organization header and, for staff, the location header; without a location, staff roles give no permissions because roles are per location. It answers 400 without an organization, 403 when the caller has no access there. The answer has these parts: the access version; the organization and location ids; the super-admin and owner flags; the list of active feature keys; the granted permissions with their scope (or true); the roles (id, name and template key); the employee id; the home page; and the clinic's sidebar layout, which is null while the clinic uses the default. GET /access/catalog (needs admin.roles.manage) returns the catalog, bundles and role templates for the roles screen.

Technical references: backend/src/access/access.controller.ts · MeAccessController · AccessCatalogController

57.6 In the browser

Status: [Implemented]

  • AccessProvider loads /me/access for the active organization and location. The data is fresh for 30 seconds and refetched when the window regains focus, when the realtime socket announces access.changed and after a reconnect.
  • useAccess() returns can(permission), which takes one permission or a list and means any-of; canAll(list) for all-of; scope(permission); feature checks; the owner and super-admin flags; the home page and the sidebar layout. The <Can perm="..."> component wraps content the same way. When no payload exists yet for a super admin on a setup page, a fallback allows everything; a loaded payload is always the source of truth.
  • Route gate. Each route file declares staticData: { can: ... }. One component, RouteAccessGate, mounted in the root route (__root.tsx), reads the requirement of every matched route and shows the No access page when any requirement fails. While access is loading it shows a skeleton; if loading fails it shows "Couldn't load your access" with a retry button. Routes without a requirement pass.
  • Sidebar. The sidebar comes from a developer-owned registry of 39 items. Each item declares its own requirement: a permission (any-of), superAdminOnly (six items: Organizations, Subscriptions, Lab Directory, Form schemas, Workflows, Stage templates), labMember (the Lab portal item) and ownerOrSuperAdmin (the flag exists but no item uses it today). The clinic's saved layout only arranges, renames and hides these items; items a user may not open are removed before display. Registry items that the layout forgot appear in a trailing "More" section so a new page never disappears silently.
  • Home page. After sign-in, the role's home page is used, then the clinic's home page, and the page is opened only if the user passes the same sidebar and route checks; otherwise the Dashboard opens.

Figure 57.2 — The No access page shown when a role lacks the permission of the page.

The screenshot was taken on 2026-10-23 in dark theme and shows the former working name of the product in the corner; the product is now called the Platform and each clinic sets its own name. A test user in a custom role opened a page their role does not allow. The sidebar is short: Dashboard, and under "Clinic" only Patients and Appointments, with Settings and the user at the bottom. The main area is titled "No access" and shows a shield icon, a Roman-Urdu headline meaning that the user has no permission for this page, an English sentence saying the user does not have permission and should ask the clinic owner to add the page to their role, and a button, "Go to my home page". The user can click the button to go to the role's home page, or to the Dashboard if the role has none.

Technical references: web-app/src/features/access/components/AccessProvider.tsx · RouteAccessGate.tsx · NoAccess.tsx · web-app/src/features/access/lib/access.ts · web-app/src/features/access/nav/nav.registry.ts · resolveNav.ts · homeRoute.ts · web-app/src/routes/__root.tsx

57.7 How fast a change reaches users

Status: [Implemented]

Each organization has a counter, organizations.access_version.
