It is raised by one after any committed change that can alter someone's access: employment roles (any column), assignments (role, location, organization, active flag, portal access or linked login), organization feature flags, ownership, location feature overrides and sidebar layout changes. An entity subscriber does this automatically for writes made through the data layer, once per transaction after the commit and never on rollback. Code that uses raw SQL or database cascades must bump explicitly; the employee delete path does.

Figure 57.3 — Sequence from an owner's role change to the refreshed browser tabs.

The diagram has six participants: the Owner, the API process, PostgreSQL, the AccessChangeBus, the QueueGateway and a Staff browser tab. (1) The owner saves a role change. (2) The API commits the role row. (3) The API increments access_version of the organization. (4) The API publishes the organization id and new version to the bus. (5) The bus drops cached access contexts of that organization. (6) It notifies listeners in this process and, through Redis, in the other processes. (7) The gateway emits access.changed to the organization's room. (8) The browser tab calls GET /me/access. (9) The API answers with new permissions and features. (10) The sidebar and buttons update and the route gate checks again.

The timing rules are:

  • Version cache. Each process caches the current version of an organization for 15 seconds. The bus updates it at once in every process that hears the change.
  • Context cache. Access contexts are cached in process memory, at most 10,000, for at most 5 minutes, keyed by user, organization, location and version. A new version means a new key, so stale entries are never used.
  • Redis. One Redis channel carries access-change messages between API and worker processes. If Redis is down, only the process that made the change learns at once; the others catch up within 15 seconds, when their cached version expires.
  • Feature cache. The enabled-feature set is cached for a short time and dropped by the same bus.
  • Browser. Open tabs refetch when told, on focus, and in any case after 30 seconds of staleness.

In practice, an owner's change reaches other staff within seconds, and within 15 seconds even when Redis is unavailable. A person who is already inside a permitted request is not interrupted.

Technical references: backend/src/access/version/access-version.service.ts · AccessVersionService · access-version.subscriber.ts · access-change-bus.ts · web-app/src/features/access/hooks/useAccessSocket.ts

57.8 The lab portal is a separate door

Status: [Implemented]

Lab staff do not use the clinic guards for their screens. Every lab portal controller uses its own LabPortalGuard after the global guards (which skip these routes as context free). It rejects any request carrying clinic headers (400 LAB_PORTAL_CLINIC_CONTEXT), so lab and clinic scopes cannot mix. It requires an active membership of an active lab; the lab is named by an x-lab-id header, or is the user's only lab (several labs without a header gives 400 LAB_SELECTION_REQUIRED). Another lab's id looks exactly like a lab that does not exist (403 LAB_ACCESS_DENIED). A lab role list on the handler (lab admin or technician) is checked against the membership. Super admins hold no lab membership and are refused. Chapter 41 describes the portal itself.

Technical references: backend/src/labs/portal/lab-portal.guard.ts · LabPortalGuard · backend/src/labs/portal/lab-memberships.ts

57.9 Row-level security does not exist

Status: [Not implemented]

The database has no row-level security policies. Tenant isolation is enforced by the application: handlers filter every query by the organization (and often the location) taken from the validated tenant context, and by applyScope for own, location and organization reach. A bug in a query that forgets the organization filter would therefore not be stopped by the database. The safeguards are the coverage test, the single @ActiveTenant() source of the organization, and code review. Chapter 8 describes the tenant model.

57.10 Limitations and known gaps

  • Tenant isolation is application-level only (section 57.9).
  • A handler without a marker passes the access guard at runtime; only the coverage test prevents it.
  • Contexts and version numbers are cached in process memory; with Redis down, other processes may lag up to 15 seconds.
  • An access token already issued is not re-checked against the session; permissions, however, are checked on every request from the access context, so a role change takes effect without a new token.
  • The ownerOrSuperAdmin sidebar flag is unused today.

57.11 Owner's FAQ

I removed a permission from a role. When does it stop working? Within seconds for open screens (the browser is told over the realtime connection) and on the next request on the server. At worst 15 seconds if the message bus is down.

A user opens a page by typing its address. Can they bypass the sidebar? No. The route gate shows No access and the API refuses the data calls with 403 NO_PERMISSION. Hiding a sidebar item is cosmetic; the checks are the permission on the route and on the API.

Does the sidebar layout give anyone access? Never. The layout only arranges pages the registry knows; every item still needs the viewer's permission.

Can the database stop one clinic seeing another's data? Not by itself. The application filters every query by organization; there are no database row-level policies.

Who can see which patients? The scope of patients.view: a doctor sees own patients, front desk sees the location, an admin sees the organization (Chapter 11).

What does 402 mean? The clinic's subscription expired; the clinic is read-only until a payment is recorded (Chapter 45).

Chapter 58 — Clinic customization

This chapter describes how a clinic shapes the Platform to its own way of working: which features are on, which roles exist and what they may do, how the sidebar is arranged, how the application looks, and where each role starts. It is written for the product owner, who needs to know what an owner can change without a developer and what only the platform team can change. Four setup screens carry this work: Features, Roles and permissions, Sidebar and Branding and theme. The permission model behind them is in Chapters 10 and 11 and the access mechanics are in Chapter 57; this chapter restates what is needed and describes the screens.

58.1 The four setup screens

Status: [Implemented]

Screen Route Sidebar label (section "Clinic setup") Permission to open
Features /admin/features Features admin.features.manage
Roles /admin/roles Roles & permissions admin.roles.manage
Sidebar builder /admin/navigation Sidebar admin.nav.manage

Every save on these screens increases the organization's access version or invalidates the settings cache, so changes reach other users quickly (Chapter 57, section 57.7).

58.2 Features screen

Status: [Implemented]

What it does. Lets the owner switch the features in the clinic's plan on or off for the whole clinic, or switch one off at a single location. A feature is only available if the platform team has entitled the clinic to it; the owner then decides whether it is enabled; and a location override can switch it off at one branch. Chapter 10 describes the three switches and the catalog in full.

Figure 58.1 — Features screen (screenshot pending).

The page is titled "Features" with the subtitle "Turn the features in your plan on or off for the clinic, or for one location." Features are listed in rows, each with a name, a switch and a button that opens the locations sheet. A filter row narrows the list. Features the clinic is not entitled to cannot be switched on. If there are no features the page says "No features yet" and that the platform has not set up any features for the clinic.

How the user does it.

  1. Open Features in the sidebar.
  2. Move a switch to turn a feature on or off. Turning a feature off first opens a dialog titled "Turn off ?" that lists the permissions the feature carries and the roles that will lose them. This is the impact preview.
  3. Click Turn off to confirm.
  4. To switch a feature off for one branch only, open the locations sheet and move the switch of that location.

Behind the scenes — technically.

Action Endpoint
List features for the clinic GET /admin/features
Impact of turning one off GET /admin/features/:key/impact
Switch on or off PATCH /admin/features/:key
Switch off or on at one location PUT /admin/features/:key/locations/:locationId

The table lists the four endpoints; all need admin.features.manage. The impact call returns the catalog permissions the feature carries and, for each active role of the organization that grants any of them, the permissions it would lose. Turning on a feature the clinic is not entitled to gives 403 NOT_ENTITLED. Every change writes an audit_logs row; a super admin acting inside a clinic is recorded as the platform.

What it does. Lets the owner (or anyone with admin.roles.manage) create custom roles, copy a system role, choose a level for each module, set a home page and see members. Chapter 11, section 11.5, describes the rules in detail: escalation protection, reason for high-risk grants, read-only system roles, unique names and the ban on deleting a role that has members.

Figure 58.2 — The role editor for a custom role, showing None, Basic and Full per module.

The screenshot was taken on 2026-10-23 in dark theme and shows the former working name of the product in the corner. It shows a custom role open in the editor. Status: [Implemented]

Status: [Implemented]

What it does. Lets the owner rename, hide, group and reorder the pages in the sidebar for the whole clinic. Each person still sees only the pages they may open, so the layout can never give access.

Figure 58.3 — Sidebar builder (screenshot pending).

The page is titled "Sidebar" with the subtitle "Rename, hide and reorder the pages in your clinic's sidebar. Each person still sees only the pages they have access to." A line at the top says whether the clinic uses the standard sidebar or a custom one, or that there are unsaved changes. The buttons are Discard changes (when dirty), Reset to default and Save. How the user does it.

  1. Open Sidebar under Clinic setup.
  2. Drag pages between sections or the tray, rename sections and pages, hide pages, add groups.
  3. Choose a clinic home page.

Rules and validations.

  • At most 20 sections; labels at most 40 characters; at most 100 items in a list.

  • Footer items (Settings) stay pinned and cannot be arranged.
  • Pages the layout forgets appear in a "More" section, so nothing disappears by accident.

The cascade.

Figure 58.5 — The theme cascade from code default to the effective theme, with locks.

The flowchart reads from top to bottom. The code default (for example the name "Clinic Portal") feeds the Platform value set by the super admin. That feeds the Organization value set by an owner with admin.theme.manage. That feeds the Location value, which may set only the name and logos. The last box is the effective theme returned by GET /theme. Two dotted arrows from the Platform and Organization boxes straight to the effective theme show that a lock stops the walk: a value locked at a higher level wins over anything set lower down.

Logos. A logo is uploaded with POST /uploads, which accepts one file up to 15 MB; the theme screen accepts images up to 2 MB and stores the returned address as the value.

Brand colour contrast check. When the owner picks a colour, the screen checks it against accessibility rules. It warns if the button text on the colour has less than 4.5 to 1 contrast, and warns if the colour on a white page has less than 3 to 1 (links and outlines will be hard to see, and a darker shade is used for brand text). When both pass, the screen says "Contrast OK" with the ratio. The warning is advice; it does not block saving.

Public theme for the login page. GET /public/theme/:organizationId (optionally with a location) is public and returns theme tokens only, nothing else about the clinic. An unknown organization gets the platform theme. The login page learns which clinic to show from an organization parameter in the address or from the last clinic used in that browser. The browser also keeps a copy of the last theme and its colours so the loading screen is on-brand before the server answers; local storage is used only for this convenience.

Figure 58.6 — Location branding (screenshot pending).

The sheet is titled "Location branding" with the text "A branch can show its own name and logo. Empty fields use the clinic's." It opens from the button on the theme page. Action Endpoint Permission

58.9 Limitations and known gaps

  • The sidebar layout is per clinic only; per-role layouts are not written yet (the column exists).
  • The owner cannot add new sidebar pages or permissions; both are fixed in code.
  • Only the name and logos can be customized per location.
  • The brand colour check is advice, not a rule.

58.10 Owner's FAQ

Who can switch a feature on that my plan does not include? Only the platform team, by entitling it. The owner can only enable features the clinic is entitled to.

If I hide a page in the sidebar, can people still open it? Yes, by address, if their role allows it. Hiding is cosmetic; use roles to remove access.

Can each branch have its own logo? Yes. Each branch can have its own name and light and dark logos; the colour and mode are clinic wide.

Why can I not change the colour? The platform team may have locked that key for clinics. The screen marks such a key as locked at a higher level.

Where do I set what a role sees first? On the role's Home page tab. The clinic-wide fallback is on the Sidebar screen.

What happens to people when I turn a feature off? They lose the permissions that belong to the feature at once, and the dialog before you confirm lists the roles affected.

Chapter 59 — Notification mechanics

This chapter explains how a notification travels inside the Platform, from the business event that causes it to the bell icon where a staff member reads it. It is written for the product owner who wants to understand the pipeline and its guarantees. The Notifications module chapter (Chapter 44) describes the settings screen, the event catalog and what users see; this chapter covers only the mechanics. Today the Platform delivers notifications in the application only: WhatsApp, SMS and email are prepared in the code but have no real sender.

59.1 The pipeline

Status: [Implemented] for in-app delivery. [Not implemented] for WhatsApp, SMS and email.

A notification event is a named thing that happens, such as order.submitted or item.ready (21 are seeded, all about lab orders, shipments, stages, appointments linked to labs and payments). When a workflow step runs the notify effect, the Platform decides who should be told, whether each person wants it, what the message says and when it may be sent. The result is one row per person and channel in a table called notification_outbox. A separate loop in the worker process sends those rows later. This is the transactional outbox pattern: the notification row is written in the same database transaction as the business change, so it exists only if the change was committed.

Figure 59.1 — The path of a notification from the business event to the inbox.

The flowchart reads from top to bottom. A "Business event" (for example order.submitted) triggers the "notify effect", which runs inside the transaction of the change. The effect asks the "Recipient resolver" for the audiences and people to tell. For each person and channel a "Decision" step applies the switches, the patient's opt-out and quiet hours. A "Template" step renders the message, filling placeholders. The result is stored in the database table notification_outbox, one row per person and channel. The "Relay in the worker", woken by a database NOTIFY and by a two-second poll, claims due rows. The "In-app provider" writes the user's copy into user_notifications, which is the bell inbox. A second branch, the "Dev log provider", handles WhatsApp, SMS and email by writing the message to the server log instead of sending it.

Technical references: backend/src/notifications/services/notification.service.ts · NotificationService.enqueue · backend/src/notifications/effects/notify.effect.ts · backend/src/notifications/delivery/

59.2 Event, recipients and audiences

Status: [Implemented]

The notify effect names an event code (and may narrow the audiences). An unknown code fails the whole transition, so a typo can never silently drop messages. Who receives the message is decided by a recipient resolver registered per kind of subject: the module that owns the subject says how to find its doctor, coordinator, lab and patient. Today only the lab order workflow registers one, so lab events are the only ones that produce notifications.

There are four audiences: patient (the only external audience), doctor, coordinator and lab. A recipient is a user (a signed-in person), a patient or a lab contact. The same person listed twice, or under two audiences, gets one row per channel. If an event is not meant for an audience, enqueueing for it fails with NOTIFICATION_AUDIENCE_INVALID. A patient is looked up in the same organization, so a clinic can never message another clinic's patient.

Technical references: backend/src/notifications/effects/notification-recipients.registry.ts · NotificationRecipientsRegistry · backend/src/notifications/notifications.enums.ts

59.3 Rules and the decision order

Status: [Implemented]

For every recipient and channel the Platform makes one decision. The first check that matches wins:

  1. An internal audience with a mandatory event on the in-app channel is queued, ignoring settings.
  2. If the audience's master switch is off, the row is stored as skipped_disabled.
  3. If the rule for this event and channel is off, it is skipped_disabled.
  4. If the patient opted out of the channel, it is skipped_opt_out.
  5. If the time is inside the audience's quiet hours (and the channel is not in-app), it is held_quiet_hours until the window ends.
  6. Otherwise it is queued for now.

Skipped rows are still written, so the clinic can see in its message log why nothing was sent. Defaults apply when a clinic has set nothing: the patient audience and every patient rule are off; internal audiences are on, with in-app on and the external channels off. The channels offered per audience in code are in-app only for doctor, coordinator and lab, and none for patients, so patients receive nothing today.

Quiet hours are a start and end time per audience. The window can cross midnight (for example 22:00 to 08:00); equal start and end means no window. They use the audience setting's timezone if it names one, otherwise the timezone of the location the event belongs to (Chapter 62), otherwise UTC. In-app messages are never held, because they are silent.

Technical references: backend/src/notifications/decision/notification-decision.ts · decide · quietHoursEnd

59.4 Templates

Status: [Implemented]

A template has a subject, a body, a channel, a language (English, Urdu or Roman Urdu) and optional provider reference. The body uses placeholders such as {clinic_name} and {recipient_name}, plus the event's own. An unknown placeholder becomes empty text so no raw braces ever reach a person. The Platform picks the clinic's own template in the person's language, then the platform's template in that language, then the same two in English. A rule can name a specific template. If no template exists, the event's name and description are used.

Technical references: backend/src/notifications/templates/template-render.ts · renderTemplate · pickTemplate

59.5 Outbox, relay and sending

Status: [Implemented]

Figure 59.2 — Status lifecycle of a row in notification_outbox.

The diagram starts at a dot and shows several entry points. A row is created as queued when the decision allows sending, as held_quiet_hours when it falls inside quiet hours, as skipped_disabled when a switch or rule is off, as skipped_opt_out when the patient opted out, and directly as failed when the channel needs an address and the recipient has none. A held row becomes queued when the relay claims it once the quiet window has ended. A queued row becomes sent when the provider accepts it. A queued row whose send fails stays queued and is tried again after a pause. It becomes failed on a permanent error or at the fifth attempt. sent, failed and both skipped statuses are final. The status delivered exists in the code for providers that report delivery but nothing sets it today.

The relay (NotificationRelayService) runs only in processes that run jobs, which is the worker. It is woken at once by a database NOTIFY sent inside the enqueue transaction (so it fires only on commit) and also polls every two seconds, which picks up retries and quiet-hours rows that are due. If the NOTIFY connection fails, it logs a warning and relies on polling.

Sending works like this:

  • A row is claimed with one short statement that locks it so no other worker takes it, adds one to its attempt count and pushes its due time out by a five-minute lease. If a worker dies mid-send, the row reappears after the lease.
  • The provider is called with no transaction open; the result is written back only if this claim is still the latest.
  • A failure is retried after 30 seconds, 2 minutes, 10 minutes and one hour; the fifth failure makes the row failed. A provider can mark an error permanent to skip retries.
  • Delivery is at least once. The in-app copy is protected by a unique link to the outbox row, so a retry after a crash never shows the same message twice.
  • Batches of 50 are processed until nothing is due.

Providers. The in-app provider writes user_notifications (user, event, title, body, link, read time). The development provider logs WhatsApp, SMS and email messages and marks them sent, so flows run end to end; it sends nothing to anyone. A real provider can take over a channel through the provider registry.

Technical references: backend/src/notifications/delivery/notification-relay.service.ts · notification-dispatcher.service.ts · in-app.provider.ts · dev-log.provider.ts · channel-provider.registry.ts

59.6 The inbox and the settings screen

Status: [Implemented]

The bell shows the signed-in user's inbox through GET /me/notifications (paged, with an unread-only filter), GET /me/notifications/unread-count, POST /me/notifications/:id/read and POST /me/notifications/read-all. These routes are context free: a user's inbox spans every clinic they work at, and lab users have no clinic location. Clinic settings are under /notification-settings and need notifications.settings.manage: the overview with master switches and quiet hours, audience updates, the rules matrix, templates (create, change, reset to platform wording) and the message log. A patient's channel preferences are read with patients.view and changed with patients.edit. Chapter 44 describes these screens.

59.7 Limitations and known gaps

  • Only lab-related events exist; no appointment reminders or billing notices are produced.
  • WhatsApp, SMS and email have no provider; patients cannot be reached.
  • Only the lab workflow registers recipients.
  • Inventory alerts are not notifications; they go to the server log only (Chapter 63).
  • The status delivered is never set.

59.8 Owner's FAQ

If a lab order is rolled back, is a notification still sent? No. The notification row is part of the same transaction and disappears with it.

Why did a staff member not get a message? Check the log in notification settings: it shows each row with its status and reason, such as an audience switched off or a rule disabled.

Can I send reminders to patients by WhatsApp? Not yet. The decision logic and templates exist, but the channel is commented out and no provider is connected.

What happens if the worker is down? Rows stay queued in the database and are sent when the worker returns; nothing is lost.

Can quiet hours delay an in-app message? No. Quiet hours apply only to external channels.

Chapter 60 — Audit logging

This chapter explains how the Platform records who changed what and when: the history tables, the modules that write to them today, who may read them and what is kept for how long. It is written for the product owner, who must be able to answer an auditor's question honestly. The most important message is that audit coverage is uneven: patients and several administration areas are recorded in detail, while appointments, employees, payroll and organizations are not yet recorded in the general audit log.

60.1 The history tables

Status: [Implemented]

The Platform has several history tables, written by different modules at different times.

Table Written by What a row says
audit_logs the shared audit service One change: entity type and id, action (create, update, void, delete, export, view_sensitive), the changed fields before and after, actor, actor side (clinic, lab, platform, system), IP address and request id
status_history the shared audit service One state change: from state, to state, action code, actor, channel (app, portal, magic link, proxy, QR), reason
billing_audit_logs billing services One billing event with before and after, reason, amount, actor and the actor's role
queue_events the queue orchestrator One queue event with a running sequence number, status before and after
prescription_history the prescription service One prescription event: created, amended (with a full snapshot of the earlier version), finalized, printed, shared

The table lists the five history tables and what each row records. audit_logs and status_history are the general tables. The other three are older, module-specific histories that stay as they are.

Append only. audit_logs and status_history are protected by database triggers that reject any update or delete, so a row, once written, cannot be changed through the application or by accident. commission_entries has a similar trigger (Chapter 35). billing_audit_logs, queue_events and prescription_history are append-only by convention: the code only inserts, but no trigger enforces it.

Written in the same transaction. The shared service always writes in the caller's transaction, so the history commits or rolls back together with the change. An update that changed nothing writes no row.

Subject. Each general row can carry a subject_id, the record whose history it joins. For example, a patient's vitals row carries the patient as subject, so one query returns the patient's whole history.

Technical references: backend/src/common/audit/audit.service.ts · AuditService · backend/src/common/audit/entities/ · backend/src/migrations/1792490000000-lab-management-foundation.ts · backend/src/billing/audit/billing-audit.service.ts · backend/src/queue/entities/queue-event.entity.ts · backend/src/prescriptions/entities/prescription-history.entity.ts

Figure 60.1 — Writers, history tables and readers.

The flowchart reads left to right. A box "Service change" (patients, roles, features, theme, sidebar, subscriptions) leads to "Same database transaction", which writes two tables: audit_logs (before and after of changed fields) and status_history (state changes). Three other writers stand alone: "Billing services" write billing_audit_logs, the "Queue orchestrator" writes queue_events and the "Prescription service" writes prescription_history. All five tables feed a single box, "Readers", which names the patient audit trail, the billing activity feed and the queue history.

60.3 Reading the history

Status: [Partial]

Reader Endpoint Permission Screen
Patient audit trail GET /patients/:id/audit-trail admin.audit.view A history sheet on the patient page, shown only to holders of the permission
Queue history of a session GET /queue/sessions/:id/events admin.audit.view Queue history

Entity timelines for labs lab endpoints lab permissions Activity timelines on lab pages

The table lists the readers. The patient audit trail merges audit_logs and status_history for the patient and every record under them, newest first (up to 200 entries), and the values are redacted for readers who lack the clinical or document permissions. The permission admin.audit.view is "View the audit log" in the Admin group; the owner and super admin hold it, and the Admin system role holds the whole Admin group by default (Chapter 11).

There is no organization-wide audit page: no screen or endpoint lists all changes of a clinic, searches by user or date, or exports the log. The general tables can be read only through the entity or subject timelines in the table and, for developers, in the database.

60.4 Retention

Status: [Not implemented]

The Platform has no retention or purge policy for audit data. The audit tables are append-only, so nothing deletes them. The only clean-up job in the area removes queue idempotency keys older than 24 hours and published realtime outbox rows older than 7 days (Chapter 63), which are technical records, not history. security_logs and session rows are also never purged. A clinic with a legal retention limit has no built-in way to apply it.

60.5 Who is the actor

Each general row stores the user id, the actor side and, when available, the IP address and a request id taken from an x-request-id header if the caller sent one. The side is clinic for clinic staff, lab for lab members, platform for a super admin and system for background jobs. A super admin acting inside a clinic is recorded as platform.

60.6 Limitations and known gaps

  • Appointments, staff data, payroll and organization settings have no audit history.
  • No organization-wide audit viewer, filter or export.
  • No retention policy.
  • Three of the five history tables are append-only by convention only.
  • Reading sensitive patient data is not logged; the action view_sensitive exists but is not written by any reader.
  • Encounter notes in progress are not audited; the plan is one snapshot at completion (not built).

60.7 Owner's FAQ

Can I see who edited a patient's phone number? Yes, if you hold admin.audit.view: open the patient and the audit history. It shows the old and new value, who and when.

Can I see who cancelled an appointment? Not from an audit log today. Appointments are not audited. The appointment row itself shows its status and cancellation reason.

Can someone delete a history row to hide a change? Not through the application. For audit_logs and status_history the database itself rejects updates and deletes.

Who is told when patient data is exported? Nobody is notified, but each export writes a record with who, when, how many rows and the filters.

How long are audit records kept? Forever, because nothing deletes them.

Chapter 61 — Error handling

This chapter describes how the Platform reports problems: the shape of every API answer, the families of error codes, how validation and database conflicts become messages, how retries stay safe, and what the web app shows the user. It is written for the product owner and for support staff who read an error message and need to know what it means. Chapter 5 traces one request through the system and shows the main status codes; this chapter goes into the error side in more detail.

61.1 The envelope

Status: [Implemented]

Every controller answers inside one JSON envelope built by ResponseWrapper. On success the fields are data (the payload), message (for example "Patient created successfully"), isSuccess (true) and httpStatusCode (always 200 in the envelope, even when the HTTP status is 201). On failure the global exception filter GlobalExceptionFilter builds the same envelope with isSuccess false, the real HTTP status in httpStatusCode, a short message for people, a devMessage with a technical text for developers and an error field holding the exception body. The web app reads res.data.data on success and err.response.data.message (or error.code) on failure.

Technical references: backend/src/common/dtos/ResponseWrapper.ts · backend/src/common/exceptions/HttpExceptionHandler.ts

61.2 What the filter does with an error

Status: [Implemented]

Figure 61.1 — How an exception becomes an envelope and a message on screen.

The flowchart reads from top to bottom. An "Exception anywhere" in the request reaches GlobalExceptionFilter. The filter asks whether it is an HTTP exception. If yes, the request keeps its own status and body, with a code, a message and any extra fields. If no, which means an unexpected failure, the answer is 500 with the message "Something went wrong". Both branches build the envelope: isSuccess false, message, devMessage and error. The web app then shows a toast, an ErrorState panel or a friendly text chosen by the error code.

Categories of error:

  • Expected HTTP errors. Business rules and security refusals are thrown as typed exceptions with a status and, in most modules, a machine-readable code. The message is written for the user.
  • Validation errors. The global validation pipe rejects bad input (section 61.3). Several messages are possible; the envelope's message shows the first one.
  • Unexpected errors. Anything that is not an HTTP exception, such as an unhandled database failure, is logged with its stack on the server and answered as 500 "Something went wrong". The user-facing text never contains internals.
  • Rate limit. A throttled request is answered 429 with "Too many requests. Please try again later." and a number of seconds to wait (Chapter 56).

Every error is logged by the application logger together with the request address.

61.3 Validation

Status: [Implemented]

The global validation pipe converts input to the types named in each request class and has whitelist and forbidNonWhitelisted on. A request that contains a field the API does not define is rejected with 400, not silently ignored, and a field with a wrong type or format is rejected with a message such as "email must be an email". Request classes use validation decorators for lengths, formats, enumerations and nested objects. The same rules appear in the web app as form schemas, so most mistakes are caught before the request leaves the browser; the server rule is the one that counts.

61.4 Error code families

Status: [Implemented]

Status Code or family Meaning
400 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REQUIRED, REASON_REQUIRED, INVALID_PERMISSIONS, validation messages The request is incomplete or malformed
401 (message only) No token, expired token or bad token; the web app tries to refresh
402 SUBSCRIPTION_EXPIRED The clinic is read-only because its subscription lapsed
403 NO_PERMISSION with the missing permissions, NOT_ENTITLED, ESCALATION, SYSTEM_ROLE_READ_ONLY, SETTING_LOCKED, FORBIDDEN, LAB_ACCESS_DENIED The caller is not allowed
404 NOT_FOUND, BILLING_NOT_FOUND, LAB_NOT_FOUND, and similar The record does not exist in this organization
409 DOCTOR_DOUBLE_BOOKED, VERSION_CONFLICT, STALE_VERSION, ALREADY_CHECKED_IN, ACTIVE_WITH_OTHER_DOCTOR, DOCTOR_BUSY, ROLE_NAME_TAKEN, ROLE_HAS_MEMBERS, REQUEST_IN_FLIGHT, BILLING_DUPLICATE, PLAN_LIMIT and similar The request conflicts with the current state or with another request
422 INVALID_TRANSITION, IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED, NOT_TODAY, LATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED, SESSION_NOT_OPEN, many BILLING_*, FORM_* and WORKFLOW_* codes The request is well formed but the rules refuse it
429 MAGIC_LINK_RATE_LIMITED and the login throttle Too many requests
500 BILLING_INVARIANT_VIOLATION, WORKFLOW_MISCONFIGURED, anything unexpected A bug or a broken money rule
503 LOCK_TIMEOUT The queue was busy; retry

The table groups the codes by HTTP status and shows what each family means. It lists examples, not every code. The codes are thrown by several module-specific error builders, each of which passes the code in error.code:

  • Billing (billing-errors.ts): about 40 BILLING_* codes plus COMPENSATION_* and COMMISSION_* for the commission rules. Each maps to a fixed status, for example allocation larger than the balance is 422 and a duplicate is 409.
  • Queue (queue.errors.ts): NOT_FOUND, FORBIDDEN, INVALID_TRANSITION, SESSION_NOT_OPEN, DOCTOR_BUSY, VERSION_CONFLICT, ALREADY_CHECKED_IN, ACTIVE_WITH_OTHER_DOCTOR, LATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED, NOT_TODAY, LOCK_TIMEOUT, IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_*, REQUEST_IN_FLIGHT, REASON_REQUIRED.
  • Workflow engine (engine-errors.ts): form, workflow and stage template codes, INVALID_TRANSITION, TRANSITION_FORBIDDEN, TRANSITION_INPUT_REQUIRED, TRANSITION_REASON_REQUIRED.
  • Labs (lab-errors.ts, plus lab billing, catalog, orders and payables): LAB_* codes, including LAB_PORTAL_CLINIC_CONTEXT and LAB_SELECTION_REQUIRED.
  • Notifications (notification-errors.ts): NOTIFICATION_* codes and PATIENT_NOT_FOUND.
  • Access and features: NO_PERMISSION, ESCALATION, INVALID_PERMISSIONS, NOT_ENTITLED, SETTING_LOCKED, PLAN_LIMIT.

DOCTOR_DOUBLE_BOOKED is the appointment overlap error (Chapter 29): the database rejects two bookings of one doctor at overlapping times, and the service turns the failure into a 409 with that code.

Technical references: backend/src/billing/common/billing-errors.ts · backend/src/queue/queue.errors.ts · backend/src/engine/common/engine-errors.ts · backend/src/labs/common/lab-errors.ts · backend/src/notifications/notification-errors.ts · backend/src/access/decorators/access.decorators.ts

61.5 Safe retries: idempotency keys and If-Match

Status: [Implemented]

Two mechanisms protect against double clicks, flaky networks and two people editing the same record.

Idempotency-Key. A client sends a header Idempotency-Key (1 to 150 characters) on actions that must not run twice. The server stores the key, a hash of the request and, once finished, the response, inside the same transaction as the work. If the same key arrives again with the same request, the stored answer is replayed and nothing runs twice. The same key with a different request gives 422 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED. The same key while the first request is still running gives 409 REQUEST_IN_FLIGHT. A missing key where one is required gives 400 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REQUIRED. The key is required on every queue change, on patient check-in from an appointment, on money-moving lab billing posts and on the workflow engine transitions; the web app creates a fresh key for each open sheet or action. Queue idempotency keys are deleted after 24 hours by a nightly job.

If-Match and versions. Records that two people may edit carry a version number. A client may send If-Match: <version> (queue entries, lab order actions) or the version in the body; the server checks it while holding a row lock and, if the record has moved on, answers 409 with VERSION_CONFLICT or STALE_VERSION and the current state or version. The web app reloads and asks the user to try again, with texts such as "Someone else changed this just now. The latest version is loaded".

Technical references: backend/src/common/idempotency/idempotency.service.ts · IdempotencyService · backend/src/common/errors/optimistic-lock.ts · assertVersion · backend/src/queue/decorators/queue-request.decorators.ts

61.6 Database constraints become messages

Status: [Partial]

The database enforces uniqueness and exclusion rules, and several services translate the database error into a clear conflict. The translation is per service; there is no global mapping.

  • Exclusion constraint on appointments (no_doctor_overlap): Postgres error 23P01 becomes 409 DOCTOR_DOUBLE_BOOKED. Compensation plan versions and lab prices use similar exclusion constraints with their own messages.
  • Unique violations (23505) are translated in billing, lab billing, lab orders, lab catalog and lab payables into codes such as BILLING_DUPLICATE.
  • Foreign key violations (23503) are translated when deleting an employee that is still referenced.
  • Lock timeouts in the queue become 503 LOCK_TIMEOUT.

A database error that no service translates reaches the filter as an unexpected error and is answered as 500 "Something went wrong". A duplicate patient number or purchase order number, for instance, would currently surface this way (Chapter 62).

61.7 In the web app

Status: [Implemented]

  • 401 and refresh. The shared axios client refreshes the access token on a 401 and retries once (Chapter 56).
  • Toasts. Mutations report failures with a toast (the library sonner, at the top right, closable, 4 seconds). Many hooks have a helper that reads err.response.data.message and falls back to a text such as "Failed to create item". About 180 places raise an error toast.
  • Friendly code maps. Billing, labs, lab orders, lab catalog, lab payables, lab billing and the engine studio each have a small map from an error code to a plain sentence, for example the billing code for a missing document code becomes "Set a document code for this location in Billing settings first." If a code has no entry, the server's own message is shown, then a generic text.
  • Stale screens. The queue hook shows "Someone else just changed this patient — showing the latest." as a warning on VERSION_CONFLICT and refreshes the screen.
  • Page states. Every list or detail screen uses LoadingSkeleton while loading (table, cards, stats or detail shape), EmptyState when there is nothing (icon, title, message and an optional action) and ErrorState when a request failed (title "Something went wrong", a sentence and a Try again button). A route-level error boundary, RouteError, shows the error message with a retry button for render failures.
  • Access errors. A missing route permission shows the No access page, not an error (Chapter 57). The access gate shows "Couldn't load your access" if /me/access fails.
  • Query settings. Queries retry twice and mutations once, with 5 minutes of freshness.

Technical references: web-app/src/lib/api.ts · web-app/src/lib/query-client.ts · web-app/src/features/billing/lib/billing-errors.ts · web-app/src/features/engine-studio/lib/studio-errors.ts · web-app/src/features/queue/hooks/useQueueAction.ts · web-app/src/components/feedback/ErrorState.tsx · EmptyState.tsx · LoadingSkeleton.tsx · web-app/src/components/shared/RouteError.tsx

Figure 61.2 — How an expired access token is replaced without the user noticing.

The diagram has three participants: the Screen, the apiClient axios instance and the API. The screen sends request A. The client sends A with an expired access token. The API answers 401 "Token has expired". The client marks A as retried and starts a refresh. It sends POST /auth/refresh with the cookie. The API answers with a new access token and a new cookie. The client stores the token and context, sends A again with the new token, gets a 200 envelope and returns the data to the screen. A note says that if the refresh fails, the stored login is cleared and the browser goes to /login. While one refresh is running, other requests that fail with 401 wait in a queue and are retried with the new token.

61.8 Limitations and known gaps

  • Error messages are in English. Only the No access headline carries a Roman-Urdu line.
  • Code-to-sentence maps exist for some modules only; others show the server's text.
  • There is no central error-tracking service; errors are written to the server log.
  • Database errors are translated service by service, so an untranslated one shows as a generic 500.
  • The error body includes a developer message field in every failure.

61.9 Owner's FAQ

A user says "Something went wrong". What now? It is an unexpected server error. Ask for the time and the page; the server log holds the cause. Other failures give a specific message.

What does 402 mean? The subscription expired; the clinic is read-only until a payment is recorded.

What does "Someone else changed this" mean? Another person saved the same record first. The latest data is loaded; redo the change.

What happens if the receptionist double-clicks "Check in"? The second click carries the same idempotency key, so the first result is returned and only one token is issued.

Does the API ignore fields it does not know? No. It rejects them with 400.

Chapter 62 — Time, money and document numbers

This chapter explains three rules that run through every module: how the Platform decides what time it is for a clinic, how it stores and calculates money, and how it numbers invoices, patients, orders and other documents. It is written for the product owner, because mistakes in these three areas, a wrong day, a wrong rupee or a duplicate number, are the ones that clinics notice first. The chapter states the rules, where they are followed strictly, and where the code still departs from them.

62.1 Clinic time

Status: [Implemented] for the rule. [Partial] for coverage: some jobs and statistics still use the server clock.

The rule. Every clinic date and time follows the location's timezone (the timezone of the location, for example a Pakistan or a Gulf timezone). Working hours, appointment availability, the same-day duplicate check, the queue's day boundary, token days and quiet hours all use it. A clinic in one timezone and a server in another still agree on what "today" means for the clinic.

How it works. ClockService is the single source of "now" and "today" for clinic logic. Its main functions are:

  • now(): the current instant (tests can replace it).
  • timezoneFor(locationId): the location's timezone name, defaulting to UTC when the stored name is not valid, cached for 60 seconds.
  • today(timezone): the location-local date as YYYY-MM-DD.
  • wallClock(timezone, instant): the local weekday and HH:MM.
  • dayRange(timezone, date): the start and end instants (in UTC) of a local day.
  • at(timezone, date, time): the instant when the clinic's wall clock reads a given date and time.

The code rule is: never use new Date() together with setHours() for a clinic day or time, because those use the server's timezone. Appointments, queue and notifications follow it (Chapters 29, 30 and 59).

Where the server clock is still used. These places do not use the location's timezone:

  • Scheduled jobs. Daily and monthly jobs run on the worker's server timezone, for example the 01:00 credit expiry, the 02:30 billing check, the 08:00 inventory alert and the payroll run at 05:00 on the 1st (Chapter 63 and Appendix E). The queue's day-end job is an exception: it decides what a past clinic day is from each location's policy.
  • Credit expiry. The check works out "today" from the server's local date, so a prepaid credit can expire a few hours early or late for a clinic in another timezone.
  • Statistics. The financial summary takes its default date and its month list from the server date.
  • Numbering years. The year inside purchase order and prescription numbers is the server's year.
  • Leave balance year uses the server year.
  • The lab catalog calendar fixes its "today" to one specific timezone (Asia/Karachi) regardless of the location.
  • Exports that print a date (patient export file name) use the server date.

For a clinic whose timezone differs from the server's by a few hours, the differences matter only near midnight or at month boundaries.

Technical references: backend/src/common/clock/clock.service.ts · ClockService · backend/src/common/clock/tz.util.ts · backend/src/billing/patient-credits.service.ts · backend/src/billing/financial-summary.service.ts · web-app/src/features/lab-catalog/lib/money.ts · catalogToday

62.2 Money

Status: [Implemented]

What is stored. Money has two storage styles, depending on the module:

Style Where Meaning
numeric(12,2) rupees Patient billing: charges, invoices, payments, refunds, ledger entries Exact decimal with two places
bigint paisa Commissions (rules, entries, settlements, compensation plans), the lab billing tables (invoice, credits, payments), and a few billing fields Whole number of the smallest unit
decimal(10,2) Inventory prices and quantities, payroll records, employee salary on assignments Exact decimal

The table shows the three styles. A paisa is one hundredth of a rupee; "PKR" is the default currency and not a limit. Amounts cross the API as numbers with at most two decimals in the billing module, and as integer paisa in the lab and commission modules.

How it is calculated. All billing math is done in integer paisa so that no floating-point error can creep in. money.ts holds the helpers: toPaisa and fromPaisa, sumPaisa, percentOf and basisPointsOf. A percentage with up to two decimals is turned into basis points (17.5 percent becomes 1750) and applied with exact big-integer arithmetic.

  • Rounding is half up (0.5 paisa rounds to the next whole paisa), the same everywhere, including tax.
  • Splitting. When an amount is shared in proportion (for example tax spread over charges), each share is rounded down and the leftover paisa go to the largest share, so the shares always add up exactly to the total.
  • Database columns are read through transformers: numeric comes back from the database as text and is rounded to two decimals; bigint comes back as text and is converted to a number, which is exact for any clinic amount.

Figure 62.1 — How an amount typed by a person travels to the database and back.

The flowchart reads top to bottom. A user types 4500.50. The web app converts the text to 450050 paisa with integer-only code (no floating point). The API receives the amount as rupees or paisa depending on the field. Server code calculates in integer paisa with half-up rounding. The value is stored in the database as numeric or as bigint paisa. When the screen reads it back, the web app formats it with the organization's currency.

Tax is exclusive. Prices are before tax. Tax equals the taxable amount (the sum of active charge net amounts after discounts) times the rate, rounded half up once per invoice. The total is subtotal minus discount plus tax. The rate is copied onto the invoice when it is issued from the location's billing settings, and later edits use that copy, not the current setting. Tax is spread over the invoice's charges so that payments can be allocated charge by charge; tax is never revenue and never earns commission. Lab invoices use the same half-up rounding and keep tax in its own paisa column.

Currency. Each organization has a currency (default PKR). It is returned with the organization list after sign-in. The web app's activeCurrency() and useCurrency() read it, and formatPaisa writes amounts as "PKR 4,500.50". Number grouping uses a Pakistani locale. The currency is a display label: there is no conversion and no multi-currency ledger.

Technical references: backend/src/billing/common/money.ts · money-column.ts · paisa-column.ts · backend/src/billing/tax/invoice-tax.ts · backend/src/organizations/entities/organization.entity.ts · web-app/src/lib/currency.ts · web-app/src/features/lab-catalog/lib/money.ts

62.3 Document numbering

Status: [Partial]. Billing and lab documents are numbered safely; some older numbers are not.

There are four numbering families.

Family Documents Format How it counts
Per location, per type, per year Patient invoices (INV), receipts (REC), refunds (RFD) location code, type, year, five digits, for example MAIN-INV-2026-00001 Table document_sequences
Per organization sequence Lab order (LAB), shipment (SHP), lab invoice (LINV), lab receipt (LRC), payment reversal (LRV), credit note (LCN), lab refund (LRF), vendor bill (VB), vendor payment (VP) prefix and at least four digits, for example LAB-0001 Table number_sequences
Count plus one in application code Patient number, treatment plan number, patient-page prescription number P-00001, TP-00001, RX-00001 Number of existing rows plus one
Last number plus one in application code Purchase order number, prescription number from the prescriptions module PO-2026-00001, RX-2026-00001 Reads the latest row and adds one

The table lists the four families with their formats. Invoices, receipts and refunds need the location's document code (2 to 6 letters or digits, set in billing settings and locked after the first invoice); without it the Platform refuses to issue the document.

The safe families. The first two families use a database counter row that is locked until the surrounding transaction ends. Concurrent requests wait their turn, no number repeats, and a rollback gives the number back, so numbers have no gaps. The service refuses to run outside a transaction. Invoice sequences restart each year, per location. Lab sequences never restart.

The risky families.

  • Patient, plan and prescription numbers (count plus one). The next number is the count of rows for the organization plus one. Two registrations at the same moment can compute the same number, and the second save fails on the unique index. Patients are deleted permanently, so after a deletion the count drops and the next number can repeat one that is still in use (the patient count includes soft-deleted rows but not permanently deleted ones). The result in either case is a failed save that the user sees as a generic error, not a wrong document.
  • Purchase order and prescription numbers (last plus one). The next number reads the most recent row of the organization and adds one, with the year taken from the server clock. Two simultaneous requests can read the same row. In addition, the unique index on the purchase order number and on the prescription number covers all organizations together, so two clinics that both reach the same sequence in the same year would collide.

These are reliability risks, not security ones. A collision stops the save; it does not issue a duplicate.

Technical references: backend/src/billing/numbering/document-sequence.service.ts · DocumentSequenceService · backend/src/common/sequences/number-sequence.service.ts · NumberSequenceService · backend/src/patients/patients.service.ts · generatePatientNumber · backend/src/inventory/services/purchase-order.service.ts · generatePoNumber · backend/src/prescriptions/services/prescription.service.ts · generatePrescriptionNumber

62.4 Limitations and known gaps

  • Several jobs and statistics use the server timezone, not the clinic's.
  • Two storage styles for money (decimal rupees and integer paisa) exist side by side; conversion happens at module boundaries.
  • Count-based and last-number-based document numbers can collide under concurrency, and purchase order and prescription numbers are unique across all clinics together.
  • No multi-currency support or conversion.
  • Tax is exclusive only; there is no tax-inclusive pricing.

62.5 Owner's FAQ

What time does "today" mean for my branch? The branch's own timezone, set on the location.

Why can a daily job run at an odd hour for my clinic? Jobs follow the server's timezone. A job set for 01:00 runs at 01:00 server time.

Can an invoice number repeat? No. Invoice, receipt and refund numbers come from a locked counter per branch and year.

Can two patients get the same patient number? The database refuses a duplicate, so the second save fails and must be tried again.

Are my prices with or without tax? Without. Tax is added on top at the rate set for the branch when the invoice is issued.

Can I invoice in another currency? You can set the organization's currency label, but there is no conversion.

Chapter 63 — Realtime updates and background jobs

This chapter explains the two ways the Platform acts without a user clicking: it pushes live updates to open screens over a socket connection, and it runs timed jobs and background loops in a worker process. It is written for the product owner who must understand which processes to run and what happens when Redis or the worker is down. Appendix E holds the full job table; this chapter restates the essentials and explains how the pieces fit together. The queue module (Chapter 30) and notifications (Chapters 44 and 59) are the main users of these mechanisms.

63.1 Process roles

Status: [Implemented]

The backend is one program that starts in one of three roles, chosen by the start command.

Role Start file Serves web requests and sockets Runs jobs and relays Needs Redis
api main.api.ts Yes No Yes, to receive events
worker main.worker.ts No Yes Yes, to send events
all main.ts Yes Yes No

The table shows the three roles. In production, run two or more api processes behind a load balancer and exactly one worker. In development, the single all process does everything and needs no Redis, because the relay hands events directly to the local socket gateway. The job scheduler is enabled only in processes whose role is not api, so adding API processes never duplicates a job.

Figure 63.1 — The browser, two API processes, one worker, PostgreSQL and Redis.

The flowchart reads left to right. The Browser talks to API process 1 and API process 2 over HTTP and Socket.IO. Both API processes read and write PostgreSQL. The Worker process, marked "run exactly one", also uses PostgreSQL. The worker publishes events and a heartbeat to Redis. Redis delivers them to both API processes through a subscription. A further arrow shows an API process using Redis for the access change bus, which is how one API process tells the others that access changed (Chapter 57).

Technical references: backend/src/common/runtime/process-role.ts · backend/src/main.ts · main.api.ts · main.worker.ts · backend/src/app.module.ts · AppModule.forRole

63.2 The realtime gateway

Status: [Implemented]

What it does. Pushes small "something changed" messages to open browser screens so that the reception board, doctor screen, waiting-room display and permission-aware screens stay live without constant refreshing.

How it connects. A Socket.IO gateway listens at the path /realtime of the API. The web app connects with websocket transport and passes its access token in the handshake. The token is verified once, when the socket connects. A browser with no token may connect anonymously, but may join only the public display room. After connecting, the client sends a subscribe message naming a room; the server answers with success or a reason.

Rooms.

Room Who may join What it carries
session:<id> Users with access to the queue session's location Events for one doctor's queue (doctor screen, reception)
location:<id>:board Users with access to the location Events of every queue at the location (reception board)
location:<id>:display Anyone, no sign-in Waiting-room TV events; payloads carry token numbers and doctor names, never patient names
org:<id> Users with access to the organization (super admin, owner, or an active staff assignment) The access.changed event with the organization id and the new version

The table lists the four room types. Anything else gets "Unknown room"; a room the user may not enter gets "No access to this room".

Events are nudges. A message carries a sequence number (seq). The browser keeps the sequence of the snapshot it loaded, ignores older or duplicate messages and fetches a fresh snapshot when it sees a newer one. This makes delivery at least once safe, because a duplicate does nothing.

Technical references: backend/src/queue/realtime/queue.gateway.ts · QueueGateway · web-app/src/features/access/hooks/useAccessSocket.ts

63.3 From a commit to a screen: outbox, relay, Redis

Status: [Implemented]

When a queue action changes state, the same database transaction also writes an event row in the outbox table and sends a database NOTIFY, so an event exists only if the change was committed. The outbox relay in the worker takes unpublished rows (up to 100 at a time, locking them so a second relay would skip them), publishes each to one Redis channel, waits until Redis accepted the whole batch and only then marks the rows as published. If Redis is down, the batch is rolled back and tried again every second. It is woken by the NOTIFY and also polls every second as a fallback. Every API process subscribes to the channel and emits each message to its own local sockets, so a browser connected to any API process sees every event. Chapter 5, section 5.8, shows this as a sequence diagram.

Heartbeat and watchdog. The worker publishes a heartbeat to the same channel every 5 seconds. Each API process runs a watchdog: it considers the bus healthy only while it is subscribed and has seen a heartbeat within 15 seconds. When the bus is unhealthy (Redis or worker down), the API process refuses new socket connections and drops existing ones, using a transport close so that browsers keep trying to reconnect. Screens then fall back to polling about every 10 seconds and reload their data once the socket returns. At start-up the gateway stays closed until the first heartbeat arrives.

Access changes. The access change bus is a second, separate path on its own Redis channel. When an organization's access version is bumped, the bus notifies the local caches and the local gateway, and publishes to Redis so the other processes do the same. Each process then emits access.changed to its sockets in the org:<id> room. This path does not use the outbox or the worker (Chapter 57).

Single-process mode. In the all role, the relay publishes straight to the local gateway.

Technical references: backend/src/queue/realtime/outbox-relay.service.ts · OutboxRelayService · redis-realtime.publisher.ts · redis-realtime.subscriber.ts · realtime-bus.ts · in-process-realtime.publisher.ts · backend/src/access/version/access-change-bus.ts

63.4 Scheduled jobs

Status: [Implemented] (the inventory alert job is [Partial])

All jobs run in the worker (or the all process). The schedules are in server time; none sets a timezone.

Job Schedule What it does
Queue no-show marker every 60 seconds Marks a booked patient as no-show once they have not checked in by the start time plus the location's maximum lateness
Queue call timeout every 15 seconds Skips a called patient who never came, when the queue policy sets a timeout
Queue session day-end every 5 minutes Closes empty queue sessions of a past clinic day; leaves non-empty ones open and logs an alert
Queue cleanup daily at 03:15 Deletes queue idempotency keys older than 24 hours and published outbox rows older than 7 days
Patient credit expiry daily at 01:00 Marks prepaid credits past their expiry date as expired
Billing invariant check daily at 02:30 Recomputes billing totals, checks money rules including the commission ledger and logs any break
Month-end payroll 05:00 on the 1st of each month Generates payroll records for the month just ended for every active location; locations already generated are skipped
Inventory alerts daily at 08:00 Counts low-stock and soon-expiring items and writes a warning to the server log only

The table lists the eight timed jobs. The first four keep the live queue consistent; the others handle daily and monthly housekeeping. Appendix E gives the same table with statuses and references. The queue day-end job is the only one that respects each location's clinic day, taken from its queue policy.

Background loops. Three loops run continuously in the worker. The queue outbox relay (section 63.3). The notification relay, which is woken by a database NOTIFY and polls every two seconds, sends notification rows to the inbox (Chapter 59). The heartbeat is published every 5 seconds. Both relays follow the outbox pattern: a change and its message commit together, and a separate loop delivers the message later. If the database NOTIFY connection drops, each relay logs a warning and keeps working by polling.

Other timers. The in-memory rate limit tables in the authentication guards and the magic-link throttle are swept every minute or when they grow large; they do not need the worker.

Technical references: backend/src/queue/jobs/queue-jobs.service.ts · backend/src/billing/patient-credits.service.ts · backend/src/billing/invariants/billing-invariant.job.ts · backend/src/payroll/payroll.service.ts · backend/src/inventory/services/inventory-alerts.service.ts · backend/src/notifications/delivery/notification-relay.service.ts · docs/handbook/src/appendix/appE-scheduled-jobs.md

63.5 Limitations and known gaps

  • Exactly one worker must run; nothing in the code stops a second worker, and a second worker would run each timed job a second time (the relays are safe with several workers, the timed jobs are not guaranteed to be).
  • Job times follow the server timezone, not the clinics'.
  • Inventory alerts reach only the server log, not any user.
  • Realtime depends on Redis in production; without it screens poll about every 10 seconds.
  • The access token is checked once when a socket connects; the connection continues after the token expires.
  • There is no clean-up job for session rows, security logs or the notification outbox.

63.6 Owner's FAQ

What happens if Redis is down? Realtime stops: the API refuses sockets and screens poll every ten seconds, so they update a little later. Access changes still reach the process that made them at once and the others within 15 seconds.

What happens if the worker is down? No timed jobs run, no notifications are sent and no queue events are published. Rows wait in the database and are processed when the worker returns. Screens fall back to polling.

Can I run two workers for safety? No. Run exactly one. A second worker would repeat the scheduled jobs.

Do I need Redis on my laptop? No. The single all process does not need it.

Can the waiting-room TV show patient names? No. The public display room carries token numbers and doctor names only.

Part 8 — Current status

Chapter 64 — Feature Status Matrix

This chapter lists every feature described in the module chapters (28 to 45), the workflow chapters (46 to 55) and the cross-cutting chapters (56 to 63), one row each, with its status label. It is for the owner who needs to know what is really built before promising anything to a clinic. The status of each row was merged from the notes of the chapters and checked against the chapter text; where a chapter and its notes differed, the chapter wins.

64.1 How to read the matrix

Each row has four columns: the chapter number, the feature as a user would name it, the status label and a one-line note. The four labels mean the following.

  • [Implemented]: built end to end. The backend and logic exist and a web screen uses them, or it is a backend-only job by design.
  • [Partial]: some of it exists. The note says what is missing, for example "backend only, no screen calls it".
  • [Not implemented]: planned, seeded, commented out or only mentioned. It must not be described as working.
  • [Unverified]: the code could not confirm it. The note says what could not be confirmed.

The workflow chapters (46 to 55) follow one business process across several modules, so many of their rows restate a feature that already has a row in a module chapter. They are listed separately so that each workflow can be judged on its own, and the totals in Section 64.5 report modules, workflows and cross-cutting chapters separately to avoid counting the same feature twice. No application was run while the handbook was written, so every label comes from reading the code.
