The module chapters hold 324 rows: 246 Implemented (76 percent), 60 Partial, 15 Not implemented and 3 Unverified. The workflow chapters hold 82 rows and the cross-cutting chapters 62. Adding modules and cross-cutting rows, which do not overlap, gives 386 distinct rows with 290 Implemented, 69 Partial, 24 Not implemented and 3 Unverified. The grand total of 468 includes the workflow rows, which repeat module features.

The pattern behind the numbers is consistent. The Partial label is almost always "the backend exists but no screen reaches it" or "the data is recorded but no rule reads it", so a Partial row is usually a small piece of web work or a decision, not a missing engine. The Not implemented rows are mostly features a clinic would expect from a mature product (patient messaging, reminders, attendance, deductions, audit coverage). The Unverified rows are concentrated in inventory, where a foreign-key mismatch could make writes fail at run time, and in one job-behaviour question during read-only mode. Chapter 65 lists each gap with its severity, and Chapter 67 lists the questions that decide what to build next.

Chapter 65 — Known Gaps

This chapter collects every gap found while the handbook was written: features that do not exist, features that exist in the backend but cannot be reached from the web app, settings that do nothing, data-integrity oddities and places where older documents describe something the code no longer does. It is for the owner who has to decide what to fix, build or promise before more clinics go live. Each gap states what it is, why it matters to an owner, which chapter holds the evidence, a severity and a suggested next step.

65.1 How severity is judged

Severity is judged by the effect on a live clinic, not by the effort to fix it.

  • High: the problem can stop daily work (registering a patient, writing a prescription) or put the business at risk, and it can happen in normal use.
  • Medium: a clinic would notice and need a workaround, or an expectation set by the product screens is not met, but daily work continues.
  • Low: a convenience, a cleanup or a feature most clinics can live without.

No application was run while the handbook was written, so every gap was found by reading the code. Where a gap depends on behaviour that was deduced but not observed, the text says so.

65.2 Features that are not built

These features are absent. Some have a seeded feature key or a database table that suggests they exist; none of them works.

Gap Why it matters to an owner Evidence Severity Suggested next step
No messages to patients by SMS, WhatsApp or email, and no appointment reminders Clinics cannot remind patients of visits, so no-shows are handled by phone calls only. The notification pipeline already exists, but the only active channel is the in-app inbox for staff and lab members. Chapters 44, 59 Medium Decide on a provider (Question 3 in Chapter 67), then switch on the patient audience and add a reminder event and job.
No renewal or trial-ending messages to clinic owners An owner learns of an expiring trial only from the banner inside the app. Expiry puts the clinic in read-only mode. Chapters 45, 53 Medium Send an email to the owner at fixed days before expiry.
No patient portal Patients cannot see their own records or invoices online. The feature key was retired. Chapters 1, 28 Low Treat as a roadmap item; no work needed for current clinics.
No online booking and no recurring appointments Every booking is made by staff, and a course of visits must be booked one by one. Chapter 29 Low Roadmap items.
No insurance claims and no online payment gateway Insurance details can be stored (backend only) but no claim is created. Payments are recorded by staff, never collected online. Chapters 28, 34 Low Roadmap items; confirm whether target clinics need them.
No server-generated PDF receipts or invoices Receipts and invoices are printed from the browser (A4 and 80 mm). They cannot be emailed or stored as files. Chapters 34, 48 Low Add a PDF generator only if sending receipts to patients becomes a requirement.
No attendance tracking Payroll uses salary and commission only; there is no record of who came to work. Leave exists but is not read by payroll. Chapter 37 Medium Decide whether attendance is wanted at all; if so, design it with payroll deductions.
No payroll deductions, tax or bank files Net pay always equals gross pay, so deductions and withholding must be done outside the Platform. Chapters 38, 51 Medium Define the deduction rules the target market needs, then add them to payroll generation.
No deploy or continuous-integration configuration The repository holds no Dockerfile, pipeline or hosting configuration. How the Platform is deployed lives in people's heads. Chapter 6 High Write down and automate the build, migration and process-role steps before more clinics depend on it.
Chairs exist as a table only The chairs entity has no module, no endpoint and no screen. Chapters 12, 26 Low Remove the entity or build the module; the rest of the Platform does not need it.
No lab order can be started from the consultation workspace Doctors must leave the consultation and use the Lab orders page. Lab orders carry no link to the encounter. Chapters 31, 48 Low Add a button that opens a lab order with the patient and doctor prefilled.
No structured allergy list and no drug-interaction check Allergy alerts are text chips built from free-text fields. A doctor can prescribe a drug the patient is allergic to without any warning. Chapter 31 Medium Add a structured allergy list first; a drug check can follow.
No way to assign an existing employee to a second location The only way to create an assignment is to create a new employee, and a phone number that already exists is refused. A doctor who works at two locations cannot be set up. Chapters 37, 47 Medium Add an endpoint and screen that create an assignment for an existing employee.
No SOAP note entity or note templates Visit notes are four fixed text fields. Clinics that need structured notes cannot have them. Chapter 31 Low Defer until a clinic asks.
No manual commission adjustment The source type exists in the ledger but nothing writes it, so a one-off correction to a doctor's commission needs a database change. Chapter 35 Low Add an adjustment screen with a reason and an audit row.
No per-location patient visit statistics The patient_visits table is never written, so the endpoint always returns an empty list. Chapters 17, 27, 28 Low Drop the table and endpoint, or fill it from encounters.
No organization-wide audit viewer and no audit for appointments, employees, payroll, organizations or locations The owner cannot answer "who changed this?" for bookings, staff records or payroll. Only patient records have a history screen. Chapter 60 Medium Extend the audit calls to the missing modules and add one viewer screen.

The most important rows are the missing deploy configuration, which is an operational risk, and the missing second-location assignment, which blocks a normal multi-branch clinic. Everything else is either a feature a clinic would ask for later or a gap that staff can work around manually.

65.3 Built but unreachable from the web app

In these cases the backend is finished, or nearly so, but no screen calls it, so the feature cannot be used by a clinic. Each one is usually a small piece of web work.

Gap Why it matters to an owner Evidence Severity Suggested next step
The inventory page has no sidebar entry and nothing links to it Stock, suppliers and purchase orders work, but a user can only reach them by typing the address. Most staff will never find them. Chapters 39, 55 Medium Add a sidebar entry; resolve the foreign-key question in Section 65.6 first.
Unapply a payment has no screen An invoice that has any payment on it cannot be cancelled from the web app, because cancelling needs the payments released first. The workaround is a refund. Chapters 34, 52 Medium Add an Unapply action to the payment detail.
Patient treatment plans have no screen Creating, updating and tracking plans, turning plan items into charges and the plan billing summary exist only in the backend. Doctors cannot plan a course of treatment in the Platform. Chapters 28, 33 Medium Build the plan screens, or remove the backend if plans are not wanted.
Payroll: put on hold, CSV export and payslip PDF have no buttons An owner cannot give staff a payslip or export a month for an accountant from the Platform. Chapters 38, 51 Medium Add the three buttons; the endpoints exist.
Lab portal: charge requests and file upload have no portal control A lab cannot ask for an extra charge or attach a file from the portal, so these happen by message or phone. Chapters 40, 41 Medium Add the two forms to the portal order page.
Lab portal: no notification inbox Lab members receive in-app notifications that link into the portal, but the portal layout has no bell to show them. Chapters 40, 41 Medium Add the bell to the portal header.
Cancel one lab item has no screen Stopping one item of an order in progress is not possible from the web app. Chapter 40 Low Add a Cancel item action on the order detail.
Recalls, referrals, feedback, insurance and the communications log The component that shows them is never mounted, and recalls have no component at all. The data model is ready. Chapter 28 Low Mount the tab or drop the claim; update the older documents that call it implemented.
Blacklist a patient The flag can only be set through the API, and it blocks nothing when set. Chapter 28 Low Decide what blacklisting should do (see Section 65.4), then add the control.
Override booking rules The API flag and permission exist, but no booking screen sends it, so no one can book outside working hours or past the daily limit. Chapter 29 Low Add an override option for users who hold the permission.
Cancel reasons The API stores a reason code and note; the screen sends neither and shows no confirmation. Chapter 29 Low Add the reason dialog.
Phone pre-check at registration The endpoint and hook exist but no component calls them. The server rejects duplicates at save with a conflict message. Chapter 28 Low Call the hook on the phone field.
Credit packages and patient credits Backend only, and credits are not a payment method. Chapter 34 Low Decide whether prepaid packages are wanted.
Plan billing summary, daily financial summary and several billing helpers Endpoints and client functions exist but no component renders them. /financial-summary redirects to the dashboard. Chapters 33, 34, 36 Low Remove unused code or build the screens.
About ten dashboard widgets that still use mock data They are not on the live dashboard but remain in the code and could be mistaken for real features. Chapter 36 Low Delete the mock module.
Queue: next-patient preview, queue history, the doctor's own session read and session creation Backend only. The queue works without them. Chapter 30 Low Add a history screen for supervisors if audit of the queue is needed.
Prescriptions: edit one medicine line, duplicate, change history viewer, lookup by appointment Backend only. The history read and the duplicate action are also likely to fail (see Section 65.6). Chapter 32 Low Fix the two defects, then add the screens.
Employee portal-access switch and some schedule calls The endpoint exists, but the switch is set through the employee form instead. /employees/create exists but nothing links to it. Chapter 37 Low Clean up.
Lab: vendor bill header edit, manual bill lines, using lab advance on bills, impressions to the lab, service categories, specialty enablement Endpoints exist; no buttons call them. Chapters 40, 42, 43 Low Build when the workflow is needed.

The Medium rows share one theme: a flow is half-finished at the boundary between backend and web. Finishing the inventory entry, the unapply action and the payroll buttons would remove most of the daily friction an owner would see.

65.4 Seeded but inert

These things look real in the catalog, a table or a setting, but nothing reads them or acts on them.

Gap Why it matters to an owner Evidence Severity Suggested next step
Legacy organization settings (booking defaults, advance booking days, cancellation notice, late fee percentage and old feature switches) An owner can save these values and nothing changes. Only a location settings screen reads the old feature switches to hide sections. Chapters 9, 14 Medium Remove the screen or wire the rules (Chapter 67, Question 5).
Blacklisted and inactive patient flags A blacklisted or inactive patient can still be booked, queued and billed. Staff may assume the flag protects them. Chapter 28 Medium Decide the intended rule and enforce it at booking and check-in.
Availability overrides and approved leave They can be recorded and edited, but booking, validation, the calendar, the queue and payroll never read them. A doctor on approved leave can still be booked. Chapters 29, 37 Medium Make booking and the calendar read them.
Feature keys that gate nothing (comms.in_app, comms.whatsapp, hr.commissions) Switching these on or off has no effect. Twelve more keys for unbuilt features are deactivated at every start and are hidden. Chapters 10, 35, 44 Low Retire the three keys or attach checks.
Notification events that are never emitted (order.overdue, shipment.dispatched, tryin.appointment_due, appointment.rescheduled_lab_delay) Clinics can edit the wording of messages that will never be sent. There is no overdue job. Chapters 40, 44 Low Add emitters or remove the events.
Quiet hours, patient opt-outs and the delivered status Quiet hours are saved but never hold in-app messages. The outbox status delivered is never set. The opt-out screen is commented out. Chapters 44, 59 Low Fix or remove.
The queue.display.manage permission It is in the catalog and in the Receptionist template but nothing checks it. Chapter 30 Low Attach it to display management or drop it.
Email verification The verification state is stored but nothing is gated by it. Chapters 45, 56 Low Decide whether unverified owners should be limited.
Dead schema and code (the table for linked external sign-ins, the deprecated refresh-token column, unused queue and database packages, per-role sidebar layouts that are never written, unused audit and history values, unused magic-link limits) They add noise for the next developer and imply features that are not there. Chapters 4, 13, 15, 32, 40, 58, 60 Low Clean up in one pass.
Settings registry beyond theme The generic cascading settings store holds only theme keys. Chapter 58 Low Move new settings onto it or leave as is.

The Medium rows are the ones that mislead: a screen or flag that implies protection or behaviour the Platform does not provide. Cleaning them up costs little and removes false assurance.

65.5 Data-integrity oddities

These are places where the data model can produce a wrong or failing result in normal use. Several were deduced from code and constraints and not reproduced.

Gap Why it matters to an owner Evidence Severity Suggested next step
Patient numbers are "count plus one", but patients can be permanently deleted After any patient is deleted, the next registration computes a number that already exists and fails on the unique index. Because the count does not change, every later registration fails the same way. This was confirmed by reading the code. Chapters 28, 62 High Use the safe sequence mechanism that billing uses, and stop hard-deleting patients that have history.
Prescription numbers are unique across the whole Platform, but are numbered per organization The first prescription of a second clinic in the same year is numbered like the first clinic's first one and violates the unique key. This was confirmed by reading the code, but not run. Chapters 19, 32, 62 High Make the number unique per organization, or use a Platform-wide sequence.
Purchase order numbers have the same flaw Same cause, in inventory. A second clinic's first purchase order collides. Chapters 23, 39, 62 Medium Same fix.
Other count-plus-one numbers (treatment plan, legacy prescription, employee code) and unlocked "last plus one" numbering They can repeat after a delete or when two people save at the same moment. Chapters 28, 33, 37, 62 Medium Move to the sequence mechanism.
Login id stored where an employee id is expected Several writes (inventory movements and purchase orders, prescription duplication, saved doctor signatures) put a login id into columns defined as links to employees. In some tables there is no foreign key, so the value is silently wrong; where there is one, the write may fail. Not run. Chapters 28, 32, 39, 55 Medium Decide which id each column should hold and make the code consistent.
Deleting a patient or an employee is blocked by ON DELETE RESTRICT rows and fails with a generic server error The user sees "Something went wrong" instead of a reason. A code comment claims the rows cascade, but they do not. Chapters 16, 17, 28, 37 Medium Catch the foreign-key error and give a clear message, or soft-delete.
Duplicate CNIC or phone number on employee edit Reaches the database unique index and returns a generic error. Chapter 37 Low Check before saving.
Employee phone and CNIC are unique across the whole Platform By design one person record can serve several clinics, but the only creation path refuses an existing phone (see Section 65.2). A second clinic cannot hire someone another clinic already registered. Chapters 8, 37 Medium Add the assign-existing-employee flow.
Tenant columns without foreign keys on most billing, queue and lab tables, and logical references to unknown targets (dentist_id, manager_id) The database does not stop a row pointing at a missing or wrong organization. Nothing in the code explains the choice. Chapters 12, 27 Low Document the decision or add the keys.
"Append-only" tables enforced by convention only Only three tables are protected by triggers. The billing audit log, the queue log and the ledgers can be changed by anyone with database access. Chapters 26, 27 Low Add triggers to the money tables.
Jobs and statistics that use the server clock The month-end payroll month, credit expiry, daily summary, "this month" prescription counts, the lab catalog price day (fixed to one time zone) and the leave year follow the server, not the location. Wrong around midnight for locations in other zones. Chapters 38, 62 Medium Move jobs to the location clock or document the server zone.
The web app computes some appointment ranges in the browser time zone The server uses the location time zone, so a user in another zone sees shifted times. Chapter 29 Low Use the location zone in the web app.
Location defaults of UTC and USD while organizations default to Asia/Karachi and PKR A new branch created without explicit values gets different defaults from its clinic. Chapters 1, 9, 14 Low Make new locations inherit the clinic's values.
Concurrent patient imports are blocked only inside one process With several API instances two imports can run at once. Chapter 28 Low Use a database lock.
Registration compares phone numbers exactly, import compares normalised numbers The same number typed two ways can create two patients. Chapter 28 Low Normalise in both.
Queue policy values apply within about a minute, and per process The screen says changes apply tomorrow. Only the smart-queue switch is fixed per day. Another instance can use old values for up to a minute. Chapter 30 Low Correct the screen text.
Check-in lookup and no-show job: write through GET and silent SQL One read endpoint creates a session. The no-show job writes no queue event. Chapter 30 Low Log the event.

The two High rows deserve attention first because they stop core work. The patient-number problem appears after the first deletion in any clinic. The prescription-number problem appears as soon as a second clinic writes a prescription in the same year.

65.6 Unverified behaviour

These items could not be confirmed from code reading, and a real run is needed.

  • Whether the foreign-key mismatches in inventory (Section 65.5) make stock movements, purchase orders and goods receipts fail at run time. Chapter 39 labels three features Unverified for this reason.
  • Whether the prescription change-history read fails because it asks for a relation that is not declared, and whether duplicating a prescription fails on the doctor foreign key. Chapter 32.
  • Whether background jobs keep running while a clinic is read-only. The read-only rule is an HTTP guard, so the answer is probably yes. Chapter 53.
  • Whether a local PostgreSQL without SSL works with the connection settings. Chapter 7.
  • Which account type to create in User Admin for a person who works only for a lab, and the exact sequence a super admin must follow to create an owner login for a clinic created from the Organizations screen. Chapters 41 and 46.
  • Whether storage settings make uploaded patient documents and prescription PDFs publicly readable by address. Chapters 28 and 32.

65.7 Documentation drift

Several older documents describe a Platform that no longer exists. The outdated ones should not be used. Chapter 68 lists each conflict with evidence. The gaps that matter for planning are these.

Gap Why it matters to an owner Evidence Severity Suggested next step
The root project instructions describe a frontend layout, a four-guard chain, "stub" modules and path-prefix skips that the code does not have A new developer or an AI assistant that follows them will look in the wrong places. Chapters 4, 5, 8 Medium Update the instructions file to match the code.
Five historical documents (hand-off note, project overview, audit, plan and the old billing context pack) are outdated They list fixed problems as open and built features as missing. Chapter 68 Medium Archive them or mark them superseded by this handbook.
The first inventory of the documents marked recall, feedback and referral as implemented through a CRM tab The tab is never mounted. This handbook corrects that to Partial. Chapters 28, 68 Low Use the handbook as the source of truth.
Some screen texts claim behaviour that does not exist (starting a patient plan from a template, queue settings applying "from tomorrow", a lab access panel saying a link expires after a day) Staff are told something false. Chapters 30, 33, 40 Low Correct the texts.
The generated data-model catalog has two known defects (shifted notes for ten inventory tables, a false trigger claim on form schema versions) Anyone reading the catalog directly can be misled. Chapters 23, 26 Low Fix the generator.

Documentation drift is Medium at worst, but it compounds: every wrong document is a future wrong decision.

65.8 What to do first

The gaps fall into a clear order. First fix the two High data-integrity gaps (patient numbers after deletion and per-organization prescription numbers), because they break core work and will appear in normal use. Second, write down the deploy procedure, because it is the only High gap that is not a code defect. Third, finish the half-built flows that cost clinics time: the inventory sidebar entry, the unapply action, the payroll buttons and the lab portal forms. Fourth, remove or wire the settings that imply protection, such as the legacy organization settings and the blacklist flag. Everything else is roadmap work that depends on the answers in Chapter 67.

Chapter 66 — Risks

This chapter lists the risks an owner carries by running the Platform as it is today: risks in the data model, risks in how it is operated, observations that a regulator or a careful customer might ask about, and security risks described at category level only. It is for the product owner, who decides what to fix before more clinics rely on the Platform. Nothing in this chapter was tested by running the application; every item comes from reading the code and the generated data-model catalog.

66.1 How to read the risks

Each risk has a likelihood in normal use (Likely, Possible, Unlikely) and an impact on a live clinic (High, Medium, Low). Security items are grouped by category and deliberately contain no file paths, endpoint paths, secret values or exploit detail, because this text is shared outside the engineering team. The engineering team holds the detailed findings separately.

66.2 Data-model risks

Risk What can happen Likelihood Impact Evidence
Count-plus-one and last-plus-one numbering After a permanent delete, or when two people save at the same moment, a patient, plan, employee or purchase order number can repeat and the save fails. Likely for patients after any delete High Chapters 28, 62
Platform-wide unique keys with per-organization numbering Prescription and purchase order numbers restart for each organization but are unique across all of them, so a second clinic collides with the first. Likely in a multi-clinic deployment High Chapters 19, 32, 39, 62
Login id stored in employee-id columns Some writes put a user id where an employee id is expected. Without a foreign key the value is silently wrong; with one the write may fail. Possible Medium Chapters 28, 32, 39
Tenant columns without foreign keys Most billing, queue and lab tables keep organization and location ids with no foreign key, so the database cannot reject a wrong tenant id. Unlikely Medium Chapters 12, 27
"Append-only" promised by comments only Only the commission ledger, the audit log and the status history are protected by triggers. The billing audit log, the queue log, the ledgers and the allocation table rely on application code. Unlikely Medium Chapters 26, 27
Duplicate concepts Two prescription tables, two audit mechanisms, two number-sequence mechanisms, two outbox tables and two feature-switch mechanisms coexist. A change to one can miss the other. Possible Medium Chapter 27
Deletes blocked by RESTRICT keys Deleting a patient or employee with history fails with a generic error. Likely Low Chapters 16, 17
Schema drift between development and production Development builds the schema from the entities; production applies a reviewed diff. Two migrations were written before later entity changes, so production needs the diff applied. Possible Medium Chapters 6, 12
Mixed timestamp types Older tables use timestamps without a time zone, newer ones with. Unlikely Low Chapter 12

The two numbering rows are the most urgent because they fail in ordinary use. The rest are latent: they cost nothing until a clinic hits a particular edge.

66.3 Operational risks

Risk What can happen Likelihood Impact Evidence
Exactly one worker process The worker runs the outbox relay, the notification relay and all eight scheduled jobs. Two workers would duplicate jobs; none would stop live queue updates, notifications and nightly checks. There is no supervision described. Possible High Chapters 6, 63
In-memory rate limiting Login and other limits are counted in one API process. With several instances the limit multiplies, and a restart clears it. Likely when scaled out Medium Chapters 6, 56
Server time zone for jobs No schedule sets a time zone, so jobs follow the server clock, not each location. Likely Medium Chapters 6, 62, 63
No deploy or CI configuration There is no pipeline, container file or hosting description in the repository. Builds and releases depend on individual knowledge. The built output path also differs from the one in the start script. Likely High Chapter 6
Dependence on Redis Realtime updates, access-change propagation and settings caches use Redis. Without it clinics see stale screens for up to the fallback interval. Possible Medium Chapters 54, 63
Per-process caches The subscription decision (30 seconds), access context (5 minutes), version (15 seconds) and queue policy (60 seconds) are cached per process. Likely Low Chapters 30, 45, 57
Nightly jobs only log The money invariant check and the inventory alert job write to the log. Nobody is told unless someone reads it. Likely Medium Chapters 34, 39
Calendar licence The appointment calendar uses premium resource views from a third-party library, and the licence key in use is a non-commercial one. Likely Medium Chapter 29
Seeded data re-created at boot Seeds run in the worker as well as the API and recreate a deleted system role, and re-seed starter plan templates when a clinic has none. Possible Low Chapters 11, 33
Unrun test coverage of behaviour The handbook was written by reading code. The access and billing suites exist, but the findings here were not reproduced. Possible Medium Chapter 64

Of these, the single worker and the missing deploy configuration matter most, because a failure there is silent and affects every clinic at once.

66.4 Compliance-sounding observations

These are observations, not legal conclusions. A clinic or a regulator may ask about them; the Platform makes no compliance claim, and earlier screenshots that showed such claims were excluded from the handbook.

  • No retention policy. Nothing purges or archives old sessions, security logs, audit rows, notification messages or consent signatures. Network addresses and browser strings are kept indefinitely.
  • Audit coverage is partial. Patient records, billing, prescriptions and queue events keep history. Appointments, employees, payroll, organizations and locations do not, and there is no organization-wide viewer.
  • No row-level security. Tenant isolation is application-level only. The queue sets database session values for tenant and location, but no database policy uses them.
  • Patient documents on external storage. Documents, insurance images and prescription PDFs are stored with an external provider and referenced by address. Access to those addresses is not decided by the Platform's permissions.
  • Consent signatures inside the database. Signature images are stored inline in the consent row, and immutability of consents is a convention, not a database rule.
  • Message text in logs. The stand-in delivery provider writes message bodies and recipient addresses to the application log, which would be unsuitable once real patient channels are switched on. Outbox rows also keep rendered text.
  • No second factor or lockout. Accounts rely on a password with a short minimum.

66.5 Security risks by category

These categories summarise findings from all chapters. They contain no locations, paths or exploit detail by design.

Category Summary Impact Chapters
Tenant isolation checks missing on some endpoints A few reads or writes do not filter by organization or location, or do not verify that referenced records belong to the caller's organization or patient scope. A few reads apply organization scope where the permission has a narrower scope. High 19, 30, 32, 33, 34, 42
Application-level isolation only No database row-level policies back up the application checks, so one missed check is a data leak. Medium 8, 30, 57
Committed credentials in test scripts Test scripts and a fixture in the repository hold a database connection and test passwords. They need rotation and removal from history. High Inventory of documents
Token handling and logging A legacy realtime gateway logs token-related data and accepts any origin. Real-time connections check the token once and outlive its expiry. A revoked session's access token stays valid until it expires. High 56, 57, 63
Input from clients trusted The server fetches a signature image address supplied by the client. An upload route is open to any organization member. Upload size and type are only partly restricted. Some edit screens send whole rows. Medium 28, 32, 58
Information exposure in errors The error envelope carries raw internal messages for unexpected errors. Medium 5, 61
Public routes by design The waiting-room display and lab magic links need no login by design, using an identifier or a bearer token as the credential. They rely on expiry, revocation and throttling, and the throttle is in memory. Medium 30, 40, 41
Secret reuse The signing secret for magic links falls back to the access-token secret when its own is missing. Medium 40, 41
Authentication hardening Short minimum password, two different minimums on two paths, no lockout, no second factor, no logging of wrong passwords, no rate limit on two sensitive endpoints. Medium 56, 45, 47
Authorization granularity Some actions need only a broad read permission, and one payroll permission guards all payroll data. Medium 37, 38, 40
Audit and retention Missing audit for personnel and payroll data; no retention. Medium 13, 60
Money-moving replay protection Idempotency keys are required for most money actions but optional for one vendor payment path. Low 42
Third-party licence See the calendar licence in Section 66.3. Medium 29

The high-impact rows are tenant-isolation gaps, committed credentials and token handling. The others are hardening work that lowers the chance and the blast radius of a mistake.

66.6 What to fix first

Fix the committed credentials first: rotate them and remove the files from history, because the exposure already exists. Then close the tenant-isolation gaps and the token logging, since a single missing filter lets one clinic read another's data. Third, fix the two numbering collisions, which break daily work. Fourth, document and automate deployment and decide how the single worker is supervised. After these, add audit coverage for staff and payroll and a retention policy, then harden authentication and the realtime token check. The rest can follow the roadmap.

Chapter 67 — Open Questions

This chapter lists the decisions and facts that only the product owner can supply. They come from the notes of every handbook chapter, from the questions in the generated organizations and locations chapter, from the ambiguities in the generated entity catalog and from items the code could not settle. Each question has the context and the reason the answer matters, so the answers can steer what is built, fixed or removed next.

67.1 Product direction

  1. Which patient channels will the Platform use, and who pays for them? Context: the message pipeline is built, but only the in-app channel for staff and lab members is active. WhatsApp, SMS and email to patients are commented out, and a log stand-in takes their place. Why it matters: reminders, receipts and lab-delay messages all wait on this choice, and it also decides the privacy and logging work needed (Chapter 66).
  2. Should owners get trial-ending and expiry messages, and how many days ahead? Context: only an in-app banner warns today; no renewal email is sent. Why it matters: expiry puts a clinic in read-only mode, so a missed warning is a lost day of work and a support call.
  3. Should the Platform have a patient portal, online booking and recurring appointments? Context: all three were planned and their feature keys were retired. Why it matters: it decides whether the retired keys are deleted or the work is scheduled.
  4. Are insurance claims and an online payment gateway required for target clinics? Context: insurance details can be stored (backend only) and no claim or gateway exists. Why it matters: these are large features, and the answer avoids building them early or promising them.
  5. Is attendance wanted, and should payroll have deductions, tax and bank files? Context: payroll is salary plus commission; deductions are always zero; leave is recorded but not read. Why it matters: payroll is the most legally sensitive money flow, and clinics will ask.
  6. What should a blacklisted or inactive patient be prevented from doing? Context: both flags are informational and block nothing. Why it matters: staff may rely on them, and the answer defines the rule to enforce at booking, check-in and billing.
  7. Should the product name be fixed? Context: the handbook calls it "the Platform" and each clinic sets its display name; the default is "Clinic Portal". Older documents and some stored keys carry a former working name. Why it matters: it decides what is cleaned out of the code and which documents can be reused.

67.2 Clinics, locations and subscriptions

These come from the generated organizations and locations chapter.

  1. Should a clinic created by a super admin start on a trial, or stay unmanaged? Context: unmanaged clinics have no expiry and no plan limits. Why it matters: it decides whether all clinics are subject to billing.
  2. When a clinic pays for a lower plan during a higher-plan trial, should the payment downgrade it at once? Context: recording a payment overwrites the plan with the paid plan. Why it matters: it can silently remove features during a trial.
  3. Should deactivating a clinic also make it read-only and end sessions? Context: today deactivation only hides the clinic at login. Why it matters: owners may still hold working sessions, and the subscription guard is not involved.
  4. Can a clinic have more than one main branch, and which becomes main when one is deactivated? Context: the main-branch flag is not exclusive. Why it matters: reports and defaults may pick the wrong branch.
  5. Should new branches inherit the clinic's time zone and currency, and should changing the clinic's time zone update existing branches? Context: locations default to UTC and USD while organizations default to Asia/Karachi and PKR; the setup wizard updates branches but later changes do not. Why it matters: it controls every date and amount a branch shows.
  6. Should the legacy organization settings be removed or wired? Context: booking defaults, advance booking days, cancellation notice, late fee percentage and old feature switches are saved but read by no backend rule. Why it matters: owners may think these rules are in force.
  7. Who is the location manager meant to be, an employee or a login, and what powers should a manager have? Context: the column's target is not stated anywhere. Why it matters: a branch-manager role needs a definite owner.
  8. Should staff without the locations permission read booking-related location settings? Context: slot length and daily cap sit on a screen that needs the manage permission. Why it matters: receptionists may need to see the limits.
  9. Which account type should be created for a person who works only for a lab, and what is the exact sequence to create an owner login for a clinic made by a super admin? Context: both were deduced, not run. Why it matters: onboarding instructions must be correct.

67.3 Data model and numbering

  1. Which id should the dentist_id columns hold (employee or login)? Context: the teeth chart, plans, recalls and feedback store a value with no foreign key and no stated target. Why it matters: reports that join to the person need a defined meaning.
  2. Which id should doctor signatures, inventory movements and purchase orders store? Context: code passes a login id into columns that are, or look like, employee links. Why it matters: the inventory writes may fail, and signatures are keyed per login across clinics.
  3. Should prescriptions and purchase orders be numbered per organization or across the Platform? Context: the numbers restart per organization but are unique everywhere. Why it matters: it decides which side of the conflict to change.
  4. Should patients ever be permanently deleted? Context: deletion breaks numbering and fails when billing exists. Why it matters: it decides between soft delete and a clear refusal.
  5. Is the missing foreign key on tenant columns deliberate? Context: most billing, queue and lab tables omit it without comment. Why it matters: it decides whether to add keys or document the choice.
  6. Which duplicate concepts should be merged? Context: legacy and new prescriptions, two audit mechanisms, two sequence mechanisms, per-visit tables with unclear roles. Why it matters: each duplicate doubles the work for every change.
  7. Should the append-only money tables get triggers like the commission ledger? Context: three tables are protected; others are promised by comments. Why it matters: it is the cheapest strong guard for financial records.
  8. Should the unused tables and columns be dropped (linked sign-ins, per-visit summary, deprecated refresh token, chairs, legacy inventory table)? Why it matters: they mislead readers and the generated catalog.

67.4 Operations and security

  1. Where and how is the Platform deployed, and who supervises the single worker? Context: no deploy configuration exists. Why it matters: exactly one worker must run, and nothing here shows how that is ensured.
  2. Should the scheduled jobs use each location's time zone? Context: jobs follow the server clock. Why it matters: payroll month, credit expiry and day-end alerts depend on it.
  3. What is the data retention policy for sessions, security logs, audit rows, messages and consent signatures? Why it matters: it is the first question a regulator or clinic will ask.
  4. Is the calendar library licence suitable for a commercial product? Why it matters: it is a legal exposure that can be solved by buying the licence or changing the component.
  5. Should audit extend to appointments, employees, payroll, organizations and locations, with one viewer? Why it matters: owners cannot otherwise answer who changed a record.
  6. What should be done about the committed test credentials? Why it matters: rotating them and cleaning history should be scheduled, not assumed.
  7. Should public lab links and the TV display remain unauthenticated by design? Why it matters: it defines the acceptable exposure and the expiry rules.

67.5 Behaviour to confirm by running

  1. Do inventory writes fail because of the id mismatch? Why it matters: it decides whether inventory can be opened to clinics at all.
  2. Do the prescription change history and duplicate actions fail? Why it matters: they are small fixes if confirmed.
  3. Do background jobs continue while a clinic is read-only? Why it matters: payroll and invariants could be skipped or not.
  4. Are uploaded patient documents and PDFs publicly readable by address? Why it matters: it depends on the storage settings, not on the code.
  5. Which currency column do billing screens read, the location's or the organization's? Why it matters: a mismatch shows the wrong currency label.
  6. Does the lab ever receive a magic-link message in practice? Why it matters: today the contact channel is a stand-in, so links must be copied by hand.
  7. Should lab orders link to the appointment and treatment? Context: the API accepts both, the web app never sends them. Why it matters: try-in scheduling and case reporting depend on it.
  8. Is a printable lab invoice or receipt needed? Context: none was found. Why it matters: lab patient invoices cannot be handed to patients otherwise.

67.6 How the answers are used

The product questions (Section 67.1) set the roadmap. The clinic and numbering questions (Sections 67.2 and 67.3) decide small fixes that remove the High and Medium gaps in Chapter 65. The operations and security questions (Section 67.4) decide the order in Chapter 66. The questions in Section 67.5 need someone to run the application and watch, and they should be answered before the related work is planned.

68.2 Documents and how far they can be trusted

The following documents are current or mostly current and may be used, with the corrections in the table: the generated entity catalog and the organizations and locations chapter, the access-control guide, the database migrations guide, the root readme (for the process split and counts) and the appointments and queue guide.

The following are outdated and should not be used for decisions: the hand-off note (it mentions an appointment token that no longer exists and fixed problems), the project overview (it predates access control, billing version two and the lab modules), the audit file (seven of its ten most serious findings are fixed), the plan file (its checklist is stale) and the old billing context pack (it describes replaced code). The two stock starter readmes carry no project information. The design mock-up file in the repository root uses a former name and does not describe the current screens. The root project instructions are partly outdated and need an update before they are given to a new developer or an assistant.

68.3 The CRM tab correction

The first document inventory marked recall, feedback and referral as implemented through a CRM tab on the patient page. The code shows that backend endpoints exist but the tab component is never mounted in the patient detail page, so those features cannot be reached by a user, and recalls have no component at all. The handbook therefore labels them Partial. Any plan or sales material that repeated the earlier claim should be corrected.

68.4 Using this chapter

Treat the handbook as the source of truth and the code as the final authority. When a document in the table is edited, update the row, so it does not return as a source of confusion. Chapter 65 lists the same drift among the known gaps, and Chapter 67 asks which documents the owner wants archived.

Appendices

Appendix A — Glossary

This glossary defines every entity, role, feature, status label and key term used in the handbook, once, in alphabetical order. It is for anyone reading a single chapter on its own, including readers who start in the middle. Where the code uses a different name from the screen, the code name follows in parentheses. Terms that exist only in the database are shown with their table name.

A

Access context — the resolved permissions of one user at one organization and location, which answers "can", "scope" and "decide" for a request (AccessContext).

Access marker — one of @Can, @AnyMember, @Public, @RequireSuperAdmin or @ContextFree; every endpoint handler must carry one, and a unit test fails when one is missing.

Access token — the 15-minute token kept in the browser's memory and sent with every request.

Access version — a counter on the organization (access_version) raised whenever roles, features or navigation change, so every process and screen knows to reload access.

Active feature — a feature that is in the active catalog, entitled, enabled and not switched off at the current location.

Active queue entry — a queue entry in status waiting, called, in consultation, on hold or skipped.

Advance — patient money received and not yet allocated or refunded; it is calculated (amount minus allocated minus refunded) and has no table of its own. A lab advance is the same idea for lab payments.

Allocation — a signed record of how much of a payment was applied to a charge or released back (payment_allocations).

Amended prescription — a signed prescription that was edited and not signed again (status AMENDED, version increased).

Append-only — a table whose rows are never changed or deleted. Only commission_entries, audit_logs and status_history are protected by a database trigger; others are append-only by convention.

Appointment — a booking: one patient, one doctor, one location, a start time and a duration (appointments). Also called a booking before arrival.

Assignment — an employee's link to an organization and a location with an employment role, a staff login and portal access (employee_org_location_assignments).

Attachment — a file on a lab order or item (attachments).

Audience — who a notification is for: patient, doctor, coordinator or lab.

Audit log — the generic append-only change history (audit_logs).

Autosave — saving shortly after the user stops typing, without a Save button.

Availability override — a one-date exception to a doctor's weekly schedule (doctor_availability_overrides); recorded but never read by booking.

B

Basis points (bps) — a rate stored as an integer where 10,000 means 100 percent and 4000 means 40 percent.

Bell — the header icon that opens a user's in-app inbox (user_notifications).

Billing audit log — billing's own audit trail with before and after snapshots (billing_audit_logs).

Billing v2 — the code's name for the current charge-based billing design.

Blacklisted patient — a patient flagged as not to be served; informational only, it blocks nothing.

Booking — see Appointment.

Bundle — a ready-made per-module level on the roles screen: None, Basic or Full.

C

Cancel reason code — the structured reason stored when a booking is cancelled (patient_left or other).

Case profit — revenue minus lab cost, case expenses and doctor commission for one lab order.

Cash close — an immutable end-of-period count of a location's counter (cash_closes); each payment account has a line with expected, counted and variance.

Chair — a treatment chair of a location; the table exists but no module uses it (chairs).

Change history — the per-patient audit timeline merged from the audit log and the status history.

Channel — how a notification is delivered: in-app, WhatsApp, SMS or email. Only in-app is active.

Charge — one billable line for a patient; the atomic unit of billing (charges).

Charge request — an extra charge a lab asks for after an order is submitted (order_charge_requests).

Clinic default layout — a sidebar layout with no role, applied to every role of a clinic (nav_layouts).

Clinic overview — the dashboard of patients, appointments and waiting (/clinic-overview).

Clinic time — dates and times computed in the location's time zone through ClockService.

Collected basis and billed basis — whether profit-and-loss revenue is counted from money received or from invoices issued.

Commission basis — whether a commission rate applies to the net or gross charge amount.

Commission entry — one signed change in commission earned on one charge or lab invoice line; append-only (commission_entries).

Commission rule — an override of a compensation plan for one service or service category (commission_rules).

Communications log — a manual record of calls and messages with a patient (patient_communications).

Compensation plan — one dated version of how an assignment is paid: salary, commission or both (compensation_plans).

Config Studio — the super admin area for form schemas, workflows and stage templates (routes under /studio).

Consent — a signed patient consent with the signature image stored in the row (patient_consents).

Consultation workspace — the doctor's one-screen visit page where notes, treatments and prescriptions are recorded.

Consumption template — a standard kit of materials for a procedure (consumption_templates).

Convert to walk-in — closing a too-late booking as a no-show and adding the patient to the same queue as a linked walk-in.

Credit note (lab) — a reduction of an issued lab invoice; money already paid above the new total returns to advance (lab_credit_notes).

Credit package — a prepaid credit offer of an organization (credit_packages); backend only.

Custom discount — a discount not taken from a discount type; it needs a permission and a note.

Custom role — a role created by a clinic, in contrast to the five system roles.

D

Daily booking limit — the most live bookings a location accepts on one local day (default 50).

Dental info — the single dental health and habits sheet of a patient.

Dev-log provider — the stand-in delivery provider that writes patient-channel messages to the application log instead of sending them.

Direct costs — lab bills plus doctor commissions in the profit-and-loss statement.

Discount type — an owner-defined discount preset (discount_types).

Doctor screen — the My queue page where a doctor runs their own queue.

Doctor share — the commission a payment would record, shown to authorised users while collecting payment.

Doctor signature — one saved signature image per login, placed on prescriptions (doctor_signatures).

Document code — the two- to six-character location code at the start of invoice, receipt and refund numbers.

Document sequence — the per-location, per-type, per-year counter behind billing numbers (document_sequences).

Double-booking constraint — the database rule that refuses overlapping live bookings of one doctor (no_doctor_overlap).

Dry run — an import request that checks rows without saving them.

E

Early window — minutes before the booked time from which a checked-in patient counts as due (default 15).

Effect — a code handler that a workflow transition may run (workflow_effects).

Employee — the person record of a staff member, shared across organizations (employees).

Employee code — a per-organization code such as EMP-001 on an assignment.

Employment role — see Role.

Encounter — the clinical record of one consultation (patient_encounters).

Entitled — a feature the super admin has granted to an organization, with an optional trial end date.

Entity catalog — the generated field-level reference of every table.

Envelope — the JSON shape every endpoint returns (ResponseWrapper): data, message, success flag, status code, error and developer message.

Escalation protection — the rule that a non-owner cannot grant a permission or scope they do not hold.

Estimate — a lab invoice in draft: editable, unnumbered, nothing owed.

Exclusive tax — tax added on top of the price at issue, using the location's rate.

Expense — one clinic running cost at a location (expenses).

External lab — a lab serving many clinics.

F

Feature — a feature key such as billing.invoices that an organization may be entitled to and enable.

Feature impact — the permissions and roles that stop working when a feature is turned off.

Finance overview — the owner's profit-and-loss dashboard (/finance).

First come, first served — the queue mode that calls patients in arrival order; the alternative is the smart queue.

Force complete — completing a consultation on the doctor's behalf.

Form schema — the stable identity of an order form (form_schemas); its versions are form_schema_versions.

G

General ledger — double-entry bookkeeping in paisa, written only for lab money (ledger_journals, ledger_journal_lines).

Global guard — a guard run on every request; there are five: JWT, tenant context, feature flag, access and subscription.

Global role — a user-level role; its only value is super admin.

Grace period — three days after a subscription ends during which the clinic still works, with warnings.

H

Heartbeat — a Redis message the worker sends every five seconds; API instances refuse sockets after fifteen seconds without one.

High-risk permission — one of 13 permissions marked high risk; granting it needs a reason.

Home page — the page a role's members open after sign-in.

I

Idempotency key — a request header that makes a retried action run once (idempotency_keys).

If-Match version — the entry version a screen sends so that a stale action is refused.

Impact preview — the dialog that lists what stops working when a feature is turned off.

Implemented — status label: built end to end, with a screen or by design a backend job.

Implies — permissions granted automatically with another (for example create implies view).

In-house lab — a lab owned by one clinic and serving only it.

Inactive patient — a patient hidden by the active filter with all records kept.

Inbox — a user's own notification rows shown behind the bell.

Invoice — an issued document grouping a patient's charges; there are no drafts (invoices).

Item stage — one try-in round of one stage of a lab item (order_item_stages).

J

Journal — one balanced double-entry posting; a journal line is one debit or credit side.

K

KPI strip — the six summary tiles at the top of the Appointments page.

L

Lab — a dental laboratory, external or in-house (labs).

Lab admin — a lab member with full portal rights for one lab.

Lab billing settings — per-organization lab tax rate and due days.

Lab coordinator — a clinic user holding both permissions needed to act for a lab that does not answer.

Lab directory — the platform list of labs kept by the super admin.

Lab link — a clinic's connection to a lab, with status, payment terms and patient data level (lab_clinic_links).

Lab member — a user who works at a lab as lab admin or lab technician (lab_members).

Lab order — a lab case: items for one patient, doctor and lab (lab_orders).

Lab order item — one piece of work with frozen price snapshots (lab_order_items).

Lab-only user — a user with lab memberships and no clinic access, kept inside the lab portal.

Lab payable — what the clinic owes a lab.

Lab portal — the area where lab members work on orders, production, billing and their team.

Lab service — one product a lab makes, such as a crown (lab_services).

Lab statement — a lab's monthly statement reconciled against bills (lab_statements).

Lab technician — a lab member who works the queue but cannot answer orders or manage the team.

Lane — one doctor's column on the reception board for a date.

Last accessed context — the organization and location saved on the user and pre-selected at next sign-in.

Late grace — minutes after the booked time within which an arriving patient keeps appointment priority (default 10).

Legacy baseline — the first migration, recorded as applied and never executed.

Legacy organization settings — the organization_settings table, editable but read by no backend rule.

Legacy quick prescription — a prescription in the older patient_prescriptions table.

Live slot check — the debounced server check the booking dialog runs while open.

Location — a branch of an organization (locations).

Location override — a switch that turns an enabled feature off at one location.

Lock (setting) — a flag freezing a setting's value for lower scopes.

Locked feature — a feature the owner cannot switch on because it is not entitled or the trial ended.

Logical reference — an id column that points to another row without a foreign key.

M

Magic link — a no-login link for a lab to one order; only a hash of the token is stored (magic_links).

Main branch — a location flagged as the clinic's main one; the flag is not exclusive.

Mandatory event — an event whose in-app message to internal audiences cannot be switched off.

Manual payment — a subscription payment recorded by a super admin.

Maximum late — minutes after the booked time after which check-in is refused and the booking becomes a no-show (default 45).

Medicine directory — the clinic's list of medicines (screen label "Medicines").

Modular monolith — one backend application split into domain modules.

Money invariants — ten rules checked every night by the billing job.

Monorepo — one repository holding both the backend and the web app.

N

Needs pricing — a flag on a charge created without a resolvable price; it blocks invoicing until priced.

Nightly job — a scheduled task such as the money invariant check.

No-show marker — the background job that marks unattended bookings as no-shows.

Not implemented — status label: planned, seeded, commented out or only mentioned.

Notification event — a platform-defined kind of event that can notify someone (notification_events).

Notification outbox — one message to one recipient on one channel, written in the same transaction as its cause (notification_outbox).

Notification rule — a clinic's on/off switch for one event, audience and channel.

Notification template — wording of one event on one channel in one language.

Number sequence — a per-organization counter for numbers such as LAB-0001.

O

Onboarding pending — a flag on the organization that is true from signup until the setup wizard is finished.

Order template — a saved starting point for a lab order.

Organization — one clinic business; the tenant (organizations).

Outbox (realtime) — table of realtime messages written in the same transaction as a queue change (outbox).

Outbox relay — the worker loop that publishes unpublished outbox rows.

Override booking rules — the permission to book outside weekly hours or past the daily limit; it never bypasses the double-booking check.

Owner — the user who owns an organization and has all permissions in it.

P

Paisa — the integer minor unit of the rupee; 100 paisa is one rupee.

Partial — status label: some of it exists; the note says what is missing.

Patient — the patient record, one per patient per organization (patients).

Patient data level — per lab link, whether the lab sees the full name or only the patient code.

Patient import — bulk creation of patients from a spreadsheet through parse, dry run and batches.

Patient lab invoice — a patient invoice for lab work (lab_invoices).

Patient ledger — one-sided statement rows per patient (ledger_entries).

Patient number — the per-organization patient identifier, P- plus five digits.

Patient scope — the reach of the patient view permission: own, location or org.

Payment — money received from a patient; it belongs to the patient, not to an invoice (payments).

Payment account — one way a location receives money: cash, bank or wallet.

Payment status — the computed invoice status unpaid, partially paid, paid or overdue; never stored.

Payroll record — one employee's pay for one month at one location (payroll_records).

Permission — a key such as billing.invoice.void granted to a role.

Pinned version — the workflow template version stored on a lab order or item when it is created.

Plan template — a predefined treatment plan offered when recording treatment (plan_templates).

Platform default — a form, stage or workflow template with no owner organization.

Polymorphic reference — a type plus id column pair that can point at different tables.

Portal access — the assignment flag that lets a linked staff login sign in at that location.

Prescription — the current prescription record (prescriptions).

Prescription preset — a reusable set of medicines for the builder; stored in treatment_plan_templates and unrelated to plan templates.

Price override — a location or doctor price for a catalog service (service_prices).

Price policy — the rule that only a holder of the price override permission may change a catalog charge's price; others give a discount.

Print layout — the look of a printed prescription (prescription_templates).

Process role — which half of the backend a process runs: all, api or worker.

Proxy update — clinic staff recording a lab's answer for a lab that does not respond.

Purchase order — an order to one supplier for one location (purchase_orders).

Q

QC — the lab's own quality check between finishing and ready.

Queue entry — a patient's place in a queue session (queue_entries).

Queue history — the append-only log of queue changes (queue_events).

Queue policy — queue settings at organization level with location override (queue_policies).

Queue session — one doctor's queue for one clinic day at one location (queue_sessions).

Quiet hours — a daily window in which non-in-app messages are held.

R

Read-only mode — the state of an expired clinic: reads work and writes are refused with a payment-required error.

Ready to bill — the desk list of patients with an unbilled charge on a chosen day.

Recall — a planned future check-up with a due date (patient_recalls).

Reception board — the Queue tab showing every doctor's lane.

Refund — money returned to a patient, always from advance (refunds).

Refund source — a previous payment from which a refund draws.

Rejoin policy — where a skipped patient goes when rejoined: end, original position or manual.

Remake request — a request to make an item again, with a responsible party.

Report definition — a registered report with key, columns, filters and one query.

Resolved price — the price a service gets: doctor override, then location override, then catalog default.

Retired feature key — a catalog key with no code behind it, deactivated at every start.

Revision — a numbered change of a submitted lab order, or the counter raised by each invoice edit.

Role — an employment role with permissions and a home page (employment_roles); "system role" for the five templates, "custom role" for clinic-made ones.

Room — a Socket.IO channel a screen subscribes to.

Route file — a thin web file declaring a URL, an optional permission and the page to render.

Row scope — the filter that limits rows to own, location or organization.

S

Scope — how far a permission reaches: own, location or org.

Selection engine — the pure function that decides whom Call next picks.

Service catalog — the organization's list of billable services (services).

Service day — the clinic day a queue session belongs to, using the location time zone and a cutoff.

Service mapping — which lab service fulfils which clinic billing service.

Session (login) — one signed-in device with a hashed refresh token (user_sessions).

Settings registry — the cascading settings store (config_values).

Settlement — a batch of unsettled commission entries paid through one payroll record.

Setup wizard — the three-step owner onboarding at /setup.

Shipment — a parcel between clinic and lab with a QR token (shipments).

Smart queue — the calling order that weighs emergencies, due appointments, starvation and returns from tests.

Snapshot (commission) — the doctor, plan and rate stored on a charge when it is created.

Specialty — a clinical specialty the engine is configured for.

Staff login — a user account linked to an employee through assignments.

Stage template — the try-in rounds a kind of lab work goes through.

Starter templates — the twelve default plan templates inserted for a clinic with none.

Starvation guard — the rule that calls the longest-waiting ordinary patient after a limit.

Status history — the append-only log of status changes (status_history).

Stock movement — one signed change to an item's stock (stock_movements).

Subscription status — the derived state of a clinic's plan: trial, active, grace, expired or unmanaged.

Super admin — the Platform operator with a global role, exempt from tenant checks.

Supplier — a vendor of stock.

synchronize — the ORM setting that builds the schema from entities; on in development, off in production.

T

Teeth chart snapshot — one append-only chart of a patient's teeth in FDI notation.

Tenant context — the active organization and location of a request.

Tenant headers — the two request headers that carry the active organization and location.

The Platform — the name used in this handbook for the whole multi-tenant clinic management product. Each clinic sets its own display name; the default is "Clinic Portal".

Token (queue) — the number a patient holds in a doctor's queue, with a letter prefix.

Transactional outbox — writing a message in the same transaction as the change and delivering it afterwards.

Treatment — work actually performed on a patient (treatments).

Treatment plan — planned work for a patient (patient_treatment_plans).

Trial — the 14-day Professional plan period given at self-signup.

TV display — the public waiting-room page showing tokens being served.

U

Unapply — releasing a payment's allocations back to advance; backend only.

Unbilled charge — an active charge not yet on an invoice.

Unmanaged clinic — an organization with no trial and no paid date: no limits and no expiry.

Unverified — status label: could not be confirmed from the code; the note says what.

Urgent priority — an authorised emergency flag with a reason that puts a patient first.

User — a login account for the whole Platform (users).

V

Variance — counted minus expected money for a payment account at cash close.

Vendor bill — what the clinic owes a lab for an order (vendor_bills).

Vendor payment — money the clinic paid a lab.

Visit notes — the doctor's free-text notes for an encounter.

W

Walk-in — a patient who arrives without a booking and is added directly to a queue.

Warranty — a period after delivery, 12 months by default (item_warranties).

Watchdog — the API check that refuses sockets when no heartbeat arrives.

Weekly working hours — a doctor's recurring working block for one weekday.

Work order — the printable sheet with a QR code and instructions, without prices.

Worker — the process running the outbox relay, notification relay and scheduled jobs; exactly one may run.

Workflow template — a state machine for orders, items or stages; its versions are draft, published or retired.

Z

Zero-priced charge — a charge created at zero because no price could be resolved; see Needs pricing.

Appendix B — Entity Index

This appendix lists all 153 database tables of the Platform, with the entity class, the owning backend module, the business purpose and the chapters that explain each table. It is for engineers and owners who meet a table name and need to find out what it is. The list was built from the generated entity catalog and checked against the data-model chapters (Chapters 12 to 27).

B.1 How to read the index

The owning module is the backend folder whose entities directory defines the class. The chapter columns give the data-model chapter that describes the table's structure (Part 4) and the module or cross-cutting chapter that explains its behaviour. Some class names differ from the table name; for example the class CatalogService is the table services. Table names are shown exactly as in the database.

Appendix C — API Endpoint Summary

This appendix maps the Platform's backend API, one line per controller file. A controller is a group of related endpoints that share a URL prefix. The backend has 80 controller classes in 74 files, with 593 endpoints in total. Where one file holds two small controllers, they share a line. Four of those endpoints belong to the Google and GitHub sign-in controller, which exists in the code but is not registered, so those routes do not exist at runtime. The full method-by-method detail of each endpoint is described in the module chapter named in the last column.

C.1 How every endpoint is protected

Every request passes five global guards in this order:

  1. JWT. Checks the sign-in token, except on routes listed as public.
  2. Tenant context. Checks that the user belongs to the organization and location named in the request headers.
  3. Feature flag. Checks features required by @RequireFeature.
  4. Access. Checks @Can permissions.
  5. Subscription. Blocks writes when a clinic's subscription has expired (read-only mode).

Each endpoint also declares how access is decided:

  • @Can(…): needs specific permissions. This is the normal case.
  • @AnyMember: any member of the organization may call it.
  • @Public: no sign-in, such as the TV display or a lab magic link.
  • @ContextFree: the handler checks access itself, because it runs before a location is chosen or outside a clinic.
  • @RequireSuperAdmin: platform staff only.
  • Lab portal: routes under /lab-portal/… use a separate lab-member guard instead of clinic permissions.

A test fails the build if any endpoint has none of these.

Technical references: backend/src/app.module.ts (guard order) · backend/src/access/access-coverage.spec.ts · backend/src/labs/portal/lab-actor.ts · LabPortalController

Appendix D — Permission Catalog

This appendix lists every permission the Platform knows. There are 70 in total, and the code defines them in one file. A permission is the smallest unit of access a role can be given, for example "void an invoice". An owner never invents new permissions. Instead, the owner combines these 70 into roles, using None / Basic / Full bundles per module or the Advanced mode for single permissions.

Five rules decide how a permission behaves:

  • Feature. Each permission belongs to one feature. When that feature is not active for the organization, or is switched off at a location, the permission is dropped while access is worked out. It is not deleted from the role, so switching the feature back on restores access exactly as it was.
  • Scope. Some permissions carry a scope: own (only records linked to the user, such as a doctor's own patients or queue), location (the active location) or org (every location of the organization). A wider scope includes the narrower ones.
  • Also grants. Some permissions automatically include others. For example, editing patients includes viewing them.
  • Risk. Permissions marked "high" ask for a confirmation and a reason when an owner grants them in the roles screen.
  • Who holds what. Owners and the super admin hold every permission. Staff hold only what their role at the active location grants. A missing permission means no access: the system is fail-closed.

The tables below are grouped by the module the roles screen lists them under. Each row gives the permission key exactly as the code spells it, the label the roles screen shows, the feature it depends on, the scopes it accepts ("—" means it has no scope), the permissions it also grants, and whether it is high-risk.

Appendix E — Scheduled Jobs and Background Loops

This appendix lists everything the Platform does on its own, without a user clicking anything. That covers timed jobs that run on a schedule, and background loops that deliver realtime events and notifications. It also explains which server process runs each one, because running a job twice can cause duplicate work.

E.1 Where background work runs

The backend is one program that can start in three process roles:

  • api role: serves web requests and the realtime socket connection. It never runs scheduled jobs, so you can run several api processes side by side without jobs running twice.
  • worker role: runs the scheduled jobs and the background relays. Exactly one worker process must run.
  • all role: does both. It is the default in development and needs no Redis.

The code enables the job scheduler only in processes whose role is not api.

Technical references: backend/src/common/runtime/process-role.ts · runsJobs · backend/src/app.module.ts · AppModule.forRole · backend/src/main.worker.ts

E.2 Timed jobs

Job Schedule What it does Status
Queue no-show marker Every 60 seconds Marks a booked patient as a no-show once they have not checked in by the appointment start plus the location's maximum lateness from the queue policy. [Implemented]
Queue call timeout Every 15 seconds Auto-skips a called patient who never came to the doctor, when the queue policy has a call timeout set. [Implemented]
Queue session day-end Every 5 minutes Closes queue sessions from a past clinic day when they are empty. Sessions that still have waiting or on-hold patients are left open for an admin and logged as an alert. They are never auto-cancelled. [Implemented]
Queue cleanup Every day at 03:15 Deletes idempotency keys older than 24 hours and published realtime outbox rows older than 7 days. [Implemented]
Patient credit expiry Every day at 01:00 Marks prepaid patient credits (from credit packages) whose expiry date has passed as expired. [Implemented]
Billing invariant check Every day at 02:30 Recomputes billing totals and checks the money rules (invariants), including the commission ledger rule, and logs any break it finds. [Implemented]
Month-end payroll 05:00 on the 1st of every month Generates payroll records for the month that just ended, for every active location of every organization. Locations already generated are skipped, so a re-run is safe. [Implemented]
Inventory alerts Every day at 08:00 Counts low-stock and soon-expiring items per location and writes a warning to the server log. No user is notified, and nothing appears in any inbox or screen. [Partial]

The table lists eight timed jobs. The first four keep the live queue consistent. The other four do daily or monthly housekeeping for credits, billing checks, payroll and stock.

Times use the server clock. None of these jobs sets a timezone, so the daily and monthly schedules follow the timezone of the server running the worker. They do not follow each clinic's location timezone. For clinics in a different timezone from the server, "01:00" or "the 1st at 05:00" therefore happens at a different local clinic time. The queue day-end job avoids this problem. It decides what "a past clinic day" means for each location from that location's queue policy (including its day cut-off) and the Platform clock, not from the server date alone.

Code comment vs code. The payroll job's comment says it runs "at 00:05 on the 1st". The schedule expression 0 5 1 * * actually means 05:00 on the 1st. This handbook follows the code.

The credit expiry job uses the server clock. It works out "today" from the server's local date rather than the location's clock. Every other clinic-day rule in the Platform uses the location's timezone, so a credit can expire up to a few hours early or late for a clinic whose timezone differs from the server's.

Technical references: backend/src/queue/jobs/queue-jobs.service.ts · backend/src/billing/patient-credits.service.ts · checkExpiredCredits · backend/src/billing/invariants/billing-invariant.job.ts · backend/src/payroll/payroll.service.ts · month-end-payroll · backend/src/inventory/services/inventory-alerts.service.ts

E.3 Background loops (always running in the worker)

Loop How it wakes up What it does Status
Queue outbox relay Database LISTEN on the queue outbox channel, plus a poll every 1 second as a fallback Takes queue events written in the same transaction as each queue change and publishes them, through Redis, to the realtime socket rooms that reception screens, doctor screens and the TV display listen to. [Implemented]
Notification relay Database LISTEN on the notification outbox channel, plus a poll every 2 seconds Delivers queued notifications to users' in-app inboxes. [Implemented]
Realtime heartbeat and watchdog Timer Checks that the Redis publish and subscribe link between processes is alive. [Implemented]

These three loops are what make the Platform feel live. The two relays follow the "transactional outbox" pattern. A change and the message announcing it are saved together in one database transaction, and a separate loop delivers the message afterwards. So a message is never lost, and is never sent for a change that was rolled back. If the database LISTEN connection drops, both relays log a warning and keep working by polling alone.

Technical references: backend/src/queue/realtime/outbox-relay.service.ts · backend/src/notifications/delivery/notification-relay.service.ts · backend/src/queue/realtime/redis-realtime.publisher.ts · redis-realtime.subscriber.ts
